name: Catalogue of Texts and Authors
intro:
The *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* is the most important Mesopotamian metatext: its compiler grouped together texts or text categories under the names of authors “from whose mouth” they purportedly stem. Works are ascribed to Ea (the god of wisdom), to antediluvian sages and semi-mythical kings; but also to famous family ancestors and scholars from a less remote past. Additionally, some compositions are said to result from divine revelation or from dictation by certain animals.  
The composition of the *Catalogue* can be tentatively dated at some point between the 10ᵗʰ (the plausible composition date of the latest works included in it) and 7ᵗʰ centuries BCE (the date of its earliest manuscripts). Furthermore, as all post-diluvian scholars mentioned in it are said to either stem from Babylon, Nippur or Eridu, a Babylonian origin of the text is more than likely. At present, the *Catalogue* is preserved in two versions: one from 7ᵗʰ century Nineveh and a less well-preserved one from Hellenistic or Arsacid Babylon. Both use the same basic pattern and overlap in some of the titles listed, but seem to belong to two divergent recensions.  
The *Catalogue* shows that Babylonian scholars wondered who created their canonical texts. This fact in itself is remarkable, since for the most part of its history Mesopotamian scholarly tradition showed little interest in understanding works of literature as creations of inspired individuals. For this reason, it has been argued that the main raison d’être of the *Catalogue* was not the concern for the biographies of individual authors, but rather the wish to underline the professional and familial heritage of the scribes whose prerogative it was to engage with and maintain cuneiform scholarship.

name: Poem of Creation (*Enūma eliš*)
intro:
The text *Enūma eliš*, also known as the *Poem of Creation*, is a Babylonian poem that narrates the creation of the universe through the battle between the god Marduk and the primeval goddess Tiamtu. The poem is divided into seven tablets, with the end of the sixth and the whole of the seventh devoted to celebrating Marduk under fifty different names. The text adapts earlier mythological material to new needs, showing a complex melting pot of religious and literary motifs.  
The date of composition of the poem is debated, with proposals ranging from the Old Babylonian period to the first millennium BCE. The most accepted view sees the poem as a composition commissioned by Nebuchadnezzar I in the course of his recovery of the statue of Marduk from the Elamites in the last quarter of the 12ᵗʰ century BCE  
The text was perhaps the most popular religious composition in ancient Mesopotamia, as evidenced by numerous references to it in letters or royal inscriptions, the existence of an Assyrianising version, and the multiplicity of school texts with extracts from the poem. It was recited in its entirety during the Babylonian New Year festival and other Babylonian rituals. The influence of *Enūma eliš* on the Book of Genesis is subject of intense scholarly discussion. It seems clear that the text was well known outside of Mesopotamia, since the philosopher Damascius was still able to provide a precise summary of its contents in the 6ᵗʰ century CE.  
G. Smith, the discoverer of the text, first reported its existence in 1875. The classic edition by King (1901) has recently been updated in the monographs by Kämmerer and Metzler (2012) and W. G. Lambert (2013). The eBL edition incorporates numerous new fragments.

name: The Elevation of Babylon
intro:
The *Elevation of Babylon* (also known as the “Hymn to Babylon and the Babylonians”) is a Babylonian hymn celebrating the god Marduk, his temple Esagil, and the city of Babylon with its inhabitants. The composition offers distinctive descriptions of Marduk’s healing powers, Babylon’s splendor, the Euphrates’ role in the city’s fertility, and the generosity of the Babylonian people. The hymn is organized into several distinct sections: an opening hymn to Marduk (lines 1–25 and 26–79), a hymn to Esagil (86–99), a hymn to Babylon (100–124), and a hymn to the Babylonians (125–158). Approximately two-thirds of the original text has been recovered, suggesting the complete work may have comprised around 250 lines.  
The text survives in twenty manuscripts dating from the 7th to the 2nd/1st centuries BCE. These manuscripts originate primarily from Sippar and Babylon, forming two chronological groups: Neo-Babylonian (626–484 BCE) and Late Babylonian (2nd/1st centuries BCE). The earliest surviving manuscript, AššSchNA1, is a school tablet from Assur dating to approximately the 7th century BCE. The absence of Old and Middle Babylonian manuscripts, if significant, suggests a composition date after the first half of the second millennium BCE. The text aligns with the ideological framework characteristic of the “Rise of Marduk,” potentially placing its composition within the same period as other Marduk-centered works copied in first-millennium schools, such as *Enūma eliš* and *Ludlul*—that is, during the second half of the second millennium BCE. The substantial number of known school manuscripts demonstrates that this text was among the most frequently copied in educational settings. Literate Babylonians presumably knew the text by heart, as school texts were typically committed wholly or partially to memory: indeed, quotations from the work appear in other contemporary texts.  
While fundamentally hymnic in genre, the text incorporates a speech introduction formula (ll. 26–27) that suggests a hybrid form combining hymn and mythological narrative. The narrative is set *in illo tempore*, at the dawn of history, with references to creation appearing at the beginning of each section.

name: Poem of Gilgameš
intro:
The *Epic of Gilgamesh* is the best-known ancient Mesopotamian text. According to the Mesopotamian tradition, Gilgameš was a king of Uruk who lived in the first half of the third millennium BC. It is unknown whether he was a historical figure; in any case, he was deified by the mid-third millennium BC.  
The most elaborate poem narrating the exploits of Gilgameš is the first-millennium version, traditionally referred to as “canonical” and attributed to an elusive figure called Sîn-lēqi-unninni. In this recension most of the episodes known in older versions are woven into a narrative framework in which king Gilgameš, confronted with mortality for the first time on the death of his friend, Enkidu, embarks on a series of adventures to achieve immortality, but fails and returns empty-handed to Uruk. This “canonical” version is known from some 75 manuscripts, the oldest from eighth-century BCE Assyria, the latest from second-century BCE Babylonia.  
The earliest tales about Gilgameš are represented by five Sumerian stories, possibly written at the end of the third millennium BCE, known in manuscripts from ca. 18ᵗʰ c. BCE. The Akkadian versions of this period are very miscellaneous, but the episodes they narrate, often overlapping with each other, have counterparts in the first-millennium recension, and in general seem compatible with its plot. In the second half of the second millennium BCE the *Epic* was at the peak of its popularity, and was exported to scribal centers in Anatolia (Ḫattuša), Syria (Emar, Ugarit), and Palestine (Megiddo), and translated into Hittite and Hurrian. However, in Mesopotamia proper only a few fragments of the *Epic* are known, many of them school tablets. In the first millennium, *Gilgameš* was only rarely copied on school manuscripts or cited in learned commentaries: the universal message it contains may have been at odds with the more local interests of scribal education of the period.  
The monumental edition of A. R. George (2003), the first of the *Epic* in over 70 years, brought *Gilgameš* into the new millennium. The eBL edition incorporates all discoveries since then, both large and small.

name: *Enūma Anu Enlil* Ištar (EAE 50–68)
intro: The *Ištar* chapter of EAE comprises tablets 50 to 68/70. Although not all tablets in the series have been fully edited or reconstructed—many exist only as partial philological editions, composites, or fragments from cuneiform commentaries and excerpts—it is still possible to outline nearly all the content of the chapter's internal sections.**EAE 50-51**Tablet 50 correlates constellations with terrestrial phenomena, while 51 deals with visibility, invisibility, and colors of several constellations. Their structure resembles that of star calendars, making it the most unique section of the EAE *Ištar* chapter.**EAE 52-53**Tablet 52-53 deal with the position, visibility, brightness, and colors of constellations like the Field, the Old Man, the Pleiades, the Jaw of the Bull, the True Shepherd of Anu, and the Arrow.**EAE 54**Tablet 54 is unreconstructed so far and its incipit is unknown. Probably concerns fixed stars.**EAE 55**The incipit of EAE 55 (split in tablets 48 and 49 according to the Aššur catalogue) is reconstructed as: “If the Yoke is high and constantly visible when it comes out.” The tablet deals with the position, visibility, brightness, and color of the constellations named ŠUDUN, *nīru*, “Yoke”, ŠU.PA, *namru*, “Bright One”, ÉLLAG, *kalītu*, “Kidney”, ŠUDUN A.AB.BA, *nīri tâmti*, “Yoke of the sea”, Ea, NUN^ki^, “Eridu”, EN.TE.NA.BAR.ḪUM, *ḫabaṣīrānu*, “Mouse”, GÍR.TAB, *zuqaqīpu*, “Scorpion”, ZI.BA.AN.NA, *zibānītu*, “Scales”, ÙZ, *enzu*, “She-goat”, and MAR.GÍD.DA, *ereqqu*, “Wagon”. It also shows connections to MUL.APIN and *Šumma Sîn ina tāmartišu* (SIT) 6. Although not every omen is reconstructed in its entirety, a sequence of 110 omens has been successfully restored. The reconstruction relies on 11 standard EAE texts, 3 text commentaries, and several excerpts and parallels. The sources primarily originate from Nineveh, written in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian ductus, with one notable exception: the Late Babylonian commentary [VAT.7830](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/VAT.7830) ([https://ccp.yale.edu/P461321]), authored by Ina-qibīt-Anu and dated to the Hellenistic period. All available sources–including EAE texts, commentaries, and parallels—have been utilized to reconstruct each composite entry.The edition of *Enūma Anu Enlil* 55 presented here was prepared by Maria Teresa Renzi-Sepe (FU Berlin) as part of the project [The Planets in Mesopotamian Culture](https://gepris-extern.dfg.de/gepris/projekt/517639233), funded by the *Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft*, and by Luis Sáenz (University of Jena) during his doctoral research. Although this section of EAE was not the primary focus of their respective PhD theses, both scholars independently began working on it after identifying numerous manuscripts through the eBL Library.**EAE 56**Tablet 56 deals with the position, visibility, brightness, and colors of planets in general.**EAE 57/58**The incipit of EAE 57 (Tablet 51 according to the Aššur catalogue) is reconstructed as: “If the Raven reaches the path of the sun, the market rate will decrease.” The tablet number is found in the colophon of one source from Nineveh, [K.2330](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/K.2330) r 7'. However, its catchline (r 6'. DIŠ ^mul^*dili-bat ina* ^iti^BÁRA IGI BURU₁₄ KUR GÁL-*ši* KIMIN SI.S\[Á\]) refers to the incipit of another tablet, known as EAE 59 in the Neo-Babylonian tablet from Nineveh [K.2907](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/K.2907) (o 35). It is, therefore, likely that the content of EAE 57 was split into two tablets, EAE 57 and 58, according to the recension to which [K.2907](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/K.2907) belonged. Interestingly, [K.2330](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/K.2330) contains many lines with two omens joined together with the *Glossenkeil*.EAE 57 deals with the position, visibility, brightness, and color of the sun, planets and constellations named UGA^mušen^/UG₅.GA, *āribu*, “Raven”, TI₈^mušen^, *a/erû*, “Eagle”, KA₅.A, *šēlebu*, “Fox”, KU₆, *nūnu*, “Fish”, NU.MUŠ.DA, *nammaššu*, “Herd”, *eru*, “Eru”, *nēberu*, “Ford”, ^d^AMAR.UTU, *marduk*, “Marduk”, LU.LIM, *lulīmu*, “Stag”, UR.BAR.RA, *barbaru*, “Wolf”, GÁN.ÙR(.RA), *maškakātu*, “Harrow”, APIN, *epinnu*, “Plow”, KA.MUŠ.Ì.GU₇.E, *pašittu*, “Pašittu”, ^d^ANZU^mušen^, *anzû*, “Anzu”, MAR.GÍD.DA, *ereqqu*, “Wagon”, AB.SÍN, *absinnu*, “Furrow”, ^d^*é-a*, Ea, AL.LUL, *alluttu*, “Crab”, MUL₅.MUL₅, *zappu*, “Bristle”, KÁR.ŠUL, U.RI.RI, UR.MAḪ, *nēšu*, “Lion”, KAL.NE, GIŠGAL.AN.NA, i.e., Jupiter, ^d^UTU, *šamaš*, “Sun”, and *dilbat*, “Venus”. EAE 57 also shows connections to MUL.APIN and *Šumma Sîn ina tāmartišu* (SIT) 6 and *Zweisprachiges Omenkompendium*.Two rubrics identify the final sections as *aḫu* omens. The first rubric appears in NinNB1 ([Rm.308](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/Rm.308)) r 30', positioned between § 93 and § 94, and counts 12 omens. The second rubric in NinNA1 ([K.2330](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/K.2330)), located just before the colophon, counts 39 omens. These two counts overlap by three omens. These *aḫu* omens, while not part of the standard EAE series (*iškāru*), nevertheless belong to its authoritative tradition. For further discussion, see F. Rochberg, *In the Path of the Moon. Babylonian Celestial Divination and its Legacy* (2010), 79-83.Although not every omen has been reconstructed in its entirety, a sequence of 121 omens (123 when counting the double entries in § 92 and § 111) has been successfully restored. This reconstruction draws upon 10 standard EAE texts, various commentaries, excerpts and parallels. The source materials primarily originate from Nineveh, written in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian script, and from Babylon in Late Babylonian script.The edition of *Enūma Anu Enlil* 57 presented here was prepared by Maria Teresa Renzi-Sepe (FU Berlin) as part of the project [The Planets in Mesopotamian Culture](https://gepris-extern.dfg.de/gepris/projekt/517639233), funded by the *Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft*, and by Luis Sáenz (University of Jena) during his doctoral research. Although this section of EAE was not the primary focus of their respective PhD theses, both scholars independently began working on it after identifying numerous manuscripts through the eBL Library.**EAE 59-63**Tablet 59-63 deal with the position, visibility, brightness, and colors of Venus. EAE 63 is called the “Venus tablet of Ammiṣaduqa”. This tablet, named after the king Ammiṣaduqa of the first dynasty of Babylon (ca. 1646-1626 BCE), has been claimed to include observational data from the Old Babylonian period, and a scheme for a 8-years period when the planet was visible and invisible. However, the date is still questionable, and it remains unclear whether the period scheme for Venus is from the Old Babylonian period or later.**EAE 64-66**Tablet 64-66 deal with the position, visibility, brightness, and colors of Jupiter.**EAE 67/69-68/70**Tablet 67/69-68/70, unreconstructed so far, possibly pertain to meteors or glows and to celestial bodies approaching one another.

name: Nergal and Ereškigal
intro:
The story of *Nergal and Ereškigal* provides an aetiology for how Nergal, god of pestilence and violent death, came to rule the Netherworld alongside his wife Ereškigal. The narrative begins with Ereškigal, bound by the laws of her own realm, being condemned to a life of solitude. Even when the other gods hold a banquet, she can only attend by proxy of her vizier, Namtar. When the mutinous young Nergal disrespects Namtar at this occasion, he is compelled to descend to the Netherworld to atone for his offense. However, his fate is altered by a combination of luck, trickery, and help by Ea: instead of being executed, he becomes Ereškigal's husband and co-ruler of the Netherworld.  
The narrative’s framework was likely composed after the Old Babylonian period to reconcile divergent regional traditions about the underworld and its divine ruler. Like [*Adapa*](/corpus/L/1/7), the myth is attested in both an abridged version from 14ᵗʰ-century Amarna and a longer version preserved in 1ˢᵗ-millennium copies.  
While the Amarna version has been known to scholarship since the early 20ᵗʰ century, the two main manuscripts of the 1ˢᵗ-millennium version were discovered only fairly recently (Ḫuzirina: 1960; Uruk: 1976). A small fragment, likely from Babylon, was published only in 2025. It remains uncertain whether the mythological fragment [BM.32667](/library/BM.32667) also belongs to this composition.

name: Adapa
intro:
*Adapa and the South Wind* tells how Adapa, in Mesopotamian tradition the first antediluvian sage who brought civilization to mankind, ascended to heaven to be held accountable for breaking the wing of the South Wind with a curse. Thanks to the instructions given to him by Ea, the god of wisdom, Adapa avoids conviction, yet wastes the opportunity to gain immortality. Because of the power bestowed on Adapa to alter reality with his speech, the composition can be read as an aetiology for the art of the “conjurer” (*āšipu*), whose practice it was to remove evil from patients by means of his – divinely-backed – words.  
The myth of Adapa’s ascent is known in several versions from the early 2ⁿᵈ millennium onward. The earlier written versions of the story, in Sumerian, are a well-preserved version from Meturan and two fragments from Nippur. The first known Akkadian version, a boiled down reading primer version, stems from 14ᵗʰ-century Amarna. In the 1ˢᵗ millennium, the text is only attested in a number of small fragments, most of which were found in the royal libraries of Nineveh (i.e. 7ᵗʰ century BCE), but which might have been written earlier (see below).  
The title “Adapa to the midst of heav\[en\],” which appears in an accession record from the same libraries ([Rm.618](/fragmentarium/Rm.618#%202)), might refer to this composition. Furthermore, the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([§0](/corpus/L/0/0/Neo-Assyrian/-#d%2B22)) cites an incipit of an unknown work (“\[…\] … from before the Flood”) as the work of Adapa himself, perhaps another reference to this text.

name: Descent of Ištar
intro:
*Descent of Ištar* is a narrative poem that recounts how the goddess Ištar decides to visit the  Netherworld, the domain of her sister Ereškigal, and is trapped there until she is rescued with the help of Ea. The short Akkadian poem (138 lines) is based on an earlier Sumerian poem that presents the story in a much fuller form (412 lines). The text displays also some similarities with other texts describing the Netherworld, such as *Nergal and Ereškigal* (L.I.6) and the *Poem of Gilgameš* (L.I.4), with which it shares some lines.  
The succinct nature of the *Descent of Ištar* poses a serious challenge for a full comprehension of its content. Interpretations of the work are largely reliant on the Sumerian version. The narrative of Ištar’s journey through the seven gates of the underworld and her subsequent imprisonment by Ereškigal is very detailed, yet other elements of the poem are rather laconic and difficult to understand. The poem provides an etiology for the *assinnu*, a cultic servant of Ištar, who is created by Ea to secure Ištar’s release. Additionally, the poem appears to reference an annual festival in which Dumuzi, Ištar’s spouse and substitute in the Sumerian myth, emerges from the underworld and returns, taking with him illnesses and malevolent demons.  
The Standard Babylonian version of the *Descent of Ištar* is known from Assur and Assurbanipal’s royal library in Nineveh. An additional version of the work was discovered in the library of the chief singer (*nargallu*) (N 3) in Assur, inscribed on an early Neo-Assyrian tablet along with a text that has been either interpreted as a celebratory heroic poem of the Assyrian king or as a parodic representation of Assyrian royal inscriptions. The context in which this tablet was written remains uncertain, but it may have been a school exercise, or it may have been excerpted for a performance.

name: Etana
intro:
The *Epic of Etana* weaves together a fable of a snake and an eagle with the tale of Etana, the childless king of the city of Kiš, and his quest for the plant of birth. In the *Epic*, the eagle’s breach of an oath earns him the wrath of god Šamaš, who condemns it to a pit. Etana rescues the eagle so the eagle, in gratitude, carries him to the heavens in search of the plant.  
The myth of Etana was probably known in the third millennium BCE, but the earliest surviving manuscripts of the *Epic*, from Babylonia and Susa, come from the first half of the second millennium BCE. Four Assyrian tablets from Aššur, belonging to at least two different manuscripts, can be dated to the second half of the second millennium BCE. In the first millennium BCE, the *Epic* is only known in the libraries of Assurbanipal in Nineveh, where at least three sets of the text were kept. The various versions differ considerably in length and wording.  
According to the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([L 0](/corpus/L/0/0/NA/-#d%2B17)), the *Epic of Etana* was composed by Lu-Nanna, the sage. The *Epic* is not known on school tablets, and its text is apparently not quoted in other compositions. However, king Etana appears frequently in other texts: the *Sumerian King List*, for example, describes Etana as “the shepherd, who ascended to heaven,” and mentions Balīḫ as his son and his successor. An Old Babylonian wisdom composition ([YBC.2394](/fragmentarium/YBC.2394)) mentions Etana’s ascension to heaven and childlessness. Later traditions present Etana as the holder of an important office in the Netherworld ([*Gilgameš* SB VII 202](/corpus/L/1/4/SB/VII#202)), and some divination texts refer to his journey to heaven as late as the second century BCE ([MLC.1874 o 33](/fragmentarium/MLC.1874#o%2033)).  
The *Epic*, first recognized in 1894, has been frequently re-edited. Large portions of the work are only fragmentarily known, and many fragments have been tentatively attributed to the *Epic* without much evidence. The eBL edition has benefitted from a digital edition kindly made available by J. Novotny.

name: Anzû
intro:
*Anzû* is an Akkadian narrative poem that tells the story of the homonymous monstrous bird that serves as the guardian of Enlil, the head of the pantheon. Anzû steals the Tablets of Destiny and seizes power among the gods, throwing the divine realm into disarray until the bird’s usurpation is ended by the warrior god Ninurta, who slays him in battle. As a reward for his deed, Ninurta is elevated to a prominent position in the pantheon. *Anzû* draws on the rich Ancient Near Eastern tradition of mythical battles between gods and monstrous creatures, most notably the Sumerian poems *Lugale* and *Angim*. The *Anzû* poem itself served as a model for later Akkadian texts such as the *Poem of Creation* (L [I.2](/corpus/L/1/2)).  
*Anzû* is known in three versions: an Old Babylonian, a Standard Babylonian, and a local version known from Ḫuzirina (Sultantepe). The concise Old Babylonian version is attested only in two fragmentary copies found in Susa, Iran. The Standard Babylonian version, with at least 499 verses spread over three tablets, is known from Babylonian and Assyrian manuscripts. An unusually large Neo-Assyrian tablet from Tarbiṣu originally contained the entire poem.  
Compared to other Akkadian narrative poems and literary texts, the number of manuscripts of *Anzû* is rather limited, so one can assume that the text was not as popular as, for instance, the *Poem of Creation*. However, recently discovered excerpts on Neo-Babylonian school tablets show that, at least in Nippur, *Anzû* played a role in elementary scribal education.  
The first fragment of *Anzû* was published by G. Smith in 1876. Several editions of the text have appeared, by Hruška, Vogelzang and Annus, and a new edition by D. Shehata has been announced. The *eBL* edition includes several newly identified fragments and offers a slightly adapted reconstruction of Tables I and II. C. Wilcke has kindly made his unpublished collations available to the *eBL* project, which has made extensive use of them.

name: The Poor Man of Nippur
intro:
*The Poor Man of Nippur* tells the story of Gimil-Ninurta, a citizen of Nippur, and the revenge he takes on the mayor of the city, who had wronged him. It is one of the few Mesopotamian stories to have survived in folklore: different versions of it spread throughout the Middle East and beyond.  
The main manuscripts of the text are two large tablets from Huzirina. The composition was also known in Gimil-Ninurta's hometown, as evidenced by an excerpt on a school tablet from Neo-Babylonian Nippur. Three Nineveh fragments of the text are also known, which differ slightly from the Huzirina version (cf. ll. 11, 16, 24, 75, 104 and 153).  
The composition is not known to have been mentioned in catalogues, nor is it cited in other compositions. The only evidence for its use in scribal training is the Nippur school tablet mentioned above.  
The text was first discovered when two large, well-preserved manuscripts of it were unearthed at Huzirina. The Nippur school tablet was published in 1974, and two Nineveh fragments were added in 2021. B. R. Foster has adapted his translation for the eBL edition.

name: Cuthaean Legend of Narām-Sîn
intro:
The *Cuthaean Legend of Narām-Sîn* presents itself as an inscription of Narām-Sîn, a 23ʳᵈ-century king of Akkad. The text claims to have been engraved on a stele kept in a temple in the city of Cutha, hence its modern title. In the *Legend*, the ruler calls on future kings to learn from his mistakes in dealing with foreign threats: a king should not go to war unless the gods order him to. Only those who have faith in the gods and act on their command, so the text goes, will prevail.  
The earliest known manuscript of the *Legend* dates to the 17ᵗʰ century BCE. The narrative later found its way to the capital of the Hittite Empire, where it is preserved in Akkadian on two prisms as well as in the form of a Hittite-language version. In Mesopotamia itself, it only resurfaces in the 8ᵗʰ–7ᵗʰ centuries BCE in Assyria; in Babylonia it continued to be transmitted even down to the first two centuries BCE.  
The text is listed in an inventory of compositions copied for the royal libraries of Nineveh ([K.13684](/fragmentarium/K.13684)+). Exercise tablets from Babylonian schools (MSS KišNBSch1, SipLBSch1) show that the text was studied in the first stages of scribal education, as was the *Birth Legend of Sargon*. The beginning of the composition inspired literary imitators, most prominently the editor of the SB *Poem of Gilgameš* ([§I.4](/corpus/L/1/4)). Apart from this famous example, there is also a parody that originated in the Neo-Assyrian court, which alludes to the Legend’s incipit and several other lines of the composition ([K.1351](/fragmentarium/K.1351)).

name: Theodicy
intro:
The *Babylonian Theodicy* (ancient title: “O sagacious mentor, come, let me tell you”) is a poetic dialogue between two parties, one of which defends the existence of divine justice, while the other challenges it.  
The *Theodicy* is perhaps the most sophisticated composition in Mesopotamian literature. It consists of 27 stanzas, each with 11 lines beginning with the same syllable: when read vertically, they form an acrostic with the name of the author, the exorcist Saggil-kīn-ubbib. The meter of the poem is very rigid: almost every verse has four metric feet divided by a caesura, and parallelism is far more common than in any other Akkadian literary text. This extreme regularity was also evident to ancient scribes, since in some manuscripts verses are divided into four boxes, each with one metrical foot. The distinct lexicon of the *Theodicy* further contributes to the complexity of the poem: recherché lemmata are used to replace common nouns, and common words are used in uncommon meanings. It is, therefore, no surprise that the *Theodicy* is one of the very few Mesopotamian literary texts that received an ancient commentary.  
The poem is mentioned in the *List of Kings and Scholars* as having been written during the reign of Adad-apla-iddina (1068–1047 BCE). This reign, politically rather unimportant, was a golden age for Mesopotamian literature, since the famous scholar Esagil-kīn-apli was also active in it. The *Theodicy* was a text reserved for initiates, and therefore played only a marginal role in elementary education. The text was, however, parodied in Mesopotamian disputations, in which animals use the bombastic language of the poem to debate more trivial questions.  
The text, christened by Ebeling “A Babylonian Qohelet” (1922), was given its current title by Landsberger (1936) in the first modern edition of the poem. The classic edition by Lambert (1960) has recently been supplemented by Oshima (2014). The eBL edition includes many new readings, such as the newly recovered title, and incorporates several new fragments.

name: *Šumma Ālu* Nabû-zuqup-kēnu (Project Ālu Geneva)
intro:
The editions of *Šumma ālu* presented here were prepared in the context of the projects “Edition of the Omen Series Šumma Alu” (2017–2021; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970](http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970)), “Typology and potential of the excerpt tablets of Šumma alu” (2022–2023; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122](http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122)), and “Edition of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s Šumma Alu series” (2024–2028; [https://data.snf.ch/grants/grant/10000955](https://data.snf.ch/grants/grant/10000955)), directed by Prof. Catherine Mittermayer at the University of Geneva and funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The complete score editions can be downloaded (PDF) at the “Archive ouverte” of the University of Geneva ([https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/](https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/); search for “Shumma alu”).  
This is the first separate edition of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s series of *Šumma ālu*. It shows important differences from the later canonical series in regard to the Tablet sequence as well as the content and structure of the individual Tablets. The separation of both versions also proved crucial for our understanding of the canonical series and resolved several inconsistencies, especially for Tablets whose previous reconstruction was mainly based on a Nabû-zuqup-kēnu manuscript.  
For some of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s manuscripts a colophon is preserved. In other cases, the attribution to Nabû-zuqup-kēnu relies on a combination of several criteria, such as the use of ten-counts in the left margin or the extent and ways in which it differs from other manuscripts from Nineveh. Where the Tablet number in Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s series is unknown, it is provisionally labeled with the number of the corresponding canonical Tablet in quotation marks (e.g., T.“10”NZK).  
The editions of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s Tablets were prepared by Kaira Boddy, Fabienne Huber Vulliet and Catherine Mittermayer.

name: *šuʾila*s to Adad
intro: According to W.R. Mayer’s catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen* (1976: 378; compare Kunstmann 1932: 83-84), there are nine incantation-prayers directed to Adad. (Not included in this count is the prayer referred to by catchline only in LKA 53 (AššNA1), rev. 10: \[EN₂^?^\] ^d^IŠKUR *tukul-tu*₂ ^d^IŠKUR LA x.) Of these nine incantation-prayers, Mayer considers five to be *šuʾila*-prayers (likewise, Frechette 2012: 252): Adad 1a, 1b, 2, 3, and 4. Only these five prayers to Adad are included in the current project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) (CASPo). The prayer Adad 6 may very well turn out to be a *šuʾila*-prayer, too, though current evidence is lacking. For the time being, Adad 6 is not included as a *šuʾila*-prayer in the CASPo corpus. Although the number of *šuʾila*-prayers to Adad is relatively high, the prayers, with the exception of Adad 1a, are not very well attested, as the following specific introductions to the prayers show. Moreover, all the witnesses to *šuʾila*-prayers to Adad indicate that these prayers were connected to some larger corpus or ritual series, though it is often difficult to be more precise, again, as the following specific introductions indicate. A general statement about such ritual uses occurs in an astrological report, [SAA 8, no. 461, obv. 7-10](https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/saao/saa08/P237874) (see Hunger 1992), which reads as follows: \[*dullu*\] *ša adad zunna ana zanā*\[*ni*\] \[*š*\]*ū līpušū u šuʾilla*\[*kkū*\] *mala ibaššû itti* \[*dulli*\] \[*lī*\]*pu*\[*šū-ma*\], “they should perform \[th\]at rainmaking \[ritual\] of Adad, and \[they should also\] perform all the ‘hand-lifting’ pr\[ayers\] that exist with \[the ritual\].”**Adad 1a**Adad 1a is the best attested *šuʾila*-prayer to Adad with four first-millennium manuscripts found in Assyria and Babylonia. Among the former are manuscripts from Neo-Assyrian Aššur (AššNA1) and Nineveh (NinNA2). The latter include Babylonian manuscripts from the Persian (BabaPer1) and Late Babylonian (BabLB1) periods. Adad 1a is one of only a few *šuʾila*-prayers (so far) in the CASPo project that is attested in a second-millennium witness. See also [Ištar 2](http://shuilas.org/Q006076.html) and [Ištar 10](http://shuilas.org/Q006084.html). The witness comes from Ḫattusa, the only site to produce such early witnesses of *šuʾila*-prayers. The two Neo-Assyrian witnesses show a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to the prayer (AššNA1, rev. 9 and NinNA2, obv. 20ˊ). The two Babylonian witnesses break off before the end of the prayer, where the rubric would be expected. HatHit1 likewise breaks off before its conclusion.As the witnesses all show, Adad 1a was variously associated with other texts, especially other prayers. In the fragments comprising [HatHit1](http://shuilas.org/P443863.html), we find an unidentified Akkadian incantation-prayer and an unidentified Sumerian prayer attested along with the text of Adad 1a, which varies significantly in this early witness from its first millennium witnesses. Although Ašš1NA1 only contains the text of Adad 1a, the incipit of an unknown prayer to Adad appears as a catchline in [rev. 10](http://shuilas.org/P413965.html) at the tablet’s conclusion, suggesting both prayers were part of a larger collection and/or ritual series. In the other Neo-Assyrian witness, [NinNA2](http://shuilas.org/P398671.html), the *šuʾila*-prayer Kaksisa 1 (obv. 1ˊ-20ˊ) precedes the text of Adad 1a (obv. 21ˊ-22ˊ, rev. 1-19), though there is no other indication or evidence—the tablet is quite incomplete—for how these texts might have been used together, i.e., in a ritual, if at all. In [BabLB1](http://shuilas.org/P549618.html), also quite fragmentary, *šuʾila*-prayer Sin 3 (obv. 1ˊ-24ˊ) and a few lines of *šuʾila*-prayer Shamash 1 (obv. 25ˊ-26ˊ) appear on the obverse, separated by an indeterminate number of lines before the text of Adad 1a picks up on the reverse. The contents of the other Babylonian manuscript, BM.38537 = [BabaPer1](http://shuilas.org/P453575.html), may shed light on the connection between these three prayers in BabLB1. In BabaPer1, the first column of the obverse preserves a part of *šuʾila*-prayer Gula 1a (i 1-19). There are no other columns preserved on the obverse. A very partially preserved column on the reverse attests a handful of lines from Adad 1a (iˊ 1ˊ-9ˊ) while the last column attests the only witness to *šuʾila*-prayer Kakkabu 5 (iiˊ 1ˊ-12ˊ). There is a catchline to Ki-Utu-prayer br 6 (see Baragli 2022: 374-377, 511-546, who notes the prayer’s use in the series *Bīt Rimki* as well as *Bīt salāʾ mê*) in line 13ˊ, which is followed by the following series information: IM.DUB.3.KAM^v^ E₂ *sa-la me-e* EŠ₂.GAR₃ *a-ši-pu*₂*-tu* NU A\[L\].TIL, “The third tablet of *Bīt salāʾ mê*, an exorcism series. Not finished.” We know from witnesses of the (very fragmentarily reconstructed) *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (known to exist in Assyrian and Babylonian recensions) that Gula 1a and Kakkabu 5 are prescribed in its cycles of prayers (Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 48\], 164 \[x + 20ˊ (= C 20ˊ)\], 166 \[x + 32ˊ (= A₁ iii 21ˊ; D 8ˊˊ)\], 175; Frechette 2012: 168, 169, 170, s.v. 7, 255). Kakkabu 5 is, in fact, the last prescribed prayer in the night cycle (Ambos 2013: 166), which may explain its final position on BabaPer1. The prayers Sin 3 and Shamash 1, both attested on BabLB1, as mentioned above, are also prescribed prayers in *Bīt salāʾ mê* (Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 47; B₂ 49\], 164 \[x + 3ˊ (= C 3ˊ)\], 166 \[y + 8ˊ (= A₂ 6; B₂3ˊˊ; C 6ˊˊb; E2ˊb)\], 175; Frechette 2012: 168, 169, 170, s.v. 7, 255). (*Nota bene:* The order of prayers varies in the different recensions of the Ritual Tablet.) Adad 1a is not currently attested in the scant remains of the series’ Ritual Tablet (in any recension). But, the placement of Adad 1a as *recitanda* on tablets attesting other prayers that are prescribed in the Ritual Tablet (so BabLB1) and on another tablet containing *recitanda* of the ritual series that also bears a scribal rubric designating the tablet as belonging to the ritual series (so BabaPer1) proves Adad 1a was used in (at least) some Babylonian version of *Bīt salāʾ mê*. (Worth noting: A person mentioned in the colophon of BabaPer1, Bēl-\[x\], son of Bēl-kēšir, of the Basia family, is likely the same person named in the colophon on [BM.36718+](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/BM.36718), rev. ii e.1, which is another tablet attesting several prayers prescribed as *recitanda* in *Bīt salāʾ mê*, though there is no explicit mention of the series on this tablet. Alan Lenzi and Frank Simons will publish BM.36718+ in coming months.)**Adad 1b-Adad 4**Adad 1b, Adad 2, and Adad 3 are all attested on only one witness; in fact, one and the same witness, NinNA1 = [K.2741+](http://shuilas.org/P394642.html), which is a collection of prayers to Adad that bears an Ashurbanipal colophon (rev. 44-56). Adad 4 is likewise attested on this tablet; and its incipit also occurs in [Sm.1117](http://shuilas.org/P425755.html) as a catchline (see rev. 8ˊ-9ˊa). With the exception of Adad 3, which is only attested by its incipit cited as a catchline (see rev. 43), K.2741+ presents the other three prayers in a uniform format: the text of the prayer, a *šuʾila*-rubric, and ritual instructions, which include the prompting situation in two of the three instances. The order of the text is as follows: Adad 4 (obv. 1-31), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. 32), prompting situation (obv. 33-35) with ritual instructions (obv. 36-41); Adad 1b (obv. 42-58, rev. 1-21), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 22), prompting situation (rev. 23) with ritual instructions (rev. 24-25); Adad 2 (rev. 26-40), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 41), ritual instructions (rev. 42); incipit to Adad 3 as catchline (rev. 43); Ashurbanipal colophon type c (rev. 44-56). The prompting situation attached to Adad 4 and Adad 1b in this witness are both related to the destructive effects of the metereological phenomena attributed to Adad’s sphere of influence, namely, thunder and lightning-effected fire.Similarly, Sm.1117 looks to be part of a collection of Adad-related prayers to avert the effects of thunder that had made a wall collapse. The series information, which occurs at the very end of the tablet, reads as follows: *ša adad rigimšu iddī-ma igāru inēʾ*, “from *the series* ‘Adad roared and the wall collapsed’” (rev. 9ˊb-10ˊ). The tablet begins with the incantation-prayer Adad 6 (see just below) on the obverse, which breaks off at what is likely the middle of the tablet’s original length. The reverse, missing about its first half, begins with a very fragmentary scribal rubric (rev. 1ˊ; see Adad 6 below) and is followed by five very fragmentary lines of ritual instructions, which conclude in a manner that suggests the material is part of a *namburbi*-ritual: *rigim adad šuātu* \[*ša*\] *ina zumrīšu ippaṭṭar*, “(The evil of) that thunder clap of Adad \[that\] *is* in his body will be released” (rev. 5ˊb-6ˊ). A scribal rubric, separated by rule lines before and after, follows in rev. 7ˊ, affirming both the effectiveness (*latkūtu*) of the material on the tablet and its Nippurean origin. After all this, the incipit to Adad 4 appears as the catchline (rev. 8ˊ-9ˊa) for the next tablet in the series identified above (rev. 9ˊa-10ˊ). Supporting the possibility that Adad 4 had a role in *namburbi*-rituals is Schwemer’s contention (2001: 667, n. 5526) that its incipit is cited in the *namburbi*-catalogue [SpTU 1, 6](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/IM.74433) (see Maul 1994: 192-195 for an edition). In Schwemer’s view (which I think is quite reasonable), the incipit cited in obv. 21ˊ should read ^d^IŠKUR^!^(UD) EN *šur-bu-u ša*₂ AN*-e u* KI*-ti*₃ *ša*₂-<*kin*₂> DUNGU-MEŠ, which is, of course, the incipit to Adad 4.**Adad 6**Given what we know about the contents of Sm.1117, Adad 6, which appears on its obverse, might have had a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to it. The fact that the prayer begins with the so-called Sumerian hymnic introduction, which overwhelming appears in *šuʾila*-prayers, though not exclusively so (see Frechette 2012: 135 with n. 46), lends support to its inclusion in the corpus. However, since there is still no evidence for an attached *šuʾila*-rubric, I exclude the text from the corpus for the time being (so also Frechette and Mayer). About the rubric in Sm.1117, rev. 1ˊ: Although I follow Schwemer in reconstructing a *šuʾila*-rubric (2001: 674) in the very broken [line](http://shuilas.org/P425755.html), that rubric was most likely attached to a different prayer to Adad (currently unknown) than the one that begins in obv. 1. It would be highly unlikely that Adad 6 originally ran to some 90 lines, which is what the tablet geometry of Sm.1117 would require of Adad 6 were it to begin in obv. 1 and run through the middle of the tablet’s reverse (see likewise Schwemer 2001: 674).

name: Righteous Sufferer (*Ludlul bēl nēmeqi*)
intro:
*Ludlul bēl nēmeqi*, also known as the *Poem of the Righteous Sufferer* and often compared to the Hebrew Bible’s “Book of Job,” is a Babylonian poem that praises the god Marduk and reflects on the human condition. Its protagonist, Šubši-mešrê-Šakkan, is a historical character known to have lived during the reign of Nazi-Maruttaš (1307–1282 BCE).  
The poem comprises five chapters, each with 120 verses. Chapter I opens with a hymnic praise of the god Marduk, which quickly turns into a monologue in which the protagonist recounts the adversities in his social life that have led him to be shunned and dejected. In Chapter II he contemplates on the source and reason for the wrongs he must endure, and the chapter ends with the description of his physical and psychological maladies. Chapter III is the turning point in the poem: Šubši-mešrê-Šakkan experiences a series of prophetic dreams that announce his recovery: indeed, the second part of this chapter and the beginning of Chapter IV describe his healing process. The still fragmentary Chapter IV possibly focuses on his penitence while the concluding Chapter V is a praise of Marduk’s healing powers, celebrated by Šubši-mešrê-Šakkan in the course of a visit to Marduk’s temple Esaĝil in Babylon.  
*Ludlul* reflects the theology of the city of Babylon, but it is known in both Babylonia and Assyria. In Babylonia, most of the manuscripts stem from Babylon and Sippar, but the poem is also quoted in tablets from Kiš and Uruk. The Assyrian manuscripts stem from Nineveh, Kalḫu, Assur and Ḫuzirīna. In Babylon, Sippar, and Assur the text was commonly copied on elementary school tablets. At Nineveh the poem and its commentary are mentioned in inventories from Assurbanipal’s libraries.  
The first editions of *Ludlul* appeared already in the 1880s, but the first modern edition is that by W. G. Lambert (1960). The structure of the poem with five chapters was established by T. Oshima (2014).

name: *Šumma Ālu* 1–21 (House, Project Ālu Geneva)
intro:
The editions of *Šumma ālu* presented here were prepared in the context of the projects “Edition of the Omen Series Šumma Alu” (2017–2021; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970](http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970)) and “Typology and potential of the excerpt tablets of Šumma alu” (2022–2023; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122](http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122)), both directed by Prof. Catherine Mittermayer at the University of Geneva and funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The complete score editions can be downloaded (PDF) at the “Archive ouverte” of the University of Geneva ([https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/](https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/); search for “Shumma alu”). The projects aim to reconstruct the canonical series of *Šumma ālu* according to the sources from Nineveh. The excerpt tablets in particular have proven crucial in determining the canonical Tablet sequence, which not always corresponds to that given by, for example, the Assur catalog. The Tablet numbering established in this way differs to that used by Freedman. In the context of the House omens, the order of the Tablets formerly numbered 7–11 is modified.  
As for the content of the individual Tablets, the new editions of T.1–T.21 differ greatly from the earlier editions by Freedman 1998. Especially the separation between the canonical series and that of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu brought about significant changes. Furthermore, through newly identified sources and new joins, the reconstructions of the Tablets could be improved upon.  
As far as possible, the editions follow Neo-Assyrian manuscripts and excerpt tablets from Nineveh. Other manuscripts, some from later periods, are included in the score insofar as they (appear to) preserve the same material. For some Tablets, a distinct Babylonian version can be detected, which is then edited separately.  
The editions of Tablets 1–21 were prepared by Fabienne Huber Vulliet, Wiebke Meinhold and Catherine Mittermayer.

name: *šuʾila* to Anu
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer lists only one incantation-prayer directed to Anu, which he also identifies as an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer (Mayer 1976: 379; see likewise, Kunstmann 1932:84 and Frechette 2012: 252). As of October 2026, the situation remains the same. Thus, Anu 1 is the only Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer included in the [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online (CASPo)](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) project.**Anu 1**There are five textual witnesses at hand to reconstruct Anu 1, three from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh (NinNA1, NinNA2, and NinNA3), one from Neo-Assyrian Ashur (AššNA1), and one from Achaemenid Babylonia (BabaPer1). NinNA1, NinNA3, and BabaPer1 are large tablets of *recitanda* for *Bīt salāʾ mê*, the only known ritual in which Anu 1 was used (see below). On NinNA1, Anu 1 occupies sixteen lines of the tablet (obv. 1-16), followed by a one line rubric (obv. 17). None of these lines is preserved beyond the first two to five signs. Since there is a total of twenty lines in the present edition of Anu 1, NinNA1 likely wrote two lines of the prayer on one line of the tablet a few times or did not include all the lines reconstructed in the present edition (see, e.g., the notes on lines 5a and 6a in the present edition). With NinNA2, only its obverse is preserved; and none of its seventeen lines of text is complete. NinNA2 breaks off after line 13 of the prayer, as numbered in the present edition. NinNA3 attests only the incipit of Anu 1, which functions as the tablet’s catchline (rev. 33). AššNA1 is the fullest textual witness, bearing fifteen lines of the prayer on its obverse and ten more on its reverse, concluding with a *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 11. The rubric probably lies at about the halfway point on the reverse, the rest of which is blank. Anu 1 is the only text inscribed on the tablet. The material on the reverse of this textual witness is easily aligned with the other witnesses (see lines 14-20 of the present edition). Unfortunately, that is not at all the case with the material on the obverse, an issue I take up below. BabaPer1, identified by Zsombor Földi (eBL) in recent years, is the only additional textual material that has come to light since Mayer’s monograph, published in 1976. BabaPer1’s colophon (e.2-4) names a certain Bel-\[uballiṭ, son\] of Bel-keshir, of the Basia family as the tablet’s owner. This individual is also known from [BM.38537](http://shuilas.org/P453575.html), which (also) preserves *recitanda* of some version of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (explicitly identified in the colophon there), as discussed in the introduction to [Adad 1a](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/1). The colophon of BabaPer1 then mentions the city Babylon (as either the home of the tablet’s owner or the source of the original from which the copy was made) and dates the tablet to the third day of some month (broken) in the thirty-second year of Darius (I), king of Persia. Thus, BabaPer1 dates to 490 BCE. Due to its fragmentary condition, BabaPer1 adds little to our textual basis for Anu 1. And in at least one case, it has contributed to the complexity of the problem of reconstructing the prayer since BabaPer1 shows one (very broken) line of the prayer whose only extant word (at the head of the line) is unparalleled in the other witnesses (see line 11 of the present edition).Four of the five manuscripts provide evidence of a *šuʾila*-rubric for Anu 1. Two of the manuscripts clearly attest the rubric. AššNA1, rev. 11 reads \[ka\]-⸢inim-ma⸣ šu-⸢il₂⸣-la ^d^a-⸢num⸣-\[kam^v^\], and BabaPer1, rev. i 11ˊ reads ⸢ka-inim⸣-\[ma šu-i\]l₂-la₂ ^d^\[a-num-kam^v^\]. The other two manuscripts, NinNA1 and NinNA3, provide indirect but compelling evidence for the attachment of the *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer. While [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P394195.html), obv. 17 reads only ka-inim-⸢ma⸣ \[...\], it is very likely that the full *šuʾila*-rubric should be restored since all the other rubrics on the tablet that are attested beyond the first few signs, namely, the rubrics in obv. 70 (on Sîn 3), rev. 18 (on Gula 1a), and rev. 55 (on Šamaš 1), are *šuʾila*-rubrics. (The rubric in obv. 35, on Nusku 3, shows the same three signs as the rubric in obv. 17. But other textual witnesses for this prayer attest it with a *šuʾila*-rubric.) Thus, Anu 1 as attested in NinNA1 likely also bore a *šuʾila*-rubric. NinNA3 provides the same kind of inferential evidence. The three prayers that are presented in full on [that textual witness](http://shuilas.org/P397497.html), Madanu 1 (obv. 1-26), Ištar 1 (obv. 28-46, rev. 1-19), and Zappu 1 (rev. 22-31), each bear a *šuʾila*-rubric (see obv. 27, rev. 20, and rev. 32), strongly suggesting that Anu 1, whose incipit is cited as the tablet’s catchline (rev. 33), should also be classified as such.In terms of textual and ritual association, three witnesses to Anu 1 are large *recitanda* tablets, attesting several prayers that were prescribed during the course of performing (some version of) the royal ritual *Bīt salāʾ mê*. The evidence for this general commonality, however, is not as simple as the statement might suggest since the series of prayers on two of the three witnesses do not follow the prescribed order of recitations in any version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (for which see Ambos 2013: 157-175).NinNA1 is the odd one out in that its presentation of *šuʾila*-prayers, including Anu 1, Nusku 3, Sîn 3, Gula 1a, Šamaš 1, and Papsukkal 1, follows the same order of *šuʾila*-prayers prescribed in an Assyrian version of the night cycle of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see Ambos 2013: 203 and 162, lines B₂ 44-B₂ 50). This strongly suggests NinNA1 is a *recitanda* tablet for that royal ritual. Indeed, Ambos has labeled NinNA1 the ninth *pirsu* of the series (2013: 203), based on the fact that the catchline for Anu 1 appears in NinNA3, rev. 33 just before the colophon, which labels that tablet the eighth *pirsu* of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see rev. 34a).That tablet (NinNA3) also presents a series of *šuʾila*-prayers, including Madanu 1, Ištar 1, and Zappu 1, before giving the incipit of Anu 1 as a catchline. But these prayers are not prescribed in the Ritual Tablet before the ones listed in NinNA1; in fact, the prayers presented serially on NinNA3 are not *at all* prescribed in this Assyrian version of the Ritual Tablet (as it is currently and fragmentarily known; see Ambos 2013: 162). In addition, although all the prayers on NinNA3 are prescribed variously by the other version of the Ritual Tablet to *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see x + 19ˊ, Madanu 1 \[= A₁ iii 7ˊ; C 19ˊ\]; x + 28ˊ, Ištar 1 \[= A₁ iii 17ˊ; D 6ˊˊa\]; x + 24ˊ, Zappu 1 \[= A₁ iii 13ˊ; D 4ˊˊa\]; and x + 6ˊ, Anu 1 \[= C 6ˊ\]), the prayers are not prescribed in this specific order (see Ambos 2013: 164-165).Prescribed order is also an issue with BabaPer1. The content of this large tablet of *recitanda* strongly suggests a connection to *Bīt salāʾ mê*, though the order of the material does not precisely fit the order of any (currently) known version of the Ritual Tablet. BabaPer1 begins with two incantations known to be used in *Bīt salāʾ mê*: EN₂ *šubtu ša ilī qurādī*, “O dwelling of the gods, the heroes” (obv. i 1-13) and EN₂ *šubtu ša ilī rabûti manzāzu ellu*, “O dwelling of the gods, the pure abode” (obv. i 14ff. \[break\]). The incipits to both incantations are cited in one version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet, but in the opposite order that BabaPer1 presents them (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 31\]). BabaPer1, obv. ii presents material that duplicates the prayer published in Livingstone’s article, “Ashurbanipal: Literate or Not?” (2007). (Alan Lenzi and Frank Simons will publish this material along with a newly identified duplicate and a discussion of the relationship of the prayer to various ritual actions prescribed for *Bīt salāʾ mê* in the near future.) After a long break between obverse and reverse, BabaPer1 attests parts of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers Anu 1 (rev. i 1ˊ-11ˊ) and Papsukkal 1 (rev. i 13ˊff.). After the break between rev. i and ii, there are the very abraded remnants of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Šulpaʾea 1. After a few lines of ritual instructions, there is the catchline to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Enlil 1a and a colophon (bottom edge 1-4), which names a scribe known to have copied *Bīt salāʾ mê* material on another large tablet of *recitanda*, as mentioned above. All the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers attested on the reverse of BabaPer1 are cited by incipit in the two different versions of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 44, Anu 1; several intervening prayers, then B₂ 50, Papsukkal 1; B₂ 38, Šulpaʾea 1, followed next by B₂ 42, Enlil 1a\]; 164 \[x + 6ˊ (= C 6ˊ), Anu 1; x + 7ˊ (= C 7ˊ), Enlil 1a; several intervening prayers, then x + 11ˊ (= C 11ˊ), Papsukkal 1; eight intervening prayers, then x + 22ˊ (= A₁ iii 7ˊ; C 22ˊ; D 2ˊˊ), Šulpaʾea 1\]). But the order of prayers attested on BabaPer1, even taking into account the breaks on the tablet, does not conform to any order prescribed in any of the versions of the Ritual Tablet.Reconstructing the precise text of Anu 1 from our current evidence is very difficult (likewise Ambos 2013: 205) since 1) all the manuscripts bearing witness to the prayer are fragmentary, 2) they do not always agree on where the prayer’s lines break, and 3) they vary in what constitutes the actual text of the prayer. Editing the available material into a unified score, as I have done in the present edition, requires decisions and assumptions (e.g., about the number of signs that could fit in a break, the number of missing lines on a side, where to begin alignment of broken fragments, etc.) that, while reasonable in my view, are also sometimes conjectural. Consider, for example, the puzzle of how to align the material inscribed on the obverse of AššNA1. Obv. 1ˊ of this manuscript reads: \[x x x (x)\] ⸢AN⸣*-e* \[x x x x x\]. The only word preserved in this line, *šamê*, occurs in *all four initial lines of the prayer*, according to the Ninevite witnesses, but at slightly different distances from the head of the line. (AššNA1, obv. 2ˊ presents a similar problem. Its only attested sign is EN, Akkadian *bēlu*, and that word occurs in several of the opening lines of the prayer, too, according to the Ninevite textual witnesses.) Based on the number of lines on the reverse of this manuscript (eleven), which is only about half inscribed, we expect about twenty lines of text on the obverse, which means we are missing maybe five lines at the beginning of the obverse. (The lower edge is preserved.) Since this manuscript often writes single lines of the prayer on two lines of the tablet, obv. 1ˊ is likely to be placed somewhere around line 3 or 4 of the prayer, as numbered in the present edition. Placing AššNA1, obv. 1ˊ in line 3 is problematic, however, since the break at the head of the line in AššNA1 (three or four signs) is too big to be congruent with the Ninevite textual witnesses in line 3, which show only one sign, DINGIR, before AN-*e*. Ambos prefers to begin AššNA1’s alignment with the other witnesses at line 1 of the prayer. But there is not enough room to fit the number of signs (at least seven) in the the break at the head of AššNA1, obv. 1ˊ, making this suggestion unlikely in my opinion. He considers beginning the alignment in line 3, as the present edition does, as an alternative (2013: 211). In fact, the size of the breaks at the heads of AššNA1, obv. 1ˊ-2ˊ might suggest that the manuscript’s alignment would better begin one line lower, putting obv. 1ˊ with line 4 and obv. 2ˊ with line 5 of the prayer. But that alignment causes other problems in lines 5 and 6 (or, rather, 5, 5a, 6, and 6a) of the prayer. Thus, in order to take into account the breaks at the heads of the lines in AššNA1, obv. 1ˊ-2ˊ as well as the issues related to the same manuscript’s alignment farther along in the prayer, I suggest AššNA1, obv. 1ˊ-2ˊ be aligned with lines 3 and 4 of the prayer but that its text in these lines differed somehow from the other two witnesses (as it does elsewhere). As one can see, there is a great deal of uncertainty in nearly every decision that leads to the solution adopted here. And this is only one of several difficult textual issues that our witnesses bring up.The present edition cannot offer a definitive reconstruction of Anu 1. We simply don’t have the evidence. Rather, it can only set out a *possible*, hypothetical reconstruction of the prayer. Joins to the present fragmentary textual witnesses along with identifications of new duplicates will be required if we wish to understand how all the pieces relate to one another or, perhaps, how they need to be treated as *not* attesting one and the same prayer.

name: Counsels of Wisdom
intro:
The *Counsels of Wisdom* is a collection of instructions on proper behavior, many of which are particularly relevant to scribes and administrators. The text contains some 150–160 verses, which can be divided into some 12–15 thematical units that discuss topics such as bad companies and marriage with slave girls and prostitutes, as well as certain aspects of a future career as vizier or official. The individual manuscripts do not separate these units by means of rulings.  
The composition is preserved on multiple manuscripts from Assyria (Nineveh, Aššur) and Babylonia (Sippar, Babylon, Borsippa, Kiš, Nippur). Although the text was composed perhaps in the second half of the second millennium BCE, all known manuscripts were written during the first millennium BCE, the latest datable one (BorPer1) was copied in the 7ᵗʰ year of Artaxerxes I or II (458/457 or 398/397 BCE).  
The text was a particularly popular school assignment: more than 40% of all manuscripts are excerpts on school tablets. *Counsels of Wisdom* is, in fact, the only Akkadian literary text that was popular both in northern and southern Babylonian schools. These school tablets are also the sole witnesses to a substantial part of the textual variants, which could therefore be regarded as mistakes. In addition, the popularity of the text was such that it is quoted or praphrased in two ancient letters.  
The first manuscripts of *Counsels of Wisdom* were published at the end of the nineteenth century; the last reconstruction appeared in 1960. The eBL edition includes a dozen manuscripts identified in the last fifty years, as well as another dozen found in the framework of the eBL project.

name: *šuʾila*s to Bēlet-ilī
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer lists three prayers directed to the goddess Belet-ili, two of which he also identifies as an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer (Mayer 1976: 379; see likewise, Frechette 2012: 252-253; compare Kunstmann 1932: 84). Mayer also lists one incantation-prayer directed to both Belet-ili and Ishtar (see Mayer 1976: 380), but its only textual witness lacks any positive indicator for its inclusion in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus. Thus, for the purposes of the present project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online (CASPo)](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html), only Bēlet-ilī 1 and Bēlet-ilī 2 are counted among the Akkadian *šuʾilas*. (It should be mentioned that one textual witness to Zarpānitu 1, *viz.* LKA 48a, names the divine addressee as Belet-ili in its rubric in [rev. 12](http://shuilas.org/P480767.html). This matter is taken up in the introduction to Zarpānitu 1 (not yet completed, as of October 2026).)**Bēlet-ilī 1**The Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Bēlet-ilī 1 is introduced with the [textual witnesses to Gula 1a](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/11) because the two prayers are nearly identical, except for the name of the divine addressee and a few other relatively minor differences.**Bēlet-ilī 2**The Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Bēlet-ilī 2 is only known from one Neo-Assyrian witness from the exorcist’s house in Ashur (Pedersén 1986: 66). The tablet is now kept in the Arkeoloji Müzeleri in Istanbul. The present edition is only based on the excavation photo PhAss 4201, made available to me thanks to the staff at the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin, and Ebeling’s old transliteration, which also seems only to be based on the photograph (1953: 136-137). (The same photograph is printed in Ebeling’s *Literarische Keilschrifttexte aus Assur* \[1953, no. 59 on Taf. VI\].) As best as I can determine, only the obverse of the tablet has been published and thus, perhaps, it is the only side of the tablet that has come down to us. The tablet preserves twenty-two lines, comprising the prayer’s opening hymn (obv. 1-13), the supplicant’s 'turning' (obv. 14-18; see Mayer 1976: 122-145 for this feature of incantation-prayers, which he labels 'Die Hinwendung'), and a few lines of petition (obv. 19ff.). This incomplete textual witness for Bēlet-ilī 2 does not preserve a *šuʾila*-rubric or a rubric of any kind since its conclusion is not preserved. A hand-raising gesture is mentioned in the body of the prayer at obv. 16, but this gesture alone is not determinative for the prayer’s inclusion in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus. The prayer is included, rather, because of the extensive opening praise and the petition for the healing of the supplicant’s body (obv. 20). These are not definitive features; but, they are suggestive (see Mayer 1976: 377 and Frechette 2012: 133-140) for the prayer’s (tentative) inclusion in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus. No textual associations or ritual uses can be determined at this time for want of evidence.

name: Dialogue of Pessimism
intro:
The *Dialogue of Pessimism* is a text in ten strophes that features a discussion between a master and his slave. In each strophe, the master informs the slave of his intention to engage in a particular activity, which is then praised by the slave. The master then declares that he will not proceed in the announced activity, and the slave proceeds to praise his decision in no less laudatory terms. Eventually, the master asks what is worth doing and the slave declares death as the only desirable outcome.  
The text is known from three manuscripts from Assur, two fragments from Nineveh, and a single Babylonian piece. The Babylonian version differs significantly from the one found in the Assyrian manuscripts. The exact date of composition is unknown, although the distribution of manuscripts suggests it may have been written during the second half of the second millennium.  
Nothing is known about the *Sitz im Leben* of the text, which is not mentioned in any catalogues or lists, nor was it used in elementary education. Scholarly opinion is largely in agreement that the dialogue should be regarded as a semi-serious composition, or as a satirical portrayal of the relationship between master and slave.  
The text was first edited by E. Ebeling in 1917, and has since been re-edited and translated multiple times. The interpretation of the text has received significant attention, particularly with regards to its serious or satirical tone, which remains a widely debated topic. No new manuscript of the text has been published since Lambert’s edition (1960); however, a large new tablet from Assur, containing additional passages, will soon be published by Anmar A. Fadhil.

name: *Šumma Ālu* 50-63 (Environment, Project Ālu Geneva)
intro:
The editions of *Šumma ālu* presented here were prepared in the context of the projects “Edition of the Omen Series Šumma Alu” (2017–2021; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970](http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970)) and “Typology and potential of the excerpt tablets of Šumma alu” (2022–2023; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122](http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122)), both directed by Prof. Catherine Mittermayer at the University of Geneva and funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The complete score editions can be downloaded (PDF) at the “Archive ouverte” of the University of Geneva ([https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/](https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/); search for “Shumma alu”). The projects aim to reconstruct the canonical series of *Šumma ālu* according to the sources from Nineveh. The excerpt tablets in particular have proven crucial in determining the canonical Tablet sequence, which not always corresponds to that given by, for example, the Assur catalog. The Tablet numbering established in this way differs to that used by Freedman. In the context of the Environment omens, this will affect especially the sequence from T.56 onward.  
As for the content of the individual Tablets, the new editions of T.50–T.63 differ greatly from the earlier editions by Freedman 2017. Especially the separation between the canonical series and that of Nabû-zuqup-kēnu brought about significant changes. Furthermore, through newly identified sources and new joins, the reconstructions of the Tablets could be improved upon.  
Complete score editions were previously not available for Tablets 50–63. As far as possible, the editions follow Neo-Assyrian manuscripts and excerpt tablets from Nineveh. Other manuscripts, some from later periods, are included in the score insofar as they (appear to) preserve the same material. For some Tablets, a distinct Babylonian version can be detected, which is then edited separately.  
The editions of Tablets 50–63 were prepared by Kaira Boddy, Catherine Mittermayer and Eric Schmidtchen.

name: *šuʾila* to Damkina
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identifies only one incantation-prayer to the goddess Damkina (Mayer 1976: 380; likewise, Kunstmann 1932: 84-85), Damkina 1, which he also labels an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer (see likewise Frechette 2012: 254). As of August 2026, the textual situation remains unchanged. Damkina 1 is the only Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer in [CASPo’s](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) corpus.**Damkina 1**There are three textual witnesses for Damkina 1, all from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh. Although the fragmentary tablets comprising NinNA2 and NinNA3 have grown since Mayer’s edition of the prayer in 1976, the new joins have not added substantially to our knowledge of the text of the prayer. NinNA1 and NinNA3 have inserted an *attalû*-formula (see lines 9b-d of the present edition), suggesting the prayer’s use in an apotropaic ritual. NinNA3, in addition, has customized its self-presentation, naming Ashurbanipal as its supplicant (see line 9a). Only NinNA2 preserves the end of the prayer, where it clearly attests a *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. 9ˊ). [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P397492.html) does not attest the end of Damkina 1 and thus offers no evidence for a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to the prayer. However, it does attest the conclusions to two other incantation-prayers on the tablet, and these both bear a *šuʾila*-rubric, Ea 1b (see obv. 8ˊ) and Ninurta 1 (see rev. 9ˊ). It is therefore likely that Damkina 1 as attested on NinNA1 would have likewise had a *šuʾila*-rubric. None of the textual witnesses preserves ritual instructions attached to the prayer. NinNa3 is extremely fragmentary and offers no evidence beyond the opening dozen lines of the text. NinNA1 breaks off just before the end of the prayer. [NinNA2](http://shuilas.org/P397501.html), the one textual witness that preserves the end of the prayer and attests a *šuʾila*-rubric in obv. 9ˊ, shows no ritual instructions in obv. 10ˊ; rather, the text of Ninurta 1 begins immediately after the rubric. In fact, there are no ritual instructions attached to any of the prayers on the tablet. This lack of ritual instructions may be explained by way of the other Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers attested on [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P397492.html) and the order in which these prayers occur: Ea 1b (obv. 1ˊ-7ˊ), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. 8ˊ), Damkina 1 (obv. 9ˊ-29ˊ \[break\]), Ninurta 1 (rev. 1ˊ-8ˊ), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 9ˊ), Gula 1b (rev. 10ˊ-36ˊ \[break\]). The last three of these prayers occur in the same order as is prescribed in the cycle of *šuʾila*-prayers in a *Bīt rimki* Ritual Tablet from Nineveh (Schwemer 2019: 56, lines 216, 218, 220 \[= A o iii 60, 62, 64\]; 76; see also Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25). In addition, the prayer that is prescribed prior to Damkina 1 on the Ritual Tablet is directed to Ea, as is the case on the present tablet, though the cited incipit on the Ritual Tablet belongs to Ea 1a (see line 214), not Ea 1b, whose incipit is unknown. For more on this issue, see the [introduction](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/8) to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Ea 1b. (Note: Damkina 1 is also followed by Ninurta 1 on NinNA2, and thus the prayers originally on that tablet may also have followed the *Bīt Rimki* order.) The Ritual Tablet prescribes an offering to each deity and then the three-fold recitation of each of the prescribed prayers (see Schwemer 2019: 56, 76, lines 213-220 = A obv. iii 57-64).

name: Advice to a Prince
intro:
The composition *Advice to a Prince*, also known as *Babylonischer Fürstenspiegel*, calls on future kings and magnates to heed justice. More particularly, it exhorts them to respect the special status of the three ancient Babylonian cities Sippar, Nippur and Babylon, whose citizens are presented as exempted from forced labor and taxes by divine decision. In a casuistic structure reminiscent of both law and omen treatises, the text lists the divine punishments reserved for the powerful who do not abide by its clauses.  
The way the *Advice* is written is remarkable in three different respects: first, both manuscripts make use of archaising syllabic sign values as well as certain linguistic features of older stages of Akkadian. Secondly, they use a plethora of logographic writings, a practice usually restricted to technical literature. Thirdly, the text omits conjunctions and relative pronouns at the beginning of lines and at times employs infinitives where finite forms would be expected. These features are probably affectations intended to increase the apparent age of the text, and their presence makes it difficult to date its composition.  
*Advice to a Prince* is attested in two manuscripts from first-millennium Nippur and Nineveh and listed in an inventory of the royal libraries at Nineveh ([K.10182](/fragmentarium/K.10182)). Furthermore, the text is quoted in a letter sent from Nippur to the Assyrian king, which asks for his support to rebuild the city.

name: *šuʾila* to Dilbat
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identified three distinct prayers to Dilbat (Mayer 1976: 429), which is the planet Venus and the celestial manifestation of the goddess Ishtar. Mayer tentatively identified only the first in his list, Dilbat 1, as a *šuʾila*-prayer. Dilbat 2, cited by incipit in a ritual tablet to *Bīt salāʾ mê*, is likely to be identified with Ištar 1 (see Ambos 2013: 165; Frechette 2012: 169). And Dilbat 3, only known by its first two words in one witness, [1879-7-8, 332, rev. 5ˊ](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/1879%2C0708.332), preserves no positive evidence for its inclusion in the corpus of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers. Unfortunately, we have very little evidence for Dilbat 1, as its brief introduction shows. The recently identified prayer to Dilbat (see Leichty, Finkel, and Walker 2019: 383) on [BM.38315](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/BM.38315) does not begin with the EN₂ superscript and is thus not included among Dilbat’s *Gebetsbeschwörungen* (for now).**Dilbat 1**The prayer is only known from one textual witness from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh, NinNA1, which has only ever been published in copy (Loretz and Mayer 1978, no. 80). No transliteration or translation has previously appeared in print. This tablet is quite fragmentary and badly abraded in some places. In fact, there are only nineteen lines of text in the prayer, none of which is preserved in its entirety and several of which offer nothing sensible at all. The rubric (rev. 4; line 20ˊ in the present edition) and two lines of ritual instructions (rev. 5-6; lines 21ˊ-22ˊ in the edition) follow the prayer’s *recitanda*. A catchline (rev. 7) and an incomplete Ashurbanipal colophon (rev. 8-13) conclude the tablet. The broken rubric reads \[ka-inim-ma šu-il₂-l\]a₂ ^mul^dil-bat-kam^v^. The raised horizontal of the right side of a LA₂ provides the smallest hint for a *šuʾila*-rubric, at least that is how I understand it for now (so already Bezold 1896: 1711). The ritual instructions prescribe an offering involving juniper, the (likely) three-fold recitation of the incantation (though this is restored), and the supplicant’s proskynesis. In the present edition, I have suggested serveral conjectural restorations in the text of the prayer. All of these should be taken as educated guesses. Although the catchline on the tablet clearly indicates another incantation-prayer was to follow Dilbat 1, this text has yet to be indentified. Thus, we can say nothing more about the prayer’s association with other texts or ritual series.

name: *Šumma Ālu* 80–120 (Human behavior, Project Ālu Geneva)
intro:
The editions of *Šumma ālu* presented here were prepared in the context of the projects “Edition of the Omen Series Šumma Alu” (2017–2021; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970](http://p3.snf.ch/project-175970)) and “Typology and potential of the excerpt tablets of Šumma alu” (2022–2023; [http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122](http://p3.snf.ch/project-205122)), both directed by Prof. Catherine Mittermayer at the University of Geneva and funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The complete score editions can be downloaded (PDF) at the “Archive ouverte” of the University of Geneva ([https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/](https://archive-ouverte.unige.ch/); search for “Shumma alu”). Most of the Tablets edited here were previously unpublished and some were even completely unknown (e.g., the garment omens of T.93). Previous reconstructions of this part of the series mix Nabû-zuqup-kēnu’s Tablet numbering with the canonical one, by which two separate Tablets are presented as “alternative” versions of the same Tablet. For example, Freedman’s T.94 (following Nötscher) is in fact T.94NZK, whereas T.94alt represents T.94 of the canonical series. For understanding and reconstructing this lesser known part of *Šumma ālu* the excerpt tablets from Nineveh were of the utmost importance (see in detail Boddy / Huber Vulliet / Mittermayer 2022).  
As far as possible, the editions follow Neo-Assyrian manuscripts and excerpt tablets from Nineveh. Other manuscripts, some from later periods, are included in the score insofar as they (appear to) preserve the same material. For some Tablets, a distinct Babylonian version can be detected, which is then edited separately.  
The editions of Tablets 80–120 were prepared by Kaira Boddy, Fabienne Huber Vulliet and Catherine Mittermayer.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Our knowledge about the omen series <jats:italic>šumma ālu ina mēlê šakin</jats:italic> has much advanced since the first manuscripts were edited. Even though the overall structure of Šumma ālu is generally well established, the final third of the series still poses considerable problems. In this article we will present a new reconstruction for the sequence from Tablet 80 to 95. As colophons with catchlines and Tablet numbers are scarce for this part of the series, we have developed a new method for the reconstruction mainly relying on clusters of excerpt tablets originating from Nineveh.</jats:p>
