name: *šuʾila*s to Ea
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identifies six incantation-prayers directed to the god Ea (1976: 380-381). (This number excludes prayers directed to Ea and another deity, namely, Ea and Šamaš 1; Ea and Marduk/Asalluḫi 1-3; and Ea, Šamaš, and Marduk/Asalluḫi 1-16, for which see Mayer 1976: 381-384.) Mayer recognizes only the first three as Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, which he numbers 1a, 1b, and 2. For the purposes of the present project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) (CASPo), all three of these prayers are included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer corpus (so also Frechette 2012: 253), even though Ea 2 does not attest a *šuʾila*-rubric. Mayer’s division of the first two prayers into 1a and 1b is in concordance with Kunstmann’s older system of numbering (1932: 85). In other cases of such a distinction (e.g., Adad 1a-1b and Enlil 1a-1b, for which see Kunstmann 1932: 83, 88 and Mayer 1976: 378, 384), the two prayers share very similar or verbatim wording over the course of a (varying) number of lines, suggesting a close literary relationship of some kind and/or doubt that the textual witnesses involved in fact present two distinct prayers. There is no such verbal commonality between Ea 1a and 1b, as Kunstmann recognizes (1932: 85); none at all, in fact. His conclusion that the textual witnesses he groups under “Ea 1b” sre ultimately witnesses to the same prayer as those he groups under “Ea 1a” is entirely based on the order of prayers on one textual witness as compared to the order of prescribed Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers in *Bīt rimki*, an issue treated in the introduction to Ea 1b below.It is important to recognize that the textual witnesses at our disposal for the reconstruction of the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ea (and other deities, for that matter) certainly provide evidence of a more complicated relationship and history than is reflected in our modern taxonomy. (When does one differentiate varying textual witnesses into two different prayers?) For purposes of continuity and user-friendliness, CASPo continues to utilize Mayer’s numbering system for the prayers of Ea (and for Akkadian incantation-prayers in general)./r/r*Nota Bene*: The left column of [BM.42325](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/library/BM.42325) presents ten lines of text of what looks to be a prayer to Ea (Leichty, Finkel, and Walker 2019: 509). The right column attests part of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Nabû 2. It may turn out that the left column preserves a previously unknown Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Ea or an unknown part of what is here labeled Ea 1b or Ea 2 (or even part of Ea 1a as represented by NinNA1₁ (+) NinNA1₂). Given the number of incantation-prayers directed to Ea (including those that address another deity along with Ea), there isn’t a sufficient basis to include the material in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus at present. It is hoped that a new join will soon change that conclusion.**Ea 1a**The textual basis for Ea 1a is fairly extensive with textual witnesses coming from most of the major first-millennium sites that have yielded tablets. (Sippar is noticeably unrepresented.) Among the Neo-Assyrian witnesses, there is one from Ashur (found in the house of an exorcist; see Pedersén 1986: 62), one from Ḫuzirina, one from Kalḫu, and four from Nineveh. The witnesses labeled NinNA1₁ and NinNA1₂ likely indirectly join (see Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 333 and already Hunt 2010: 46,n.162 \[a personal communication attributed to T. Abusch\]). NinNA3 only preserves the incipit functioning as the tablet’s catchline. And the rubric on NinNA2 identifies Marduk as the prayer’s addressee (see below). The south is represented by three textual witnesses: one from late period Babylon and two from Hellenistic Uruk. UrkHel2 only cites the incipit of the prayer. (Its colophon explicitly identifies the owner as “Iqishaya, son of Ishtar-shuma-eresh, descen\[dant of Ekur-zakir\],” who flourished c. 320 BCE. See Robson 2019: 229-235.)Although there are only a few unknowns in the reconstruction of the wording of the preserved lines of the prayer (see line 22, which is very problematic, and the gaps in lines 11ˊ-16ˊ), the textual witnesses show significant differences from one another, suggesting a complicated history of composition, adaptation, and transmission. (For speculations on diacronic development, see Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 332.) Textual variants occur in some lines of the prayer (see lines 22, 24, 26, and 29 in the present edition) while two manuscripts include an additional line of praise toward the prayer’s conclusion (see line 28a). NinNA1₁ deviates so widely after line 10 that its continuation is treated separately as lines 11ˊ-16ˊ in the present edition. NinNA1₂, however, which may indirectly join NinNA1₁, resumes in line 22 and follows the duplicates closely until its text runs out in line 27. BabLB1 may include a generic self-introductory formula (see the textual note on line 14), and HuzNA1 inserts a customized self-introductory formula with lament for a certain Banitu-teresh (see lines 14a-14e). Four textual witnesses attach a *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer (AššNA1, rev. 23; KalNA1, rev. 10; UrkHel1, obv. 9ˊ; and NinNA2, obv. 6ˊ), but do not agree on the addressee named therein. AššNA1 names Enlilbanda as the addressee; KalNA1 and UrkHel1 name Ea; and NinNA2, oddly, identifies Marduk as the addressee, resulting in its version of the prayer being cataloged as Marduk 3 with our NinNA2 as its only witness (see Mayer 1976: 395 and Frechette 2012: 260). Given how closely the text of NinNA2 follows the other textual witnesses to Ea 1a (only in lines 24-31 with a minor lexical variant in line 26), the divine name in the rubric may be a scribal mistake (see Mayer 1976: 395; Frechette 2012: 172; and Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 332; differently, Hunt 2010: 64,n.223). Another scribal issue occurs in BabLB1, which lacks the final signs of several lines (see its obv. 6ˊ\[?\], 7ˊ, 9ˊ, 10ˊ, and 12ˊ in lines 7-13 of the edition). Its *Vorlage* may have been damaged, though the scribe does not indicate such.As for textual associations and ritual uses of Ea 1a: Many of the textual witnesses to Ea 1a only bear the text of that prayer (BabLB1, HuzNA1, KalNA1, NinNA1₁ (+) NinNA1₂). And since none of these provide ritual instructions for the prayer’s use, they offer no evidence for the purpose at hand. In [NinNA3](http://shuilas.org/P397372.html), there is one line of basic ritual instructions of the kind often attached to *šuʾila*-prayers—involving a ritual assemblage (*riksu*) or censer (*nignakku*)—just before the incipit of Ea 1a is given as the tablet’s catchline (rev. 1ˊ-2ˊ). This textual arrangement suggests a ritual use for Ea 1a in conjunction with at least one other text, but nothing more can be said about this use for want of evidence. The nearly complete AššNA1 places Ea 1a among three other identifiable Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, two of which prescribe the basic ritual procedure. The full [content](http://shuilas.org/P369041.html) of this tablet runs as follows: Marduk 2 (obv. 1-25), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. 26), basic ritual instructions (obv. 27), incipit to Marduk 18 (obv. 28), Ea 1a (obv., 29-36, rev., 1-22), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 23), ritual instructions (rev. 24), incipit to Ea 2 as catchline (rev. 25), and then the colophon (rev. 26-30; see Hunger 1968, no. 225), which names Nabû-balassu-iqbi as the tablet’s owner and a junior scribal apprentice (name lost in the break) as the tablet’s copyist. The catchline suggests the tablet is part of a larger ritual series or textual collection. But, the precise purpose for this concatenation of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers on one tablet is unclear. (Incidentally, in the only [other witness to Marduk 18](http://shuilas.org/Q006116.html), which is also from Ashur and part of a concatenation of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, that prayer is also preceded by Marduk 2.) Ea 1a was certainly a prescribed recitation in the Ninevite Ritual Tablet to *Bīt rimki* (Schwemer 2019: 56, line 214 \[= A o iii 58\]; 76; see also Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25) and in *Bīt salāʾ mê*, according to one version of its Ritual Tablet. In fact, the prayer was prescribed during the latter ritual’s night cycle of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers twice, once directed to Ea (Ambos 2013: 164 \[x + 13ˊ (= A₁ iii 1ˊ; C 13ˊ)\], which is followed by Marduk 2), and once to the “star of Eridu,” ^mul^NUN^ki^, parts of Puppis and Vela (Ambos 2013: 165 \[x + 27ˊ (= A₁ iii 16ˊ; D 5ˊˊb; the incipit is mostly restored\]), and then again in the morning after the recitation of Šamaš 1 and before Marduk 2 (Ambos 2013: 168 \[y + 9ˊ (= A₂ 7; B₂ 4ˊˊ; C 7ˊˊa\]; see also Frechette 2012: 168-169). This ordering of prescribed recitations in one version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet may explain the placement of Ea 1a (without ritual instructions) before Marduk 2 on [UrkHel1](http://shuilas.org/P348682.html). Two other sources for Ea 1a show textual associations that imply a ritual use (NinNA2 and UrkHel2), both of which have been treated elsewhere. For the possibility that NinNA2, which names Marduk in the rubric, bears *recitanda* used in the morning section of *Bīt salāʾ mê*, see the second to last paragraph in the [introduction to Šamaš 1](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/31), where Ea 1a’s NinNA2 = Šamaš 1’s NinNA2 (= BMS 10). For Ea 1a’s place in a Hellenistic *namburbi*-collection, perhaps indicating its use in such rituals, see the seventh paragraph in the [introduction to Šamaš 1](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/31), where Ea 1a’s UrkHel2 = Šamaš 1’s UrkHel1 (= SpTU 2, no. 18 + SpTU 5, no. 238).**Ea 1b**Unlike Ea 1a, Ea 1b is very poorly attested with only one textual witness from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh. Only the final half-dozen lines of the prayer are attested on this one witness before the *šuʾila*-rubric in obv. 8ˊ, which names Enlilbanda as the prayer’s addressee. Three other Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers follow: Damkina 1 (obv. 9ˊ-29ˊ \[break\]), Ninurta 1 (rev. 1ˊ-8ˊ with *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 9ˊ), and Gula 1b (rev. 10ˊ-36ˊ \[break\]). Neither of the two prayers that has a rubric includes ritual instructions. This absence may be explained by the use of the prayers in *Bīt rimki* since the last three occur in the same order as is prescribed in the cycle of *šuʾila*-prayers in the Ninevite Ritual Tablet of that series (Schwemer 2019: 56, lines 216, 218, 220 \[= A o iii 60, 62, 64\]; 76; see also Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25). In addition, the prayer that is prescribed prior to Damkina 1 on the Ritual Tablet is directed to Ea, as is the case on the present tablet, though the cited incipit on the Ritual Tablet belongs to Ea 1a (see line 214), not Ea 1b. Of course, we do not know the incipit to Ea 1b, only the prayer’s concluding lines. For Kunstmann (1932: 85-86), this ordering of prayers on NinNA1 in light of the ordering of prayers in the Ritual Tablet was determinative for his classification of the textual material into Ea 1a and Ea 1b, despite the absence of any overlap in wording between their respective conclusions. His use of the a-b differentiation reflects some hesitancy to identify the two prayers outright. But, from his own description, he seems to think that the textual material involved really does reflect one prayer beginning with the incipit *šar nēmeqi* (see Ea 1a, line 1). Is it possible that the prayer edited here as Ea 1a had a different ending in one manuscript (our NinNA1 for Ea 1b) so that Ea 1a and Ea 1b are in fact one and the same prayer? Yes. But, I think it is more likely that we simply have a different prayer to Ea on NinNA1 than is prescribed in the Ritual Tablet to *Bīt rimki*. They ought to have distinct identifiers in our catalogs, in my view, rather than the a-b label, which supposes their close relationship. (For the sake of continuity and convenience, I have retained Kunstmann’s and Mayer’s labels.) Perhaps NinNA1 represents a variation in the tradition of prescribed prayers for *Bīt rimki*. Or, perhaps NinNA1 is not *recitanda* for *Bīt rimki* at all but had some other unknown purpose. These are guesses, really; we simply don’t know. To make matters more complicated: It is possible that Ea 1b’s NinNA1 represents the conclusion of what is here reconstructed as Ea 2. Until evidence connects the two, however, they retain distinct identifiers.**Ea 2**There are only two Neo-Assyrian textual witnesses at our disposal to reconstruct Ea 2. One of these (AššNA1), which happens to be the best textual witness to Ea 1a, only preserves the prayer’s incipit as the tablet’s catchline. (For more on this textual witness, its full content, and its unknown purpose for arranging four Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers serially, see the introduction to Ea 1a above.) The other, HuzNA1, is a votive tablet dedicated to Adad and belonging to a certain Aplaya, the military chief (*turtānu*), according to its colophon (rev. 10-18; see Hunger 1968, no. 407). This textual witness attests only the hymnic introduction to Ea 2. Thus, our knowledge of the prayer is limited to that initial section. It is noteworthy that the other text on HuzNA1 is also a hymnic introduction, this one to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Sîn 1 (obv. 19-28, rev. 1-8). After the last line of both hymns there is (what I argue is) a scribal annotation, labeling the preceding material an incantation (EN₂). Both annotations end with an admonition to “keep this in order” (Akk. *annâ šutēšir*; see obv. 18 and rev. 9, which are treated in the colophon section of this introduction under chapter 2) and are followed by a rule line. Whatever the original purpose for inscribing the two hymnic passages on this tablet, the content seems to have caught Aplaya’s eye sometime later. His colophon was scratched into the tablet after it had dried in a much larger script than the inscription proper. The colophon, it seems, was added to the tablet specifically to make it an appropriate votive for the military man. Because several other [textual witnesses to Sîn 1](http://shuilas.org/Q006153.html) attach a *šuʾila*-rubric to that prayer, and because two other prayers attested on AššNA1 have a *šuʾila*-rubric (Marduk 2 in obv. 26 and Ea 1a in rev. 23), Ea 2 is included among the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers by dint of textual association. As already noted in the introduction to Ea 1b, it is possible that Ea 2 is the opening hymn for the prayer that is classified here as Ea 1b.

name: *šuʾila*s to Enlil
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identifies three incantation-prayers directed to the god Enlil (1976: 384-385; compare Kunstmann 1932: 88), which he numbers 1a, 1b, and 2. For the purposes of the present project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) (CASPo), all three of these prayers are included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer corpus (so also Frechette 2012: 254), even though the very fragmentary Enlil 2 does not attest a *šuʾila*-rubric. Unfortunately, there are few textual witnesses with which to reconstruct these prayers, and none preserves clear ritual instructions (though one manuscript of Enlil 1b provides a hint of them, see below). It was Kunstmann who labeled the first two prayers Enlil 1a and Enlil 1b (1932: 88, followed by Mayer 1976: 384), suggesting their close literary relationship and/or doubt that the textual witnesses involved in fact present two distinct prayers. Indeed, parallels between the two prayers exist in seventeen lines, but only seven of these are verbatim (eight, if the emendation in Enlil 1b, line 18 is included). Leaving aside their shared concluding line (Enlil 1a, line 28 and Enlil 1b, line 38), the parallels occur in the first twenty-two lines of both prayers (as numbered in the present editions): Enlil 1a, lines 1-9, 12-13, 16-18, 21-22 parallel Enlil 1b, lines 7-22. Enlil 1a, lines 10-11, 14-15, and 19-20 lack parallels in Enlil 1b, whose lines 1-6 (which Kunstmann calls an addition; 1932: 88) and 23-37 are unparalleled in Enlil 1a. The intertextual and genetic (if any) relationships between the two prayers will be explored in a future publication. Both Enlil 1a and Enlil 1b were used in larger ritual procedures, as discussed in the specific introductions to those prayers below.**Enlil 1a**Enlil 1a is the best-attested prayer to Enlil with four first-millennium textual witnesses available for its reconstruction. There are two manuscripts from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh. One, NinNA1, attests something from all but the first few lines of the prayer while the other, NinNA2, attests only fragments of the first six lines on its obverse. (The reverse only preserves a partial Ashurbanipal colophon.) The other two manuscripts are from the south. BabaNB1 is the best witness to the text of the prayer, bearing the entire text with only a few lacunae, all of which can be restored easily. This tablet probably dates to the Neo-Babylonian period but its precise provenance in the south is unknown. The other southern manuscript, BabaPer1, is a large tablet of *recitanda* for *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see below). With regard to Enlil 1a, BabaPer1 only attests the incipit of the prayer, which functions as the tablet’s catchline (e.1). The colophon that follows (e.2-4) names as the tablet’s owner a certain Bel-\[uballiṭ, son\] of Bel-keshir, of the Basia family. He is also known from [BM.38537](http://shuilas.org/P453575.html), which (also) preserves *recitanda* of some version of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (explicitly identified in the colophon there), as discussed in the introduction to [Adad 1a](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/1). The colophon of BabaPer1 then mentions the city Babylon (as either the home of the tablet’s owner or the source of the original from which the copy was made) and dates the tablet to the third day of some month (broken) in the thirty-second year of Darius (I), king of Persia. Thus, BabaPer1 dates to 490 BCE. The two best textual witnesses, NinNA1 and BabaNB1, both attach a *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer (see NinNA1, rev. 13 and BabaNB1, rev. 9). In both cases, the rubric is immediately (and only) followed by the incipit of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Ninlil 1, which serves as the tablets’ catchlines. The two textual witnesses vary from one another in a few places (see lines 18-19, the latter of which is absent in NinNA1; and line 23) and conclude in markedly different ways after line 25. In what the present edition identifies as lines 26-28, BabaNB1 concludes with a wish for the personal gods to praise Enlil and then a promise for the supplicant himself to praise the deity. NinNA1 has none of this; rather, it concludes with a stock phrase about the unalterable divine command (see lines 26ˊ-27ˊ). As Foster points out, this is not a complete sentence (2005: 655,n.1). However, ending a prayer with such an exclamation is not unparalleled (see, e.g., Ereqqu 2 in [SpTU 4, no. 129](http://shuilas.org/P348723.html), obv. ii 47ˊ-48ˊ and Tašmetu 1 in [CTN 4, no. 168](http://shuilas.org/P363582.html), rev. i 41-43). Why the two manuscripts have the different endings is unclear at present.None of the textual witnesses currently at hand preserves ritual instructions, but we do know something about the prayer’s ritual use. Enlil 1a is a prescribed recitation in both *Bīt rimki* (Ninevite version; see Schwemer 2019: 56, line 212 \[= A o iii 56\], 76; also Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25) and *Bīt salāʾ mê* (both versions; see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 42; x + 2ˊ (= C 2ˊ), both directed to ^mul^ŠU.PA, perhaps the constellation Boötes\]; 164 \[x + 7ˊ (C 7ˊ, directed to ^d^50, Enlil\], 175; Frechette 2012: 168). In both rituals, Enlil 1a is followed by an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Ninlil. In *Bīt rimki*, that prayer is Ninlil 2. In *Bīt salāʾ mê*, it is Ninlil 5. Our two best textual witnesses to Enlil 1a, as mentioned above, both cite the incipit to Ninlil 1 as the catchline to the tablet, suggesting that that prayer, Ninlil 1, was to follow Enlil 1a. (All three prayers to Ninlil included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers [corpus](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) are currently only known by their incipit. See [here](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/22) for editions.) The insertion of the *attalû*-formula in NinNA1 (see lines 11a-c in the present edition) certainly indicates the prayer’s use in a ritual with an apotropaic purpose. Such a formula is attested in two Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers on a tablet that follows the order of prayers prescribed in the Ninevite Ritual Tablet of *Bīt rimki* and whose colophon explicitly designates the tablet as part of *Bīt rimki* (see the introduction to [Ištar 1](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/13) and [K.155](http://shuilas.org/P393771.html), obv. 12-13 in Sîn 1 and rev. 4ˊ-5ˊ in Tašmetu 1; Frechette 2012: 193-194). So perhaps we should remain open to the possibility that these two manuscripts of Enlil 1a attest a variant in the ritually prescribed recitations of *Bīt rimki*. Without further evidence, however, the precise ritual setting (if any at all) for the textual association of Enlil 1a and Ninlil 1 in NinNA1 and BabaNB1 remains open.Prescribed order is also an issue with BabaPer1. The content of this large tablet of *recitanda* strongly suggests a connection to *Bīt salāʾ mê*, though the order of the material does not precisely fit the order of any (currently) known version of that series’s Ritual Tablet (for which, see Ambos 2013: 155-175). BabaPer1 begins with two incantations known to be used in *Bīt salāʾ mê*: EN₂ *šubtu ša ilī qurādī*, “O dwelling of the gods, the heroes” (obv. i 1-13) and EN₂ *šubtu ša ilī rabûti manzāzu ellu*, “O dwelling of the gods, the pure abode” (obv. i 14ff. \[break\]). The incipits to both incantations are cited in one version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet, but in the opposite order that BabaPer1 presents them (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 31\]). BabaPer1, obv. ii presents material that duplicates the prayer published in Livingstone’s article, “Ashurbanipal: Literate or Not?” (2007). Alan Lenzi and Frank Simons will publish this material along with a newly identified duplicate and a discussion of the relationship of the prayer to various ritual actions prescribed for *Bīt salāʾ mê* in the near future. After a long break between obverse and reverse, BabaPer1 attests parts of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers Anu 1 (*šuʾila*-rubric in rev. i 11ˊ \[Anu’s name is restored\]) and Papsukkal 1 (rev. i 13ˊff.). After the break between rev. i and ii, there is the very abraded remnants of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Šulpaʾea 1 (*šuʾila*-rubric in rev. ii 21ˊ). After a few lines of ritual instructions, there is the catchline to Enlil 1a and a colophon (bottom edge 1-4), which names a scribe known to have copied *Bīt salāʾ mê* material on another large tablet of *recitanda*, as mentioned above. All the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers attested on the reverse of BabaPer1 are cited by incipit in the two different versions of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 44, Anu 1; several intervening prayers, then B₂ 50, Papsukkal 1; B₂ 38, Šulpaʾea 1, followed next by B₂ 42, Enlil 1a\]; 164 \[x + 6ˊ (= C 6ˊ), Anu 1; x + 7ˊ (= C 7ˊ), Enlil 1a; several intervening prayers, then x + 11ˊ (= C 11ˊ), Papsukkal 1; eight intervening prayers, then x + 22ˊ (= A₁ iii 7ˊ; C 22ˊ; D 2ˊˊ), Šulpaʾea 1). However, just as was the case with BM.38537, the order of the prayers on BabaPer1 does not conform to any order prescribed in any of the versions of the Ritual Tablet. It is to be noted, though, that one version of the Ritual Tablet does attest Šulpaʾea 1 followed by Enlil 1a, as in BabaPer1.**Enlil 1b**Enlil 1b is only attested in two manuscripts from Neo-Assyrian Ashur. AššNA1 preserves nearly the entire text of the prayer, followed by a *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 17). After the rubric, the remainder of the reverse is blank. There are no ritual instructions, no colophon, and no other texts copied with Enlil 1b on AššNA1. In the few places where AššNA1 is broken, the text of Enlil 1b can be restored with a high level of confidence except for the end of line 5 and the beginning of line 22 in the present edition. AššNA2 (KAR 23 + 25 = VAT 9823 + VAT 9737, respectively) is a large tablet bearing the text of seven *šuʾila*-prayers (see full contents below), copied by a junior scribal apprentice named Nabu-zeru-leshir (rev. ii 4ˊ; see Baker 2001: 911, #8), who traces his genealogy back several generations to Dadiyu, the scribe of the temple and the palace (rev. ii 9ˊ-10ˊ) (Radner 1999: 364). This textual witness incompletely attests lines 1-14 of Enlil 1b, as numbered in the present edition, and offers a few minor textual variants vis-à-vis AššNA1. Unfortunately, a fragment from the lower right corner of the reverse of the tablet (bottom of rev. i) and a flake from the upper left corner (top of rev. ii) have apparently fallen away since Ebeling made his copy in the early twentieth century. Thus, some signs that appear in his copy (see KAR 25) are no longer on the tablet and cannot be collated. The text of Enlil 1b on AššNA2 ends abruptly at the bottom edge of the first column on the reverse of the tablet. The remaining lines of Enlil 1b and perhaps several lines of its accompanying ritual instructions were inscribed at the top of rev. ii, though this portion of the tablet is not preserved. Thus, the first two preserved lines in this column are likely the very end of the ritual instructions accompanying Enlil 1b (and also the last lines of ritual content on the tablet). Only the second line offers sensible text. It reads: ⸢*x*⸣ \[... DU₁₁.GA-*su*\] ⸢ŠE⸣.GA-⸢*at*⸣, “. \[. . . his prayer (lit., speech)\] will be granted.” (The restored signs were visible to Ebeling when he made his copy; they are no longer on the tablet. See above.) Though this phrase provides nothing substantive about the ritual actions that were to accompany Enlil 1b, it may very well be a fitting conclusion to the larger ritual procedure in which Enlil 1b and six other prayers were used (see below). Because this textual witness breaks off before the end of the prayer, it does not attest a *šuʾila*-rubric for Enlil 1b. However, the other six prayers on the tablet are classified as such; thus, it is very likely that Enlil 1b on this textual witness also bore the rubric.As mentioned above, AššNA2 attests six other Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, all of which appear before Enlil 1b, which is the final prayer on the tablet. The complete content of [AššNA2](http://shuilas.org/P369009.html) is as follows: Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Nabû 1 (obv. i 1-19), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. i 20), with ritual instructions (obv. i 21-28); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Marduk 2 (obv. i 29-55), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. i 56a), with ritual instructions (obv. i 56b); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Marduk 18 (obv. i 57-69, ii 1), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. ii 2a), with ritual instructions (obv. ii 2b); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Marduk 19 (obv. ii 3-24), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. ii 25), with ritual instructions (o ii 26); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Nabû 2 (obv. ii 27-60), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. ii 61 \[restored\]), with ritual instructions (obv. ii 62); (about two lines missing before the bottom edge); (about thirty-one lines missing from the top of rev. i; i.e., the number of lines on KAR 23); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Sîn 9 (rev. i 1ˊ-11ˊ), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. i 12ˊ \[inserted in a smaller script\]), with ritual instructions (rev. i 13ˊ-20ˊ); Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Enlil 1b (rev. i 21ˊ-33ˊ) (bottom edge); (about thirty-one lines missing from the top of rev. ii; i.e., the number of lines on KAR 23); perhaps ritual instructions to Enlil 1b (rev. ii 1ˊ-2ˊ); colophon (rev. ii 3ˊ-16ˊ = Hunger 1968, no. 235, but see presently for a new reading of the first line). For a map of the tablet’s layout, see [here](http://shuilas.org/P369009_map.jpg). The gap at the top of rev. i, which is likely about 31 lines, may have only included the opening lines of Sîn 9. At present (July 2026), we do not know this prayer’s length (see Hätinen 2021: 474-476) so it is impossible to know if some other text came between Nabû 2 and Sîn 9. (Two tablets from Ashur attesting Nabû 2 continue with Tašmetu 2. See [LKA 40](http://shuilas.org/P413951.html) and [LKA 40a](http://shuilas.org/P413952.html). Tašmetu 2 is about 20 lines long and thus could fit in the gap at the top of rev. i while still leaving room for the beginning of Sîn 9. If Tašmetu 2 did follow Nabû 2 on AššNA2, it would have been the only prayer to a goddess on the tablet.) The concatenation of these *šuʾila*-prayers, according to the first line of the colophon, was to be used in a ritual performance of some kind: EN₂ *ana* \[*m*\]*u-*\[*še-piš-u*₂*-ti-šu*₂ SAR*-ma*\] *ib*₂*-ri*, “The incantations were \[written and\] collated for a \[ri\]tu\[al performance\]” (the restoration is my own suggestion; see Hunger 1968, no. 341 for the same phrase). But, the precise nature of this ritual is not specified. Oshima suggests the prayers may have been recited in *Bīt rimki* (2011: 329), though the order of prayers attested on AššNA2 does not match the order of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers prescribed in any of the attested ritual instructions (likewise, Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 341), which, as Oshima notes, remain fragmentary (see Schwemer’s new edition of the relevant material of the series’s Ritual Tablet \[2019\]). Thus, our only recourse for positing a united ritual purpose for these seven prayers is to infer that purpose from the specific content of the prayers and the ritual instructions attached to each. The following brief reflections are preliminary. A fuller study is needed, ideally when more evidence is available.The content of the opening prayer on AššNA2, Nabû 1, and its ritual instructions (obv. i 21-28) look to function as an initial salutation to gain a favorable audience with the deity (see Frechette 2012: 165-224 for this function of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers in various ritual contexts). Indeed, in the only petition of the prayer the supplicant, who, as the text constructs him, is advanced in age (obv. i 11-12, 15), requests deliverance: *kullimanni nūra*, “show me the light!” (obv. i 18), a phrase that the supplicant is required to repeat, according to the ritual instructions, just before a prescribed prostration (obv. i 27-29). Marduk 2, the next prayer on the tablet, may have a similar function since its petitions are all rather general, including wishes for life, achievement of desires, good standing and effective speech among social elites, and the presence of personal deities (obv. i 39-50). (In the only other textual witness to Nabû 1 that associates that prayer with another, the prayer is Marduk 2. But, they occur in the reverse order. See [STT 55](http://shuilas.org/P338373.html), inscribed by a junior scribe.) The ritual instructions attached to Marduk 2, like those for the next two prayers, are the standard, basic ritual instructions used with many Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers: *šumma ina riksi šumma ina nignakki teppuš*, “you do *the ritual* either with a ritual assemblage or with a censer.” They provide little overt help for understanding the distinctive ritual purpose of the concatenation of the seven prayers on AššNA2. In Marduk 18 (only known from two [textual witnesses](http://shuilas.org/Q006116.html), both from Ashur and preceded on the tablet by Marduk 2), the supplicant seeks absolution for unintended sin (obv. i 60-64). In Marduk 19 the supplicant’s only petition is for release from an interdiction or taboo (Akk. *ikkibu*, obv. ii 23). In Nabû 2 (see Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 341-349) the supplicant complains of and seeks release from several common sources of human misery, including distress, illness, witchcraft, magic, and sorcery (obv. ii 43-47, 50-52). At the end of the prayer he wishes for the presence of his personal god and protective spirit (obv. ii 56-57) and for his renewed health (obv. ii 60). The prayer clearly aligns with other rites of removal, especially in light of the phrase *lissi šār \[bēri\]*, “may it (i.e., the undesirable concern) withdraw far \[away\].” The ritual instructions for Nabû 2 on AššNA2, the only textual witness of that prayer (so far) to include them, are not well-enough preserved to provide evidence for the present purpose (see obv. ii 62). In fact, due to tablet damage, we cannot know if only the standard, basic ritual was prescribed or something more elaborate. The preserved text of Sîn 9 (a prayer also only known from two [textual witnesses](http://shuilas.org/Q006163.html) from Ashur) also wishes for the removal of something evil or negative from the supplicant’s body (the word is restored in rev. i 8ˊ), using phrases that resonate with rites of removal (rev. i 5ˊ-7ˊ). The similarities of the (rather extensive) ritual instructions attached to Sîn 9 (rev. i 13ˊ-20ˊ) to those prescribed in several other therapeutic rituals concerned with some kind of undesirable skin condition (Akk. *garābu*) may suggest the same or a similar skin condition is at issue here (see Hätinen 2021: 474). However, the one line in Sîn 9 that seems to describe a symptom uses two words from the semantic domain ‘cold’, *kuṣṣu* and *ḫurbāšu* (rev. i 3ˊ), suggesting perhaps some other concern is in focus. In any case, removal of what is undesirable is definitely the prayer’s and its ritual instructions’ goal. (Note the final ritual act is throwing everything in the river, rev. i 20ˊ.) Then comes Enlil 1b. Although AššNA2 does not preserve the last half of the prayer, it very likely preserved that part of the prayer at the top of rev. ii before the tablet was damaged. Further, it is likely that its text of this last half of the prayer followed the text of the prayer as it is preserved on AššNA1. (This manner of argumentation is less than ideal but reasonable in light of how closely the two witnesses align in lines 1-14.) The petitions in Enlil 1b are centered on the supplicant’s desire for a favorable fate (line 20), good standing among the supplicant’s superiors and peers (lines 21-25, 30), and reconciliation with and presence of his personal deities (lines 27-29, 32-34, 36) as well as reconciliation with Enlil (line 35). (The concern with social standing and the desire for the presence of the personal deities are themes present in Enlil 1a but not as fully developed as they are in Enlil 1b. See Enlil 1a, lines 21-25.) It is interesting to note the absence of any petitions for the removal of something undesirable or evil in Enlil 1b. The supplicant makes such petitions in Enlil 1a, lines 19-20, as reconstructed in the present edition, but these lines are absent—purposefully skipped?—in Enlil 1b (see lines 20-21, which compare to Enlil 1a, lines 18, 21). Perhaps the removal was considered complete after the recital and ritual actions of Sîn 9. In any case, the final line of text before AššNA2’s colophon provides a fitting conclusion to both the (presumed) ritual instructions of Enlil 1b as well as the larger ritual procedure of the seven prayers: “\[his prayer\] will be granted” (rev. ii 2ˊ). The petitions throughout the seven prayers on AššNA2 address most of the primary causes of human misery in Akkadian prayers, and the ritual instructions, at least as they are preserved, do not offer any distinctive insights (e.g., via the burning of an image of a witch). Thus, for now, it seems the larger ritual purpose for Enlil 1b amidst the other texts on AššNA2 is some kind of ritual removal and divine reconciliation.**Enlil 2**This prayer is only attested on one very fragmentary textual witness from Neo-Assyrian period Ashur. Although identified already by Mayer as an incantation-prayer to Enlil (1976: 385), this small fragment—merely the upper left corner of a tablet—was not published until 2011 (Maul and Strauß 2011: 20, no. 54). It attests only six lines, none of which is complete. There is no rubric of any kind attached to the text. And there are no other known textual or ritual associations. The text is included here as an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer tentatively due to the so-called Sumerian hymnic style hinted at in the opening two lines (see Mayer 1976: 40,n.9, who does not classify the text as a *šuʾila*-prayer; and Frechette 2012: 135,n.47; 254, who does).

name: Series of the Poplar
intro:
The *Series of the Poplar* contains a discussion between a Poplar, an Ash, and probably other trees, who each tries to establish his preeminence in the vegetal kingdom by listing their many uses and excellent qualities.  
Four sections of the text can be reconstructed at present, yielding a total of some 80 lines. The poem began with a cosmogonic introduction, now lost, followed by the description of the place of litigation, a gallery forest (*qīšu*), and the contenders, a poplar (*ṣarbatu*) and an ash (*martû*). The other preserved sections contain speeches of either Poplar or Ash, the order of which is difficult to determine. It seems likely that the *Series of the Poplar* would originally have comprised more than one chapter, in which perhaps other trees could have intervened — the poem *Palm and Vine* ([§II.12](/corpus/L/2/12)) could well be part of the *Series*.  
Three manuscripts of the text are known: two from Nineveh – apparently from different tablets – and one from Babylonia.  The series is mentioned by title in the Neo-Assyrian inventory [Rm.618](/fragmentarium/Rm.618), along with other disputation poems, and in the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([§0](/corpus/L/0/0)). According to the latter, it was written by the Babylonian exorcist Ur-Nanna, who may have lived in the second half of the second millennium BCE.  
The Nineveh manuscripts, once believed to be part of the *Epic of Gilgameš*, were edited in the 1960s; the larger Babylonian tablet received a first edition in 2017. The text is still very fragmentary.

name: Series of Ox and Horse
intro:
The *Series of Ox and Horse* is a poetic dispute between an ox and a horse and perhaps other animals. Around 200 mostly fragmentary verses are known, but it is uncertain how long the text originally was, or in which order the preserved fragments should be arranged.  
The text opens with a mythological introduction describing the arrival of the spring, which provides the *occasio litingadi*: in the lush pastures an ox and a horse meet and decide to dispute, simply for pleasure’s sake. Nine speeches of Ox and eight of Horse are preserved, concerned with a variety of topics. In the opening salvo (A+25–A+37), Ox claims that, whereas he enjoys the pasture and his calves gambol in it during the spring, Horse gruffly tramples it. In one speech, Horse (B+1–B+12) scoffs at Ox for being a pack animal; both Horse and Ox brag of their proximity to kings and princes (Ox in F+2; Horse in A+6 and C+11).  
Seven pieces of this series, all of them from Ashurbanipal’s libraries, are known. None of the pieces duplicate each other, and they can be identified solely on the basis of the presence of one of the two speech introduction formulae of the series: “Horse answered and spake a word unto the heroic Ox saying” and “Ox answered and spake unto Horse, the expert in war.” The *Series*, as well the incipit of one of its chapters are mentioned among other disputation poems in the inventory tablet [Rm.618](/fragmentarium/Rm.618#%2013). Nothing is known about the genesis of the text, but since some hippological lexemes are otherwise attested only in Middle Babylonian documents, the *Series* was probably composed in the second half of the second millennium BCE.  
The most recent edition of the series was published in the 1960s, although most fragments had already been edited in the 1920s, many of them also in G. Smith’s pioneering edition in the 1870s.

name: *šuʾila* to Guanna
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer does not list any incantation-prayers to the star Guanna (Akk. *is lê*), which is identified with the star Alpha Tauri and The Hyades, a star cluster. Thanks to the recent publication of new textual material described below, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online (CASPo)](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) can include one Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to this star (see likewise, Frechette 2012: 252).**Guanna 1**Only a very partial incipit to Guanna 1 is currently known. In fact, we only know its first word! The incipit and thus the existence of the prayer was discovered in recent years with Claus Ambos’s edition and publication of new material related to the different versions of the Ritual Tablet of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (Ambos 2013: 165 \[x + 25ˊ (= A₁ iii 14ˊ)\]; see also Frechette 2012: 252). The only textual witness to this part of the Ritual Tablet that was known prior to Ambos’s edition, K.2132 \[= Ambos’s MS D 4ˊˊb\], is broken in the line that would have attested the prayer’s incipit (compare Kunstmann 1932: 62).Guanna 1 is prescribed as part of *Bīt salāʾ mê*’s night cycle of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to various stars. The prayer is included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus because the other prayers cited by incipit in this part of the Ritual Tablet and known beyond their initial line from other textual sources are all labeled with the *šuʾila*-rubric. Compare the prayers identified in Frechette 2012: 168-169 with the manuscript information for each at [CASPo’s list of prayers](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) and the information about [rubrics](http://shuilas.org/rubrics.html) attested in each manuscript of the corpus. Nothing more is known about this prayer.

name: *šuʾila* to Gud
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer lists only one prayer to the star Gud (Akk. *šiḫṭu*), which is associated with the planet Mercury (Mayer 1976: 430; see also Frechette 2012: 254; compare Kunstmann 1932: 62).**Gud 1**Gud 1 is (still) only known from the partial citation of its incipit in one version of the Ritual Tablet of *Bīt salāʾ mê* (Ambos 2013: 165 \[x + 30ˊ (= D 7ˊˊa)\]; see also Frechette 2012: 169, 254). Although there is a second source for this line in Ambos’s edition (his MS A₁ iii 19ˊ), the line breaks just before the citation of our prayer’s incipit. Gud 1 is prescribed as part of *Bīt salāʾ mê*’s night cycle of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to various stars; it is the second to last prayer in that cycle. The prayer is included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus and the present project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online (CASPo)](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html), because the other prayers cited by incipit in this part of the Ritual Tablet and known beyond their initial line from other textual sources are all labeled with the *šuʾila*-rubric. Compare the prayers identified in Frechette 2012: 168-169 with the manuscript information for each at [CASPo’s list of prayers](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) and the information about [rubrics](http://shuilas.org/rubrics.html) attested in each manuscript of the corpus.The incipit of Gud 1, unfortunately, is only partially preserved in our one source. After the clearly preserved first two words, *aplu gašru*, there is what looks to be a ŠE, or perhaps a partial BU. (Kunstmann, apparently, read it as BU, since he gave *gitmālu* (*git*₂-*ma-lu*, git₂ = BU) as the third word of the prayer’s incipit \[1932: 62\]. Ambos leaves the signs undeciphered.) If BU is the correct reading, it raises the possibility that the next word in the incipit is *bukur*, which in turn suggests the possible restoration of the complete incipit of the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Ninurta 1, *aplu gašru bukur ellil*, “O mighty heir, firstborn of Enlil” (see Mayer 1976: 404). Although Ninurta 1 is recited earlier in the *Bīt salāʾ mê* cycle of prayers (see Ambos 2013: 164, x + 9ˊ \[= C 9ˊ\]), there are other examples of one and the same prayer being prescribed as a recitation directed first to the deity, identified by name, and then to the star associated with that deity (e.g., Ea 1a directed to Ea and then to the star of Eridu). It is possible, therefore, that Ninurta 1 could have been recited twice, too, once to Ninurta and once to the star Gud (Mercury). Ninurta, of course, was typically associated with the star Sirius (^mul^KAK.SI.SA₂). And, it should be noted, there is a prescribed *šuʾila*-prayer to that star in the *Bīt salāʾ mê* cycle of prayers (see Ambos 2013: 164 \[x + 23ˊ\], which prescribes Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Kaksisa 4). But, Ninurta is also sometimes associated with Mercury in the first millennium (see Brown 2000: 56-57). And so it is at least possible that he is addressed in that astral form, too, during the night cycle of prayers. Unfortunately, as indicated on the note to NinNA1, rev. 7ˊ in the edition, the epigraphy in our one line of evidence is not clear just before it breaks off. The sign (or signs) after (what I take to be) BU is difficult to identify. And, we may have to posit a scribal omission of KUR/KUR₂ to arrive at *bukur*. Thus, at present there is not sufficient warrant to conflate Gud 1 with Ninurta 1, though the possibility should be kept in mind. Until future evidence indicates otherwise, the prayer is treated as a separate composition in [CASPo](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html).

name: Series of the Spider
intro:
The *Series of the Spider* is mentioned in the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([§0](/corpus/L/0/0)) as the work of a son of Šumu-libši, a scholar from the city of Eridu. Since the text is classified as a *Series*, it probably comprised more than one chapter: today only the first sixty-five lines of the first one are preserved. They contain a cosmogonic prologue and the first rounds of the disputation. The prologue narrates how the universe was created and populated with creatures; at an early point, Spider appears, proclaiming itself the most splendid of all animals. The god of wisdom, Ea, intervenes and, with a ruse well known from other Mesopotamian texts, creates two rivals (“two pipsqueaks,” perhaps two insects), whose mission is to take the boastful creature down a peg. The two creatures are given the exotic names *ḫamānīru* and *ešqapīzu*, both known only in this text. The *ešqapīzu* opens with a salvo celebrating its own qualities and condemning those of its rival. At several points, Spider intervenes, apparently as a referee in the dispute. Although the end of the text is missing, it could conceivably have ended with Spider eating both contenders.  
Two manuscripts of the text are known, both from 7ᵗʰ century BCE Assyria. The first (NinNA1) was found in Nineveh, the second (AššNA1) in the library of the “House of the Exorcist,” in Assur. The text is, however, probably an older composition, perhaps from the end of the second millennium BCE.  
The Nineve manuscript was first published by G. Smith in 1876 and it found great interest in the late 19ᵗʰ century because of its alleged parallels with *Gen*. 1. The Assur manuscript, the larger of the two, appeared in the first edition of the text (2017), which is closely followed here.

name: *šuʾila*s to Gula
intro: Werner Mayer lists five incantation-prayers directed to the goddess Gula in his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen* (Mayer 1976: 387; compare Kunstmann 1932: 89-90), Gula 1a, 1b, 2, 3, and 4. He includes two additional prayers in his list, Gula 5 and 6, but places these in square brackets, indicating that these prayers are, due to content and/or structure, either marginal to the incantation-prayer category or to be excluded entirely (see Mayer 1976: 375 for the meaning of his use of square brackets). Of the five incantation-prayers in his list, only three are labeled *šuʾila*-prayers (likewise, Frechette 2012: 255), Gula 1a, 1b, and 2. As of October 2026, these remain the only known Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Gula and, thus, are the only ones included in the [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online (CASPo)](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) project.Gula 1a and 1b are so numbered because they share a great many lines and phrases in common, so much so that Kunstmann described Gula 1b as a free variant of Gula 1a (1932: 90). (Note also the similarities in the first few lines of Gula 3 and Gula 1a. In fact, they may share the same opening line \[so Mayer 1976: 387\], though the only witness to Gula 3, LKA 20, breaks off in obv. 1 before the line’s end.) To my mind, there is no clear evidence at present for thinking one prayer derives from the other rather than both being derived from a common source. In fact, the matter is even more complicated, since there is one textual witness to Gula 1b (AššNA1) that varies so significantly from the others that it could be labeled Gula 1c, as I discuss below in the introduction to Gula 1b. The Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Bēlet-ilī 1 is introduced here with the textual witnesses to Gula 1a because the two prayers are nearly identical, except for the name of the divine addressee and a few other relatively minor differences, also discussed below.As the following specific introductions show, Gula 1a and 1b are well-attested prayers that were prescribed in two different, important royal rituals. Gula 2, on the other hand, is extremely fragmentary, hardly more than a stub of a prayer on present evidence.**Gula 1a and Bēlet-ilī 1**The Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Gula 1a is known from three Neo-Assyrian witnesses from Nineveh (NinNA1, NinNA2, NinNA3), one from Neo-Assyrian Ashur (AššNA1), one from Neo-Assyrian Ḫuzirina (HuzNA1), and one from Persian-period Babylonia (BabaPer1). All but NinNA2 and NinNA3, which are fragmentary, offer very full textual witnesses to the prayer, though none is entirely complete. Attesting almost the same text, save the divine name and a few minor differences (see Lenzi 2016: 77-88), are three manuscripts of Bēlet-ilī 1. Two are from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh, NinNA1 and NinNA2. The former preserves all the lines of the prayer, but not a single one is complete. The latter attests the first half of the prayer, but again none of the lines is preserved unbroken. In addition to these two Assyrian witnesses, Bēlet-ilī 1 is attested on one witness from Neo-Babylonian Sippar (SipNB1). Although its obverse is nearly complete, its [reverse](http://shuilas.org/P480756_big.jpg) is mostly illegible. Due to the many lines in common between Bēlet-ilī 1 and Gula 1a, the gaps in the text of Bēlet-ilī 1, especially near its conclusion, can be restored with confidence.The three best textual witnesses to Gula 1a, namely, AššNA1, NinNA1, and HuZNA1, bear a clear *šuʾila*-rubric. BabaPer1 breaks off just before the end of the prayer and thus does not provide positive evidence for the rubric. However, the one other *šuʾila*-prayer attested on this witness to its conclusion (Kakkabu 5) does bear a *šuʾila*-rubric in [rev. iiˊ 12ˊ](http://shuilas.org/P453575.html), strongly suggesting that the other *šuʾila*-prayers on this textual witness would have also had the same rubric attached to them. The same inference may be made of Gula 1a as attested on [NinNA3](http://shuilas.org/P397902.html): The final lines of Nabû 3 (1ˊ-5ˊ) and its *šuʾila*-rubric (6ˊ) precedes an incomplete Gula 1a (7ˊ-14ˊ \[break\]).Two textual witnesses to Bēlet-ilī 1 attest a rubric after the text of the prayer, NinNA1 and SipNB1, though neither clearly shows the rubric’s defining word, šu-il₂-la₂. In NinNA1, the rubric breaks off after ka-inim-ma. In SipNB1, the signs are so washed out that my reading of what I take to be the rubric in rev. 11a (\[ka-inim-m\]a^?^ ⸢šu^?^⸣-⸢i\[l₂^?^⸣-la₂^?^ ...\]) remains very uncertain. (The reading of this witness is only based on an old excavation photograph; collation in Istanbul has not yet been possible.) In any case, given the commonalities between the text of Gula 1a and Bēlet-ilī 1, the latter’s inclusion in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus is virtually assured.In terms of ritual uses of Gula 1a, there are several facts about which we can be certain. First, like Gula 1b, Gula 1a contains a line that suggests its use to counter the effects of an oracle and a dream that, the supplicant fears, portends evil. Line 13 (attested in all the textual witnesses except the fragmentary NinNA3) reads, “on account of an oracle (*bīru*) and a dream (*šuttu*) that are hounding me” (compare Gula 1b, line 15, where the nouns appear in the opposite order). Second, two manuscripts, HuzNA1 and NinNA1, include rather typical ritual instructions (see Frechette 2012: 243) after the prayer and its rubric (see lines 27-28 in the present edition). Interestingly, only Gula 1a among the many other *šuʾila*-prayers included on NinNA1 (see just below) has ritual instructions attached to it. Third, Gula 1a is a prescribed recitation in the royal ritual *Bīt salāʾ mê*, according to both versions of its Ritual Tablet (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 48\], 164 \[x + 20ˊ (= C 20ˊ)\], and 175; Frechette 2012: 168, 169, 170, s.v. 7, 255). In fact, NinNA1 presents a series of *šuʾila*-prayers, including Anu 1, Nusku 3, Sîn 3, Gula 1a, Šamaš 1, and the catchline to Papsukkal 1, that follows the order of prescribed *šuʾila*-prayers in an Assyrian version of the night cycle (see Ambos 2013: 203 and 162, lines B₂ 44-B₂ 50), suggesting it is a tablet of *recitanda* for that series. Indeed, Ambos has labeled NinNA1 the ninth *pirsu* of the series (2013: 203), based on the fact that the catchline for Anu 1 appears on K.2396+, rev. 33 just before the colophon, which labels the tablet the eighth *pirsu* of *Bīt salāʾ mê*. BabaPer1 is also a *recitanda* tablet of the same royal ritual, as its colophon explicitly states in rev. iiˊ 14ˊ: IM.DUB.3.KAM^v^ E₂ *sa-la me-e* EŠ₂.GAR₃ *a-ši-pu*₂-*tu* NU A\[L\].TIL, “The third tablet of *Bīt salāʾ mê*, an exorcism series. Not finished.” Yet the order of the prayers on the tablet do not conform to either Ritual Tablet’s prescriptions of prayers. For a fuller discussion of this particular issue, see my [introduction to Adad 1a](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/1) and the remarks on the textual witness labeled BabaPer1 there (as here). Two other textual witnesses provide evidence that associates Gula 1a with another Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer, perhaps implying their ritual use together. HuzNA1 presents Sîn 3 on its obverse (with ritual instructions) and Gula 1a on its reverse (with ritual instructions). NinNA3, as mentioned above, attests the final lines of Nabû 3 and then the opening lines of Gula 1a. The order of presentation on HuzNA1 puts its two prayers in the same order as is prescribed in *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see above with regard to NinNA1), perhaps suggesting a connection to that royal ritual. Explaining the placement of Nabû 3 before Gula 1a on NinNA3 is difficult at present. NinNA3, as of October 2026, is the only [textual witness to Nabû 3](http://shuilas.org/Q006123.html) that associates that prayer with a text other than another Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Nabu. NinNA2 may attest the final line of an Akkadian incantation- or *šuʾila*-prayer and its rubric before the text of Gula 1a begins in line 3ˊ. But the identification of this prayer, if in fact it is one (there are only three signs on the two lines in question!), is unclear.The ritual use of Bēlet-ilī 1 must be inferred from the prayer itself and what little we know about its textual associations. All the textual witnesses to Bēlet-ilī 1 show the insertion of an *attalû*-formula, along with other formulaic phrases, in the prayer, indicating the prayer’s ritual use to dispel the evil of a lunar eclipse (see Frechette 2012: 193). (None of the textual witnesses to Gula 1a has such formulaic insertions!) Each witness places the formulaic insertion(s) in a slightly different place in the prayer. SipNB1 includes a customized self-introductory formula for Shamash-shuma-ukin (vassal king of Babylon, 667-648 BCE, under Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, his brother), an *attalû*-formula, a lament, and a petition to keep the evil from approaching in lines 9a-9h of the present edition. This witness may also include ritual instructions in lines 26-27 that are similar to those attached to Gula 1a, lines 27-28, though abrasion on the tablet makes this reading uncertain. NinNA1 inserts an *attalû*-formula in lines 12a-12c. NinNA2 includes a generic self-introductory formula and inserts an *attalû*-formula in lines 13a-13c. Despite their insertion of the *attalû*-formula, SipNB1 and NinNA2 also include line 13 of the prayer (see also line 13 of Gula 1a), in which the supplicant indicates that an (evil) oracle and dream have weighed him down. NinNA1 skips the line. What we can learn about the prayer’s ritual use on the basis of textual association is disappointing. Only NinNA1 provides evidence, the contents of which is as follows: Nabû 6 (obv. 1ʹ-7ʹ), rubric (obv. 8ʹ), Bēlet-ilī 1 (obv. 9ʹ-32ʹ), rubric (obv. 33ʹ), Išḫara 1 (rev. 1-30 \[break\]). How these texts might have been used together, i.e., in a ritual, if at all, is unclear.The differences between Gula 1a and Bēlet-ilī 1, aside from the obvious divine name change, are rather minor (see Lenzi 2016: 77-88). In line 7 of both prayers, the three manuscripts attesting the line in Gula 1a use the adjective *šurbūtu* to describe the goddess rather than *šaqūtu*, as in all three manuscripts attesting the line in Bēlet-ilī 1. Note, however, that two manuscripts of Gula 1a show *šaqūtu* as a variant, thus agreeing with Bēlet-ilī 1. In line 9 of both prayers, Gula 1a has the supplicant say *kâši asḫurki*, “I turn to you,” whereas Bēlet-ilī 1 reads *kâši atkalki*, “I trust in you,” a phrase that also occurs in Gula 1b, line 10. The first line of each prayer may also have differed, though such a (tentative) conclusion can only be reached at present via inference from the size of breaks in the textual witnesses. The manuscript NinNA2 for Bēlet-ilī 1 does not have room in the break at the end of line 1 (NinNA2, obv. 1) for the phrase *āšibat šamê ellūti*, which occurs at the end of Gula 1a, line 1. The same may be true for the break in Bēlet-ilī’s witness NinNA1 (obv. 9ˊ), though the matter is more difficult to assess because the break is so large. In any case, at present we do not have positive evidence for the inclusion of the celestial description of the goddess in the opening line of Bēlet-ilī 1, and we have some epigraphic basis for thinking it might have been excluded, at least in one witness. A more significant difference between the two prayers is the absence of Gula 1a, line 14 (*palḫākū-ma ātanamdar*, “I am afraid and continually anxious”) in all three textual witnesses to Bēlet-ilī 1. (One textual witness to Gula 1a, NinNA2, also leaves the line out.) Accounting for this exclusion in Bēlet-ilī 1 is likely entangled with the various insertions of formulaic phrases in the textual witnesses of Bēlet-ilī 1 (discussed above). But those insertions did not *require* the line’s exclusion, if Gula 1b is any indicator. Line 16 of Gula 1b expresses the supplicant’s fear in a similar manner as the excluded line, and Gula 1b, line 16 occurs just after the insertion of an *attalû*-formula (see lines 15a-15c) in the four witnesses attesting this part of the prayer.**Gula 1b**The Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Gula 1b is known from eight Neo-Assyrian witnesses from Nineveh and one from Ashur. Although the number of Ninevite manuscripts seems high, most of them are very small fragments, offering nothing more than a small number of incomplete lines (NinNA4, NinNA5 \[which is so small that it may not be a textual witness at all!\], NinNA6, NinNA7, and NinNA8). Both NinNA2 and NinNA3, which are larger fragments, attest about two-thirds of the prayer’s lines, but none of the attested lines is complete. It is possible that future joins will show that some of these Ninevite fragments belong to the same original tablet(s). NinNA1 is our best textual witness to Gula 1b—from Nineveh or anywhere, but it provides no evidence for lines 24-31 of the prayer. The one witness from Ashur, AššNA1, has a “landscape” rather than “portrait” format. The tablet is now kept in the Arkeoloji Müzeleri in Istanbul. The use of this tablet in the present edition is only based on the excavation photo PhAss 3982, made available to me thanks to the staff at the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin, and Mayer’s transliteration (1976: 455-456). The text on this witness follows Gula 1b, lines 1-9 in obv. 1-10, but it then diverges significantly from the other textual witnesses in its obv. 11-12 and rev. 1-7. In these lines, the goddess is once addressed by the name Baba (line 13ˊ), and the supplicant complains twice about an illness (lines 10ˊ and 15ˊ). These lines are so different from the other textual witnesses to Gula 1b that they are treated separately in the edition, numbered lines 10ˊ-17ˊ. One wonders if, in fact, AššNA1 should be treated as a textual witness to a Gula 1c. In any case, this witness certainly complicates understanding the relationship(s) of the textual witnesses to the tangle of prayers categorized under the label “Gula 1.” The Persian-period fragment from Dilbat also contributes to these complications.DilPer1 is not an actual textual witness to an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Gula at all; rather, it offers several parallels to lines in both Gula 1a and Gula 1b, especially their opening lines. Because DilPer1, line 14ˊ parallels Gula 1b, line 7, which is absent in Gula 1a, I include the text of DilPer1 in the “Unplaced Lines” sections of this page under “Chapter 1b,” *viz.*, Gula 1b. This tablet illustrates the formulaic, “mash-up” nature of the prayers as compositions and suggests that positing simple textual geneaological relationships between prayers may be overly simplistic. As mentioned in the [introduction to the prayers to Ea](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/6), the textual witnesses at our disposal for the reconstruction of the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers provide evidence of a more complicated relationship and history than is reflected in our modern taxonomy.Three Ninevite fragments, NinNA2, NinNA3, and NinNA8, bear witness to the prayer’s rubric, though all are incomplete and only one (NinNA3, obv. 22ˊ) provides clear, if also only partial evidence for a *šuʾila*-rubric: ⸢ka⸣-inim-ma šu-\[il₂-la₂ ...\]. Although the rubric to Gula 1b is not preserved in NinNA1, the conclusion to two other *šuʾila*-prayers are preserved on this [textual witness](http://shuilas.org/P397492.html) and they both have a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to them (Ea 1b in obv. 8ˊ and Ninurta 1 in rev. 9ˊ). Thus, it is likely that Gula 1b would also have had the rubric attached to its text in this textual witness. AššNA1, which bears witness to the text of the prayer all the way to its end and is blank for several lines after the prayer’s conclusion, does not attach a rubric, *šuʾila* or otherwise, to its version of the prayer.In terms of ritual uses of Gula 1b, there are four facts about which we can be certain. First, like Gula 1a (see line 13), Gula 1b contains a line that suggests its use to counter the effects of a dream or an oracle that, the supplicant fears, portends evil. Line 15 (attested in NinNA1, NinNA2, and NinNA3) reads, “on account of a dream (*šuttu*) and an oracle (*bīru*) that are hounding me.” Second, NinNA1, NinNA2, NinNA3, and NinNA6 show evidence of the insertion of an *attalû*-formula into the prayer (see lines 15a-15c), indicating the prayer was also used to counter the specific evil associated with a lunar eclipse (see Frechette 2012: 193). Third, the prayer is prescribed in the royal ritual *Bīt rimki* (see Ritual Tablet, line 220 \[= A o iii 64\]; Schwemer 2019: 56, 76; Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25). And fourth, two manuscripts, NinNA2 and NinNA8, preserve evidence of ritual instructions after the prayer and its rubric, which proves the prayer was sometimes transmitted with its own ritual instructions, though we can say almost nothing more about that ritual use, given how fragmentary these lines (and witnesses) are.The textual associations on the witnesses to Gula 1b may also point to the prayer’s ritual use in *Bīt rimki*, though this conclusion is not always certain or without complication. AššNA1, which is almost a complete tablet, only bears the text of Gula 1b (without rubric and without ritual instructions) and thus provides no evidence for textual associations. NinNA2, NinNA6, NinNA7, and NinNA8 also only bear the text of Gula 1b but are so fragmentary that this fact has no evidentiary value for the matter under discussion. (Note, however, that NinNA2 and NinNA8, as mentioned previously, do attest ritual instructions.) NinNA4 and NinNA5 are also mere fragments, but the text they bear shows a transition from one prayer to another. The identifications of the two texts involved are uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of the witnesses and the relevant lines. If the identifications hold, we have in both witnesses the ending of Ninurta 1 and the beginning of Gula 1b. And thus, these two fragments may present the two prayers in the same order as prescribed in the Ninevite *Bīt rimki* Ritual Tablet, lines 218 and 220 (= A o iii 62, 64; see Schwemer 2019: 56, 76; Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25). Perhaps future joins will confirm this interpretation. But, there are many uncertainties here, and the possibility of circular reasoning should not be dismissed too readily. The order of prayers on NinNA3, namely, Gula 1b in lines 1ˊ-22ˊ and Sîn 1 in line 23ˊ (with no intervening ritual instructions between the two), may indicate that this textual witness also bears *recitanda* for the same series (see the Ninevite Ritual Tablet, lines 220, 222 = A o iii 64, 66). Finally, there is NinNA1, which attests parts of four Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, Ea 1b (obv. 1ˊ-7ˊ with *šuʾila*-rubric in obv. 8ˊ), Damkina 1 (obv. 9ˊ-29ˊ \[break\]), Ninurta 1 (rev. 1ˊ-8ˊ with *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 9ˊ), and Gula 1b (rev. 10ˊ-36ˊ \[break\]). The last three prayers follow the order prescribed in the Ninevite Ritual Tablet of *Bīt rimki*, but matters are complicated by the presence of Ea 1b. See [the introduction to Ea 1b](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/6) for my discussion of the issues.**Gula 2**There is only one textual witness to the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer labeled Gula 2, a small Neo-Assyrian fragment from Nineveh. The fragment attests three legible but incomplete lines (2ˊ-4ˊ) before a single ruling and a fragmentary *šuʾila*-rubric (5ˊ). One line of standard ritual instructions follows in line 6ˊ, which is set off by single rulings from the rubric and line 7ˊ. The tops of a few signs in line 7ˊ indicate that another text followed Gula 2. But that text remains unidentified for now. Nothing more is known of Gula 2 for want of evidence.

name: Palm and Vine
intro:
*Palm and Vine* is a disputation poem between two litigants, Palm (designated by the rare name *arḫānû*) and Vine (Akkadian *karānu*), each of which praises its own merits and many uses, and discredits those of its rival. Fifty-four lines from the middle section of the text are preserved, which begin *in medias res* with a long speech of Palm, immediately followed by Vine’s rejoinder. Three library manuscripts of the poem are known, as well as an excerpt on a peculiar school tablet.  
The three library manuscripts, and perhaps also the school tablet, stem from Achaemenid or Hellenistic Uruk. Internal evidence, however, suggests that the poem is not a Hellenistic composition, but an older text preserved only in later manuscripts. That the text should have found echo only in one southern city is perhaps explicable if one considers that the palm is the most iconic tree in southern Babylonia. Vines, by contrast, are not native to the Uruk area: to Mesopotamian ears, a dispute between a palm and a vine (or between date beer and wine) may have sounded like a debate between the South and the North, or between native and imported produce.  
*Palm and Vine* is not mentioned in any ancient catalogue, which may suggest that it was part of a longer series, perhaps the *Series of the Poplar* ([§II.8](/corpus/L/2/8)), under which name it would have been booked by ancient librarians. The first manuscript of the text (MS UrkHel3 – a damaged tablet riddled with corruptions) was published in the 1990s; the text itself was first published in 2017, and a new manuscript came to light a year later. The present edition follows the *editio princeps* closely, but includes also a few small improvements.

name: Story of the Poor, Forlorn Wren
intro:
The minute bird called *diqdiqqu* or *duqduqqu* (“wren”) in Akkadian is a bird of proverbial small size and great ambitions. The *Story of the Poor, Forlorn Wren* describes his conflict with Eagle – paragon of pride – resolved by the Sun God.  
The opening lines represent Eagle nesting on top of a mountain, and Wren in the more humble abode of a “mountain plant.” Wren, described as “poor, forlorn” (epithets reminiscent of those given to Gimil-Ninurta in *Poor Man of Nippur*, [§I.11](/corpus/L/1/11)), is apparently prevented by Eagle from going out to feed himself, for which reason he demands justice from the Sun God. Wren concedes that “my size may be small” – after all, he is called the “one-shekel bird,” i.e., the bird who weighs only 8 grams –, but contends that he should still be allowed to subsist. The Sun God apparently punishes Eagle for its pride, whereupon Wren exhorts the “birds from the mountain and the plain” to sing the god’s praises for making him an equal to Eagle. Eagle should never boast again of the loftiness of its nesting sites, nor should Wren be ashamed of his humble abode. The poem ends with a short epimythium: the beloved of Marduk alone is allowed to nest and raise his progeny.  
The text appears to be a late composition, perhaps from the second half of the first millennium BCE. It is preserved in three library manuscripts from Babylon: one of them, MS BabPar1, dated to 69 BCE, is one of the latest datable cuneiform literary texts. In addition, two excerpts of the fable on school tablets from Babylon and Nippur are known, which shows that its celebration of the ways of the humble found the favor of the Mesopotamian pedagogues.  
The first edition of this text, still riddled with lacunas, was published in 2017.
