name: *šuʾila*s to Ištar
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identified thirteen of twenty-nine prayers directed to the goddess Ishtar as either a *šuʾila*-prayer by virtue of the presence of the *šuʾila*-rubric—his nos. 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 23—or a likely member of that class by virtue of other criteria—his nos. 3, 6, and 10, with a question mark on his nos. 11 and 12 (see Mayer 1976: 388-393; compare Kunstmann 1932: 90-94). Although Mayer excluded Ištar 13 from the corpus of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, likely because of the compound rubric in one of its textual witnesses (see below), the current project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) (CASPo), counts it within the corpus (see likewise, Zgoll 2003: 287-288 and Frechette 2012: 258). The project follows Mayer in excluding from the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus Ištar 21, an incantation-prayer directed to Kilili (i.e., Ishtar), though the ritual instructions direct the supplicant to lift his hands before its recitation (see Farber 1977: 28 for the point and pp. 57-58, lines 21-40 for the relevant text). The textual witnesses to Ištar 21 lack a *šuʾila*-rubric and the prayer itself does not show typical literary characteristics of an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer (see Frechette 2012: 219-220 for a discussion). In the fifty years since Mayer’s work, two other *šuʾila*-prayers have come to light, Ištar 30 and Ištar 31 (for the former, see already Mayer 1990: 270; for both texts as members of the corpus, see Zgoll 2003: 23-24 and Frechette 2012: 258). Also, the *Gebetsbeschwörungen* that Mayer identified as Ištar 18, known only by its incipit, has been reassigned to Ninlil (see Ambos 2013: 228 and Frechette 2012: 125). CASPo treats this text as the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer [Ninlil 5] (http://shuilas.org/prayers.html). Many witnesses to the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ishtar indicate that the prayers were accompanied by ritual actions of various kinds, though it is not always possible to identify the broader purpose of these rituals or to associate the texts with a particular ritual series. The following specific introductions will consider each prayer on a case by case basis.Zgoll edits all the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ishtar (2003) except Ištar 6, 11, and 12, and she offers close readings of Ištar 1, 2, 8, 10, and 23 that shed important exegetical and thematic light on the prayers. Her work has been foundational for CASPo and is essential for serious students of the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ishtar (and Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers in general).**Ištar 1**Ištar 1 is a very well-attested prayer with eleven first-millennium manuscripts in total. There are six Neo-Assyrian manuscripts, five from Nineveh (NinNA1, NinNA2, NinNA3, NinNA4, and NinNA5) and one from Ashur (AššNA1). NinNA3, however, only attests the incipt as a catchline, and NinNA5 preserves a mere seven, fragmentary lines of the prayer. There are five Late Babylonian manuscripts, two from Sippar (SipLB1 and SipLB2) and three from Babylon (BabLB1, BabLB2, BabLB3). BabLB1 offers only sixteen fragmentary lines. The obverse of BabLB2 attests half as many (the text on the reverse remains unidentified); likewise, the only preserved surface of BabLB3.Four textual witnesses provide evidence for a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to the prayer, though only two of these offer unambiguous support: NinNA1, rev. 20a and SipLB1, rev. 8ˊ. In SipLB2, rev. 19ˊ the operative word in the rubric, *šuʾila*, must be restored. In AššNA1, l.e. 2 (see line 30ˊ), the presence of the same word, the only word preserved on the line, is uncertain due to an abraded surface. If the reading is correct and this is the prayer’s rubric, it appears after less than thirty lines of text. A line of ritual instructions, set off by rule lines, follows this line (line 31ˊ in the edition), and then an unidentified text begins, occupying the entire (very fragmentary) reverse. This evidence makes it virtually certain that the prayer in its one witness from Ashur was substantially shorter than the prayer on some other witnesses. Although the rubric is not attested on NinNA4 (because the prayer breaks off before its end), it is quite likely that the *šuʾila*-rubric was originally included with the prayer since the *šuʾila*-prayers before (Sîn 1) and after it (Tašmetu 1) on the tablet bear such a rubric; see [obv. 28 and rev. 17ˊ](http://shuilas.org/P393771.html). For NinNA2 also the gap in rev. 22 may have contained a *šuʾila*-rubric before the ritual instructions on the same line. There is plenty of room for it.Although several witnesses only contain evidence for Ištar 1, in most cases due to their fragmentary condition (NinNA5, SipLB2, BabLB1, and BabLB3; NinNA2 is the exception), the other witnesses place Ištar 1 in relation with other Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers, and two of these also provide series information. [NinNA4](http://shuilas.org/P393771.html) is the best example of a tablet containing *recitanda* matching a series’s ritual prescriptions. Sîn 1 occupies obv. 1-28, followed by Ištar 1 in obv. 29-35, after which the tablet breaks off. The text resumes on the reverse with Tašmetu 1 (rev. 1ˊ-17ˊ) and then the incipit of Madanu 1 is inscribed as the tablet’s catchline in rev. 18ˊ. This is followed by series information for *Bīt rimki* (rev. 19aˊ) and the attachment of an Ashurbanipal colophon (rev. 19bˊ-26ˊ). The series information reads: ⸢DUB⸣.<x>.KAM\* E₂ *rim-ki*, “the <N^th^> tablet of *Bīt rimki*.” If we take into account the break, in which Nabu 2 has been entirely lost, NinNA4 attests the precise order for these prayers as prescribed in the Ritual Tablet for the series (see Schwemer 2019: 58 and 76, lines 222-230 and Frechette 2012: 178). (Note: Although the lines 230-231 direct the ritual to Nusku, the incipit cited there is identical to that for the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Madanu 1; see Mayer 1976: 406 and Frechette 2012: 170, 178, 267, 259). Similarly, the arrangement of Sîn 1 (obv. 1-29, rev. 1-8) followed by the incipit to Ištar 1 as catchline (rev. 9) on [NinNA3](http://shuilas.org/P394701.html) suggests this textual witness is also following the prescribed order of the *Bīt rimki* Ritual Tablet, though it bears no series information in its colophon. On the other end of the spectrum, [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P397497.html) is the best example of a tablet containing *recitanda* and *not* matching any known prescriptions for the series it names. The series information preserved on NinNA1 identifies its four prayers as 8*-u*₂ *pir-su* E₂ *sa-la me-e*, “the 8^th^ *pirsu* of the series *Bīt salāʾ mê*” (rev. 34a). The prayers are ordered as follows: Madanu 1 (obv. 1-27), Ištar 1 (obv. 28-46, rev. 1-21), Zappu 1 (rev. 22-32), and Anu 1 (rev. 33, where the incipit is the tablet’s catchline). Unfortunately, none of the textual witnesses for the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (in any recension) prescribes these prayers in this order (see Ambos 2013: 174-175). (*Nota bene:* The order of prayers varies in the different recensions of the Ritual Tablet.) Ištar 1 is, however, prescribed in one version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet, though in this case the prayer is addressed to ^mul^*Dilbat*, the goddess’s celestial form as the planet Venus (Ambos 2013: 165, x + 28ˊ \[= A₁ iii 17ˊ; D 6ˊˊa\]; Frechette 2012: 169). This prescribed prayer is preceded and followed by different prescribed prayers than those that appear before and after Ištar 1 on NinNA1. With SipLB1, AššNA1, and BabLB2, the placement of Ištar 1 in relation to another prayer remains difficult to explain. The incipit to an otherwise unknown incantation-prayer to the Great Gods occurs as the catchline on [SipLB1](http://shuilas.org/P480768.html) after Ištar 1 (see rev. 11ˊ; the prayer is to be added to Mayer’s catalog as *ilū rabûtu* 5; 1976: 427). The text that follows Ištar 1 on [AššNA1](http://shuilas.org/P369214.html) and the one that occurs on the reverse of [BabLB2](http://shuilas.org/P564266.html) remain unidentified.**Ištar 2**Ištar 2 is the longest Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer in the corpus. (Ištar 13 may have been similar in length, though current evidence does not allow firm conclusions. See the introduction to that prayer below.) Ištar 2 is attested on twelve first-millennium manuscripts. Although there are eight Neo-Assyrian manuscripts, five from Nineveh (NinNA1, NinNA2, NinNA3, NinNA4, and NinNA5), two from Ashur (AššNA1 and AššNA2), and one from Kalḫu (KalNA1), they are but fragments. The same is true of the Late Babylonian witnesses BabaLB1, BabLB2, and BabLB3. The prayer’s main textual witness is another Late Babylonian manuscript, BabLB1, which preserves the entire text on a [beautifully inscribed tablet](http://shuilas.org/P208501_big.jpg). According to its colophon (see rev. 56-57), this tablet was deposited in Marduk’s Esagil temple in Babylon as a votive offering. In several places, BabLB1 is the only witness to the text of the prayer. BabLB1 is also the only witness that provides clear evidence for a *šuʾila*-rubric (see rev. 50). In terms of associating Ištar 2 with other texts, BabLB1 is one of only two witnesses that provides evidence. BabLB1 connects Ištar 2 to Ištar 3, the incipit of which appears as the tablet’s catchline (see rev. 55). The other relevant witness, BabLB3, bears lines of an incantation-prayer directed to Kilili (= Ištar 21) on its reverse (compare Farber 1977: 57, lines 23-26). That incantation-prayer is prescribed in a long ritual discussed in the introduction to Ištar 23 below. None of the witnesses provides clear information about the prayer’s use in a larger ritual complex or series. Although both BabLB1 and NinNA5 attest to the ritual instructions associated with the prayer, these instructions do not provide a stated purpose for the ritual, which must be inferred from the text of the prayer itself. Frechette argues that Ištar 2 is part of an anti-witchcraft ritual based on the mention of witchcraft in the prayer (see line 55) as well as the similarities between the ritual instructions attached to the prayer and those attached to Ištar 13, which is clearly an anti-witchcraft ritual. Frechette thinks the ritual instructions for Ištar 2 may have been a shorter version of those for Ištar 13 (see Frechette 2012: 208-212).Ištar 2 is also one of only a few *šuʾila*-prayers (so far) in the CASPo project that is attested in a second-millennium witness; see HatHit1. For other examples, see Adad 1a [here](http://shuilas.org/Q006052.html) and [here](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/1) and Ištar 10 (below). The version of the prayer attested on this witness shows numerous variants from the first-millennium version of Ištar 2 and diverges significantly at the prayer’s conclusion. This version of the prayer may also be shorter than the first-millennium version, if the accepted understanding of the relationship between the manuscript’s several fragments is correct. HatHit1 might have attached a *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer, but the evidence is inconclusive. The opening three signs are mostly restored, \[KA-INIM\]-⸢MA^?^⸣, and though there is a long blank space after them on the tablet, there may be room for other components of the *šuʾila*-rubric in the break. Without more evidence, however, caution is in order (see likewise Frechette 2012: 162). No ritual instructions are attached to the prayer. Although there are a few very fragmentary lines on HatHit1 that do not belong to Ištar 2 (separated by rulings and column lines), thereby indicating the prayer’s association with other texts, the compositions to which these lines belong have not yet been identified.**Ištar 3**Aside from the prayer’s incipit appearing as a catchline in BabLB1, rev. 55 (see Ištar 2 above), the main textual witness to Ištar 3 comes from Achaemenid Uruk, UrkPer1, which provides evidence of a *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 3. After a few lines of ritual instructions, rev. 7b-8 (see lines 28b-29 in the present edition) give the prayer’s ritual purpose, namely, to turn aside divine anger. The anger seems to belong to Ishtar (see lines 6-7) since angry personal deities are not mentioned in the prayer. (Note, however, that the supplicant does wish their god or goddess to walk along side in line 16, perhaps implying their previous absence.) The divine anger has manifested itself as slander and defamation against the supplicant (see lines 11-15).UrkPer1 only bears the text of Ištar 3. As noted by Robson (2019: 232, 250 n.133), the tablet may have been copied for practical use. In terms of associations with other texts, as mentioned above, the incipit of Ištar 3 appears as a catchline on the best textual witness to Ištar 2 (BabLB1 = BM.26187). According to its colophon (see rev. 56-57), this tablet was deposited in Marduk’s Esagil temple in Babylon as a votive offering.**Ištar 4**Ištar 4 is attested in only four fragmentary witnesses, all from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh. One of these witnesses, NinNA3, only attests a few fragmentary lines of the ritual instructions and then perhaps gives the incipit for Ištar 6. The basis for its being considered a witness to Ištar 4 is slim and thus tentative. NinNA2 preserves some material of the actual prayer (see lines 1ˊ-14ˊ), but none of these lines is complete. NinNA4 is even more fragmentary, attesting only a dozen unbroken signs over seven incomplete lines. Remarkably, one of the broken signs at the end of its line 3ˊ provides the most likely reading for the end of line 17ˊ in this edition. NinNA1 is the fullest witness to the text, providing evidence for its most distinctive feature, a petition for the supplicant to conceive and give birth to a healthy child. Line 19ˊ reads: *šurkī-ma šuma u zēra lū rēmu silītī lušāpâ zikirk*\[*i*\], “Give me a child and heir (lit. a name and a seed). May my womb be a *sound* womb that I may glorify you\[r\] name.” For a discussion of this theme (also in relation to Ištar 23), see Zgoll 2003: 169-177.NinNA1 is the only witness that bears the *šuʾila*-rubric with this prayer (see rev. 1). After the ritual instructions, both NinNA1 and NinNA3 give the incipit of another prayer (see NinNA1, rev. 12 and NinNA3, 5ˊ). In NinNA1, the incipit is the tablet’s catchline and belongs to Ištar 6. In NinNA3, the incipit may belong to Ištar 6, too, though, if this is the case, the incipit varies from the other two witnesses attesting to it. See the introduction to Ištar 6 below. NinNA1 is of further interest in that rev. 13, just after the catchline and before the Ashurbanipal colophon (rev. 14-15), hints at a long ritual series to which the tablet belonged. The fragmentary line reads: DUB 1.ME 34.KAM\* EN₂ ⸢*ur*^?^⸣-\[...\], “134^th^ tablet of incantations *in the series Ur*^?^-\[. . .\]” (differently, Beaulieu and Mayer 1997: 177, who imply the tablet belongs to a series of *šuʾila*-prayers). Unfortunately, the series remains uncertain.**Ištar 5**The text of Ištar 5 is very poorly known. One Neo-Assyrian textual witness (NinNA1) preserves five fragmentary lines of the prayer at its conclusion. This prayer’s unusual final line is its most distinctive feature. It reads: *ina pušqi u dannati šūzibī*\[*nni dalīlīk*\]*i ludlul*, “Deliver m\[e\] from this difficulty and hardship, that I may sing \[yo\]ur \[praises\]” (6ˊ). A *šuʾila*-rubric and then three well-preserved lines of ritual instructions follow the text of the prayer. The divine addressee in the rubric is not named Ishtar; rather, she is identified with the epithet *Bēlet-šamê*. The general purpose of the ritual is tagged onto the final line of ritual instructions: *eṭēra u gimilta kunni*, “*The ritual is* for establishing deliverance and favorable treatment.” In terms of associated texts, the initial line of Ištar 6 occurs after the textual material associated with Ištar 5 on the final line of the obverse of the prayer’s sole textual witness.**Ištar 6**Ištar 6 is only known by its incipit. According to the combined evidence of two Neo-Assyrian witnesses from Nineveh (NinNA1, rev. 12 and NinNA3, obv. 11ˊ), the line reads: *ilti igigî bukrat sîn telītu*, “goddess of the Igigi, most capable daughter of Sin.” NinNA2, obv. 5ˊ attests a similar incipit; its mostly restored text reads: \[*ilti igigî bukra*\]*t an*\[*unnakī* ...\], “\[Goddess of the Igigi, . . . daugh\]ter of the An\[unnaki\].” If this is evidence for the incipit of Ištar 6, it is also evidence that its incipit varies among textual witnesses. Or, it may be evidence of a scribal error in writing the incipit, since one can easily imagine that the typical pairing of the Igigi and Anunnaki could have led a scribe to change *bukrat sîn* to *bukrat anunnakī* almost without thinking. Although we only know the incipit of the prayer, it seems reasonable to include the prayer in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer corpus since one of its witnesses, NinNA1 (= K.3448), includes a *šuʾila*-rubric for the prayer that precedes it, Ištar 4. (In NinNA1, the incipit to Ištar 6 serves as the tablet’s catchline.) If the identification of the ritual instructions on NinNA2 (= Sm.882) are those that accompany Ištar 4 (see the introduction to that prayer above, where Ištar 4’s witness NinNA3 = [Sm.882](http://shuilas.org/P425646.html) = Ištar 6’s NinNA2), then a second textual witness shows the incipit to Ištar 6 following Ištar 4. (But note, as mentioned just above, that this incipit may attest a variant or mistake in the wording.) In NinNA3, the incipit is preceded by the text and ritual instructions for Ištar 5. At this time, we have no further information about Ištar 6 or its ritual use.**Ištar 7**Ištar 7 is known only from one Neo-Assyrian witness from Nineveh (NinNA1). The prayer’s *recitanda* is entirely broken away on this witness, save for the last broken sign of the last line. If the reading of that sign is correct (⸢*bu*⸣), the last line of the prayer may have read \[*ilū rabûtu libbaki liṭib*\]*bū*, “may the great gods make your heart glad,” which is also the final line of Ištar 1 (see line 44). After this broken line, there is a partially restored *šuʾila*-rubric and some broken ritual instructions. The ritual instructions indicate the prayer’s purpose was to reconcile a supplicant with their personal deities (see lines 4ˊb-5ˊ). The small differences between these ritual instructions and those attached to Ištar 1 are the basis for distinguishing the two prayers (for now). Another prayer to the goddess, Ištar 8, follows Ištar 7 on this only witness.**Ištar 8**Only one Neo-Assyrian textual witness from Nineveh is available to reconstruct Ištar 8 (NinNA1), and this witness preserves little more than the prayer’s opening hymnic material. Maul and Strauß (2011: 20, 111-112) suggest that their KAL 4, no. 57 (from Neo-Assyrian Ashur) is also a witness to Ištar 8, but this fragment shows hardly any parallels to that prayer and many significant deviations from it. Frechette catalogs the same fragment with Ištar 10 (2012: 257), which seems to be an error based on his classification of [Si.59](http://shuilas.org/P480760.html). I think it best to treat [KAL 4, no. 57](http://shuilas.org/P480749.html) as an entirely different and new prayer to Ishtar, which may or may not be an Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer. The fragment is not edited here as part of Ištar 8, though it is listed as an “uncertain fragment.” Ištar 8 is accepted into the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer corpus primarily on the basis that the prayer opens with extensive praise and it is preceded in its sole textual witness by Ištar 7, which has a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to it. In addition, Zgoll has noted several echoes with Ištar 1, 2, and 10 (all *šuʾila*-prayers) in her exposition of the prayer (2003: 241-246). She speculates that the main concern in Ištar 8 may already be hinted at in line 6: To restore the supplicant’s dispersed family, a concern also expressed in Ištar 2 (246). Other than its association with Ištar 7 on its one textual witness, we have no further information about the ritual use of Ištar 8.**Ištar 9**The text of Ištar 9 is very poorly known. One textual witness from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh preserves three fragmentary lines of the prayer at its very conclusion. A partially restored *šuʾila*-rubric (line 4ˊ) and one line of very basic ritual instructions (line 5ˊ) follow. In terms of associated texts, a dozen lines from the beginning of Ištar 10 are inscribed after the textual material associated with Ištar 9 on this one witness.**Ištar 10**Ištar 10 is attested on six textual witnesses, five of which are from first millennium sites: two from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh (NinNA1 and NinNA2), one from seventh-century Sippar (SipNA1, see rev. 10ˊ, where king Shamash-shumu-ukin is named), one from Persian period Uruk (UrkPer1), and one from late period Babylon (BabLB1). The witnesses from Nineveh are quite small fragments, each bearing only about a dozen fragmentary lines of the prayer. BabLB1 also preserves very little text and is badly abraded, making its use of limited value (though see lines 22 and 24 in this edition). SipNA1 attests more than half of the text as compared to UrkPer1, but it must be used with caution as presented here because the tablet remains unpublished and still only available via Geers’s copy (see Heft AC, 14-16; see likewise Zgoll 2003: 107). Thankfully, the witness from Uruk is nearly complete, providing the main textual basis for Ištar 10; what little is lost can reasonably be restored. Unfortunately, as of late 2025, UrkPer1, held in the National Museum of Iraq (in Baghdad), could not be collated for this project (in person or from photographs). The sixth witness, Unc1, first published by Zgoll (2003: 109-114 with a copy from the hand of Claus Wilcke on p. 108), may be from the area of Emar and date back into the second millennium. The tablet lines on this witness do not correspond clearly with the poetic lines of the prayer’s text (as known in the other witnesses), and thus it is not always clear what the witness may have left out in lines 1-31. Although the other textual witnesses attest to a number of variations in the text of Ištar 10, Unc1, held in the Archäologische Staatssammlung Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte (in Munich), differs significantly, especially after line 32 of the present edition. Its conclusion is treated separately from the other witnesses (see lines 33ˊ-45ˊ). I thank Dr. Zsombor Földi for making photographs of this witness available to me for collation.Of the six textual witnesses, only SipNA1 attaches a *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer (see rev. 2ˊ). [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P397810.html) may have originally attached a *šuʾila*-rubric to Ištar 10 since the prayer that precedes it, Ištar 9, bears one in line 4ˊ, but the text breaks off before the end of the prayer and thus provides no evidence for such a rubric for Ištar 10. The rubric is absent on the well-preserved witness UrkPer1 precisely where we might have expected to find one: the prayer ends (rev. 19), there is a single rule line but no rubric after it, and then the ritual instructions begin immediately (rev. 20-22). The same can be inferred for BabLB1: The last line of the *recitanda* is followed by a ruling and then the remainder of the fragment is blank.In terms of ritual use: Unc1 has two lines of very broken ritual instructions probably involving a censer of juniper and flour (rev. 9 = line 43ˊ here). Among the first-millennium witnesses, only SipNA1 and UrkPer1 provide information about the accompanying ritual actions (rev. 3ˊ-7ˊand rev. 20-22, respectively), which include a triple recitation of the prayer along with lighting a censer of juniper, pouring out a libation of beer, and annointing the supplicant’s mouth with oil that had been sprinkled on the ground (see lines 46-48 of the present edition). Distinctively, SipNA1 also provides the supplicant an opportunity for extemporaneous prayer (see line 47a).As for associations with other texts, two very broken lines of an unidentified text follow Ištar 10 on [Unc1](http://shuilas.org/P480788.html). And Ištar 9, as mentioned in the introduction to that prayer above, precedes Ištar 10 on NinNA1. Ištar 10 is the only text inscribed on UrkPer1 and (apparently) SipNA1 as well. We have no information about the use of this prayer in a larger ritual or series.It is worth noting that Ištar 10 is quite conspicuous among the other Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ishtar due to its very short hymnic introduction (lines 1-7 in the present edition) and very long section of supplication (lines 8-40; see Zgoll 2003: 32, 128).**Ištar 11**Only one Neo-Assyrian tablet from Nineveh attests to the text of Ištar 11 (NinNA1), and only one side of that tablet is preserved. As recognized by Ebeling (1953: 128) and Seux (1976: 324, n.1, who discusses the issue explicitly), despite its lacking the EN₂ superscript and *šuʾila*-rubric, the preserved text is likely part of a *šuʾila*-prayer due to the extensive praise (see lines 1ˊ-21ˊ) and concern with personal deities (see lines 21ˊ-23ˊ). Of course, this view must be held tentatively until further evidence becomes available. In my view, the tablet’s first line is likely not the prayer’s first line. Rather, given the shape of what remains, this is the first line of the tablet’s reverse and thus we should not expect an EN₂ superscript. Oddly, the goddess’s name is never written with the divine determinative (see line 1ˊ and 7ˊ) on this textual witness, though the determinative is used in line 23ˊ with the mention of the personal goddess. Nothing is known about specific ritual uses or instructions for this prayer.**Ištar 12**There are four Neo-Assyrian textual sources treated as witnesses to Ištar 12 in the CASPo project, one from Ashur and three from Nineveh. Two of the three witnesses from Nineveh, NinNA2 and NinNA3, are mere fragments, attesting to only twelve and eight incomplete lines, respectively. NinNA1 is a large, two-column tablet that bears witness to several anti-witchcraft ritual texts, Ištar 12 among them. Unfortunately, despite now comprising nineteen fragments (compare the copy in Abusch and Schwemer’s edition with thirteen fragments \[2011, pls. 68-74\]), the tablet remains quite incomplete, a situation that especially impacts the reconstruction of Ištar 12, which occurs only in its very broken obv. ii. The witness from Ashur, AššNA1, comprises two fragments that are indirectly and uncertainly joined, LKA 58 (= Ist A 173) and KAL 7, no. 28 (= VAT 13960). (The two fragments are also institutionally separated, as the former is housed in Istanbul and the latter in Berlin.) If the two fragments are indeed part of the same ancient tablet, then, as the edition indicates, we must reckon with possible gaps between them. As a result of this poor textual evidence, the line numbering of the prayer is tentative (in both recensions, discussed below).Although AššNA1 and NinNA1 bear witness to basically the same four initial lines of the prayer (here lines 1-4 and 1a-4a), the textual reconstruction thereafter becomes complicated. The issue turns on the incongruency between the number of lines *missing* between the fragments K.11260 (one of the fragments comprising Abusch and Schwemer’s MS B₁) and K.6996 (their MS B₃) in NinNA1, which is about nine lines, and the number of lines *attested* on AššNA1, including at least obv. 5-15 (on LKA 58) and 1ˊ-6ˊ (on KAL 7, no. 28). Thus, the material for Ištar 12 in the present edition is organized under two different recensions, an Ashur recension of the prayer and a more poorly known Ninevite one. This organization allows the clearest presentation of the textual evidence while also facilitating comparison of all the textual material on the same page. Additional evidence, of course, may eventually allow a better understanding of Ištar 12 that obviates this recensional distinction.There are no ritual instructions attested for Ištar 12 as of yet. And, there are no rubrics, *šuʾila* or otherwise, attached to any textual witness associated with this prayer. However, rev. 10ˊˊ of [AššNA1]( http://shuilas.org/P413970.html) does attach a *šuʾila*-rubric to Kakkabu 1, the prayer that follows (presumably) Ištar 12 on that witness. This fact, the extensive opening praise in the prayer, and a reference to the personal god (in lines 22 and 25 of the Ashur recension) are suggestive of the prayer’s inclusion in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus, at least until future evidence indicates otherwise.Concerning textual associations: Ištar 12’s association with Kakkabu 1 in AššNA 1 is not known elsewhere, as that tablet is the prayer’s only known textual witness. As mentioned above, NinNA1 collects several anti-witchcraft rituals, one performed before Shamash (obv. i 1-ii 18ˊ), which includes the incantation-prayers Shamash 52 and Shamash 53 as well as one to the ritual torch, and an anti-witchcraft ritual performed before Marduk (rev. i 1ˊ-ii 26ˊˊ), which includes the incantation-prayer Marduk 25. The *recitanda* of Ištar 12 occurs between these two rituals (obv. ii 19ˊ-22ˊ, 1ˊˊ-13ˊˊ), immediately after the first one and followed by a substantial gap before the second one begins. Ritual instructions for Ištar 12 likely occupied at least some of the space in this gap.**Ištar 13**There are only two textual witnesses to reconstruct Ištar 13, one from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh (NinNA1) and one from Sippar (SipLB1). The former, NinNA1, comprises K.66 and the newly joined fragment K.6800, which now allows the restoration of the first several signs at the head of the opening nine lines of the prayer. NinNA1 is the only textual witness that includes a *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. 6ˊ). Due to the gaps between the obverse and reverse in both NinNA1 and SipLB1 and the manner in which these two textual witnesses overlap (and do not overlap; see presently below), we must reamin open to the possibility that this rubric in NinNA1, rev. 6ˊ might not have been originally attached to the prayer that begins in obv. 25 of the same tablet (i.e., Ištar 13; see line 25 of the present edition). Until further evidence confirms this possibility, however, I work under the assumption that the rubric does in fact belong to Ištar 13. Interestingly, this rubric is compound, labeling the text both a *šuʾila*-prayer and an *eršaḫunga*-lament. It reads: ka-inim-ma šu-il₂-la₂ er₂-ša₃-hun-ga₂ ^d^inana-ke₄, “the wording of a lifted-hand prayer, a heart-appeasing lament to Ishtar” (see line y+6 in the present edition). Why the rubric uses the compound label is unclear, especially since the text of the prayer does not show typical elements of *eršaḫunga*-laments (see Frechette 2012: 210). Frechette suggests the rubric may be attached to the prayer to emphasize the appeasing of divine anger (2012: 210-212), which is, however, a common theme in many *šuila*-prayers. I wonder if the final word of the prayer, *aḫulap*, which is *very* unusual in this position and the very epitome of lament in Akkadian prayers, influenced the addition of a lament label in the rubric.Ištar 13 is part of an anti-witchcraft ritual. The ritual begins with a long diagnostic section in which witchcraft is ultimately blamed for the supplicant’s acquisition of an adversary (*bēl lemutti*), which has resulted in the supplicant’s loss of respect and social standing (lines 1-13). This section is only attested in NinNA1. The ritual continues with a lengthy section of ritual instructions (lines 14-24), which prescribe various offerings but do not prescribe the use of any ritual effigies or any symbolic actions against the adversary/witch (as is often the case in anti-witchcraft rituals; see Abusch and Schwemer 2011: 365). In this section, NinNA1 and SipLB1 begin to overlap (see lines 20-24). The final section provides the prescribed *recitanda*, that is, the prayer modern scholarship has labeled Ištar 13. The actual length of this prayer is problematic due to the relationship of the two textual witnesses. In lines 25-33 the two textual witnesses overlap. From line 34 on, only SipLB1 continues. After line 41, it breaks off (at the end of its obverse). There is a gap of about 15-30 lines between the obverse and reverse of SipLB1 (see Abusch and Schwemer 2011: 367, 370). The text that begins on the reverse of SipLB1 (labeled x+NN in the present edition) is also a prayer to a goddess. It may or may not be the continuation of the Ištar 13. The supplicant’s lament about his loss of respect and social standing in the opening lines of this material (see lines x+1-x+8) suggests, however, that the reverse of SipLB 1 does in fact continue Ištar 13 (see also Abusch and Schwemer 2011: 370). The reverse of SipLB1 breaks off before it begins to duplicate text on the reverse of NinNA1 (labeled y+NN here), which comprises the last several lines of a prayer and its compound *šuʾila*-*eršaḫunga* rubric (as discussed above). The prayer that is attested on the reverse of NinNA1 is directed to Ishtar. If it is the conclusion of Ištar 13 (as accepted here; see likewise Abusch and Schwemer 2011: 367, 370), there is likely about 10-30 lines (see Abusch and Schwemer 2011: 367) of the prayer missing in the gap (i.e., between the end of the reverse of SipLB1 and the beginning of the reverse of NinNA1). If this reconstruction is a close approximation to the original extent of Ištar 13, the prayer is at least among the longest, and perhaps the very longest, of all Akkadian *šuila*-prayers, extending from between 90 and 120 lines.The self-contained anti-witchcraft ritual that prescribes Ištar 13 is the only composition on NinNA1, according to the present reconstruction. The same may be true for SipLB1, which, as it has come down to us, is missing (in addition to lines on its top and bottom) the first column on its obverse and thus the last column on its reverse. In any case, these two textual witnesses for Ištar 13 offer no evidence for any other textual associations or for its incorporation into a larger ritual series.**Ištar 23**Ištar 23 has at least two Neo-Assyrian textual witnesses, one from Nineveh (NinNA1) and one from Ashur (AššNA1). These two textual witnesses provide evidence enough to reconstruct most of the text of Ištar 23 with confidence. Both preserve a rubric after the *recitanda* (see rev. 30ˊ and 54a, respectively; see line 14 in the present edition). The rubric on NinNA 1 clearly labels the text a *šuʾila*-prayer; the rubric on AššNA1 likely indicates the same, though the word *šuʾila* must be restored. K.13324, here labeled NinNA2, is a third textual witness to Ištar 23 in my view, though previous editors disagree. Zgoll excludes it from her edition entirely (2003: 155). Farber treats it separately from the other witnesses (1977: 63, 99-100) and offers an admittedly speculative idea about the fragment’s genetic relationship to the other textual witnesses (1977: 32-36; similarly, Mayer 1976: 392 labels the fragment a “Vorläufer^?^ von “Ištar 22/23””). I see the textual differences in NinNA2 through the lens of textual criticism and think the fragment should be included among the witnesses to Ištar 23 until further evidence suggests otherwise. The fragment preserves only six partial lines of text on its obverse. (Its reverse bears a partial Ashurbanipal colophon.) The text on NinNA2, to the extent that it is preserved, duplicates Ištar 23 in the lines this edition labels 1, 4, 5, and 7. NinNA2 offers a minor variant in line 2, reading *apsû* instead of *erṣetu* in the stock phrase (according to NinNA1 and AššNA1) *šamû u erṣetu lirīšūnikki*. (Note also that NinNA1 and AššNA1 inscribe lines 1-2 of the edition on one line of the tablet. I assume NinNA2 did not.) NinNA2 is the only witness of the three to include what is labeled line 3 in the present edition. Of course, it is possible that NinNA2 simply added this line, though I can offer no satisfactory reason for such an addition. It seems more likely that the other two witnesses (or their respective *Vorlagen*) skipped the line via parablepsis, specifically, homoioarcton. Note that both lines 3 and 4 begin with the AN/DINGIR sign. This leaves only one other textual difference, the absence of line 6 in NinNA2. Line 6 stands out in the introductory hymn as verbless and dependent on line 5 for its meaning. Moreover, the line shows variation even among the undisputed textual witnesses. NinNA1 reads *kīma nūru puluk šamāmī* while AššNA1 reads *kīma nūru uruk šamāmī* but offers in a following (indented) line the reading in NinNA1, *nūru puluk*, as a variant. Looking at the empirical textual evidence for line 6 in all three witnesses, I think the best conclusion to draw is that line 6 was still fluid in the prayer’s transmission. Thus, despite attesting several textual variants, I see no reason to exclude NinNA2 from the textual witnesses to Ištar 23.NinNA1 and AššNA1 both place Ištar 23 directly after a long ritual for the production of a poultice, Akkadian *mēlu*, from the skin of a goat that is slaughtered and its skin tanned and colored for this specific ritual purpose. The content of this ritual includes a list of symptoms and a diagnosis, several sections of ritual instructions, and a variety of *recitanda*, including two incantation-prayers to Ishtar (= Ištar 21 and 22, neither of which are labeled with a *šuʾila*-rubric) and several bilingual incantation-prayers addressing substances (*Kultmittelgebete*) used in the tanning and dying process (i.e., milk, beef fat and ghee, and madder). See Farber 1977: 26-30 for an outline of the ritual and pp. 55-100 for his text edition. Frechette 2012: 218 provides a brief outline. Farber argues in some detail that Ištar 23 originally had no place in this extensive polutice-making ritual (1977: 29-36). Instead, he speculated that the prayer was included as an appendix to the preceding ritual material, placed there due to a common divine addressee, among other reasons (see similarly Zgoll 2003: 161 n.299 with an important difference noted just below). In Farber’s view, Ištar 23 was eventually fitted *secondarily* in a rather thoughtless manner with its own (brief and unusual) ritual instructions, which were lifted from line 20 in his edition of the poultice-making ritual. If we follow Farber, Ištar 23 was not integrated into an actual ritual but was rather a textual appendage to one in a scholastic collection of rituals loosely connected in some way to Ishtar and Dumuzi. Differently, Zgoll treats Ištar 23 and its ritual instructions as a separate ritual, concerned only with the slaughter of a goat and the burning of its heart (and not at all concerned with making a poultice from its hide). Frechette, on the other hand, while admitting the possibility of Zgoll’s perspective, argues that Ištar 23 also could have been recited in the poultice-making ritual. In his view, Ištar 23, though clearly appended at the end of the long poultice-making ritual, may have nevertheless played an integral role in it. Given the prayer’s content and the use of other *šuʾila*-prayers in lengthy rituals, Frechette thinks Ištar 23 may have had a preparatory function to the recitation of Ištar 21 earlier in the ritual, and may have been recited just at the point when the goat was slaughtered, even though this is not indicated explicitly in the ritual instructions (Frechette 2012: 216-220). Neither Farber nor Frechette takes into account the supplicant’s petition in Ištar 23 for progeny (see line 12 in the present edition), which is not at all an issue in the poultice-making ritual. This final petition factors heavily in Zgoll’s exegesis of the prayer (2003: 161-181). In my opinion, this final petition is most suggestive for seeing Ištar 23 and its brief ritual instructions as a separate but genuine ritual, just as Zgoll treats it, to obtain progeny. In support of Ištar 23’s separate consideration is the fact that [NinNA1](http://shuilas.org/P394506.html) collects three other textual units—three diagnoses with associated remedies involving medicinal-magical leather pouches (rev. 32ˊ-33ˊ, 34ˊ-36ˊ, and 37ˊ-42ˊ)—after its presentation of Ištar 23 (rev. 20ˊ-31ˊ) and before concluding with a catchline (rev. 43ˊ) and colophon (rev. 44ˊ-54ˊ). Like Ištar 23, these materials clearly have nothing to do with poultice-making.r\A final speculation about the ritual instructions: Although the desired progeny are called *zēra* and *perʾu* in line 12 of the prayer, *liblibbu* falls within the same semantic domain. It may be that the use of the slaughtered goat’s heart (*libbu*) provides an unstated connection to the desire for progeny, *liblibbu*, via the kind of near homonymy ancient scribal scholars exploited in their commentaries to forge explanatory connections.**Ištar 30**The text of Ištar 30 is very poorly known. One tiny fragment from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh (NinNA1) preserves an illegible line and then parts of two formulaic lines at the prayer’s conclusion. A few signs in line 4ˊ suggest the presence of a *šuʾila*-rubric: \[ka-inim-ma šu-il₂\]-⸢la₂⸣ ^d^+inana-\[kam\*\]. And then there are a few signs that provide evidence for some formulaic ritual instructions. No other texts are associated with this prayer on its only textual witness.**Ištar 31**Ištar 31 is attested on one very large Neo-Assyrian tablet from Kalḫu (KalNA1), which was copied by a junior scribe (whose name is lost, see rev. ii 59). The tablet was found in the vicinity of the tablet room (a pit in NT 12, probably) of Nabû’s Ezida temple (see Wiseman and Black 1996: 42, 49). A label on the tablet’s left edge identifies it as a collection of *šuʾila*-prayers to “great and exalted goddesses.” And indeed, that sums up the tablet’s [contents](http://shuilas.org/P363582.html) quite well, which are as follows: Nisaba 1 (obv. i 1-12), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. i 13-14), and ritual instructions (obv. i 15); Nisaba 2 (obv. i 16-47), truncated rubric, likely an error (obv. i 48a), and ritual instructions (obv. i 48b-50); Ištar 31 (obv. i 51-67, ii 1-10), *šuʾila*-rubric, (obv. ii 11), and ritual instructions (obv. ii 12-34), alternate ritual instructions (obv. ii 35-38); Tašmetu 2 (obv. ii 39-58), *šuʾila*-rubric (obv. ii 59), unidentified text (rev. i 1-2); Tašmetu 1, long version (rev. i 3-43), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. i 44), and ritual instructions (rev. i 45-50); Tašmetu 1, short version (rev. i 51-53, ii1-29), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. ii 30); Nanaya 1 (rev. ii 31-52), *šuʾila*-rubric (rev. ii 53), and ritual instructions (rev. ii 54-56), repeated *šuʾila*-rubric(!) (rev. ii 57); catchline to Išḫara 2, which is likely a *šuʾila*-prayer (rev. ii 58); and colophon (rev. ii 59).Ištar 31 is distinctive in that its ritual instructions are as long as the prayer itself and has, in fact, two versions of instructions. The first runs to twenty-three lines (see lines 29-51 of the present edition). The stated result of the ritual (and thus its purpose) is that god and king will be at peace with the supplicant and nothing evil will approach the person (lines 49b-52). The second set of ritual instructions, set off from the first and what follows by rulings and labeled *šanîš* in the first line, is only four lines long (lines 52-55). These instructions have been mangled in transmission and thereby shortened an indeterminate number of lines (see the note on line 53). The ritual purpose in this alternative version of ritual instructions concerns appeasing the anger of the personal deities (line 55). Given the presence of a catchline with a prayer to another goddess, it seems this collection of *šuʾila*-prayers to goddesses continued with at least one more tablet, perhaps more.

name: *šuʾila*s to Ninlil
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer lists four incantation-prayers as potentially directed to the goddess Ninlil (Mayer 1976: 380; compare, Kunstmann 1932: 100-101). Only the first two does he identify as Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers. In addition to these two prayers, CASPo also recognizes a third Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Ninlil. This prayer, known only by its incipit cited in both versions of the Ritual Tablet for *Bīt salāʾ mê*, was previously identified with Ištar 18 (see Meier 1937-1939: 43, 44,n.9; Mayer 1976: 391; and Berlejung 1996: 7, 12,n.47), but has been separated from that incantation-prayer and reassigned to Ninlil (see Ambos 2013: 162, 164, 228 and Frechette 2012: 125, 170, 265). Following the lead of Ambos and Frechette, CASPo treats this text as the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer [Ninlil 5](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html). All three prayers are only known by their incipit as cited either as a catchline or a prescribed recitation in a larger ritual, as discussed below. The ritual uses of these three Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Ninlil are discussed in the [introduction](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/9) to Enlil 1a.**Ninlil 1**Ninlil 1 is only attested as the catchline on two textual witnesses. One witness is from Neo-assyrian Nineveh (NinNA1). The other, BabaNB1, probably dates to the Neo-Babylonian period but its precise provenance in the south is unknown. These two tablets are also the best textual witnesses to Enlil 1a. No other texts or ritual instructions appear on these two tablets. The prayer is included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus because both textual witnesses attest a *šuʾila*-rubric for Enlil 1a (see NinNA1, rev. 13 and BabaNB1, rev. 9).**Ninlil 2**Ninlil 2 is only known by its incipit, which is cited in the Ninevite Ritual Tablet to *Bīt rimki* (Schwemer 2019: 56, line 212 \[A o iii 56\]; 76; see also Frechette 2012: 178; Ambos 2013: 188; Læssøe 1955: 25). The prayer is included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus because the other prayers cited by incipit in this part of the Ritual Tablet and known beyond their initial line from other textual sources are all labeled with the *šuʾila*-rubric. Compare the prayers identified in Schwemer 2019: 75-76 with the manuscript information for each at [CASPo’s list of prayers](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) and the information about [rubrics](http://shuilas.org/rubrics.html) attested in each manuscript of the corpus.**Ninlil 5**Ninlil 5 is only known by its incipit, which is cited in both versions of the Ritual Tablet to *Bīt salāʾ mê* (Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 43\]; 164 \[x + 8ˊ (= C 8ˊ)\], 175; see also Frechette 2012: 168, 170,n.6, 265). The prayer is included in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-corpus because the other prayers cited by incipit in these parts of the Ritual Tablets and known beyond their initial line from other textual sources are all labeled with the *šuʾila*-rubric (except Papsukkal 1). Compare the prayers identified in Frechette 2012: 168-169 with the manuscript information for each at [CASPo’s list of prayers](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) and the information about [rubrics](http://shuilas.org/rubrics.html) attested in each manuscript of the corpus.

name: *šuʾila*s to Šamaš
intro: In his catalog of *Gebetsbeschwörungen*, Werner Mayer identified 105 distinct prayers to Shamash (Mayer 1976: 410-422; compare Kunstmann 1932: 104-110). (This number excludes prayers directed to Shamash and another deity; e.g., Ea and Šamaš 1 or Šamaš and Marduk 1, 2, and 3, for which see Mayer 1976: 382, 409, 423.) Only the first six prayers in his catalog did Mayer identify as a *šuʾila*-prayer. And for two of these, his nos. 4 and 6, he indicated uncertainty about this identification (Mayer 1976: 410-411). The current project, [Corpus of Akkadian Shuila Prayers online](http://shuilas.org/prayers.html) (CASPo), counts all six of these prayers as members of its corpus (see likewise, Frechette 2012: 271-272) and provides reasons for the inclusion of nos. 4 and 6 in the specific introductions to those prayers below. Although the number of prayers to Shamash is relatively high, most of the prayers, at the time of this writing (May 2026), have few (nos. 3, 5, and 6) or only one (nos. 2 and 4) textual witness. The *šuʾila*-prayer Šamaš 1 is the exception: With seventeen witnesses to its text, it is among the best attested prayers in the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer corpus. (Only Marduk 2 has more witnesses.) Many witnesses to the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers to Shamash provide evidence that the prayers were accompanied by ritual actions of various kinds or were part of a larger ritual performance. However, it is not always possible to identify the broader purpose of these rituals or to associate the texts with a particular ritual series. The following specific introductions will consider each prayer on a case by case basis.**Šamaš 1**There are seventeen textual witnesses to Šamaš 1, representing most of the first millennium sites that have yielded cuneiform tablets in significant number. (Ashur is the exception.) Nine manuscripts come from Assyrian sites: six from Nineveh, three from Ḫuzirina. The remaining eight manuscripts are from southern sites, with two from unspecified Babylonian sites, four from Babylon itself, and one each from Kish and Hellenistic Uruk. (The colophon of the Uruk witness identifies the owner as “Iqishaya, son of Ishtar-shuma-eresh, descen\[dant of Ekur-zakir\],” who flourished c. 320 BCE. See Robson 2019: 229-235.) Many of the witnesses are small (BabaLB1, BabLB1, BabLB4, HuzNA3, KišLB1, NinNA5, NinNA6) to medium (BabLB2, BabLB3, NinNA2, NinNA3, NinNA4) tablet fragments, attesting only a portion of the prayer. Several witnesses provide a larger chunk of the text (NinNA1, HuzNA2) or almost its entirety (BabaNA1, HuzNA1, UrkHel1). None of the witnesses provides ritual instructions to accompany the prayer’s recitation.Variation among the manuscripts is extensive and diverse in nature. Variations within lines range from minor differences in a word or two (e.g., lines 1, 4, 8, 9, 20, 22, 24 \[likely an explanatory gloss\], 28, 32, 33) to larger variations in phrasing (e.g., line 17 and an expansion in line 15 \[see HuzNA2 and NinNA3\]). Variations also exist on the level of the whole line, with some textual witnesses inserting additional lines into the prayer (e.g., lines 16a in HuzNA2, 24a-24b in HuzNA1 and HuzNA2, and 32a in HuzNA1), omitting various lines (likely by accident, see notes on lines 7, 23, 28, 31, and 34), reversing the order of two lines (see HuzNA2, obv. 16, 17 = lines 17, 16 in the edition), or showing a completely different final line vis-à-vis the majority of manuscripts (see line 35, according to NinNA2 and HuzNA1). In addition to these variations, three manuscripts (BabaNA1, HuzNA2, and NinNA4) include a self-introductory formula and laments concerning the appearance of unfavorable signs. Though these are inserted in each witness at about the same place in the prayer (see line 17), they vary significantly from one another, as described below in the discussion of the prayer’s ritual use.Five textual witnesses attest a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to the prayer (see NinNA1, rev. 55; NinNA2, obv. 26ˊ; HuzNA1, rev. 21; BabaNA1, rev. 16; and UrkHel1, rev. 26ˊ). The prayer on all but two of the other witnesses, HuzNA2 and NinNA3, is too fragmentary to provide evidence for or against a *šuʾila*-rubric. In both HuzNA2 and NinNA3 Šamaš 1 is the only text inscribed on the tablet. The final lines on the reverse of HuzNA2 are severely abraded. It is clear that the inscription ends with a single ruling after rev. 19, and the remainder of the reverse is blank. I see no evidence for a single ruling after rev. 18. Thus, it seems unlikely that the scribe attached a *šuʾila*-rubric to the prayer, even though there is certainly room for one. Like HuzNA2, the prayer on NinNA3 ends with a single ruling after the final line of the prayer and the remainder of the reverse is blank. It has room for a rubric but clearly does not attest one. It is worth mentioning that the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer that precedes Šamaš 1 on BabLB2, Sîn 3, does have a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to it. See [BabLB2, rev. 7](http://shuilas.org/P545379.html). The order of the two prayers on the tablet suggests an association with the cycle of prayers in *Bīt salāʾ mê* (see below), and thus it is quite likely that Šamaš 1 on BabLB2 also had a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to it.As mentioned above, none of the witnesses to Šamaš 1 attest ritual instructions. There is extensive evidence, however, for the prayer’s ritual use, especially in *namburbi*-rituals and in the *šuʾila*-prayer cycle of *Bīt salāʾ mê*. First, *namburbi*-rituals.As mentioned above, three manuscripts customize the prayer with a self-introductory formula and various laments concerning the appearance of unfavorable signs. NinNA4 attests the generic “so-and-so” (Akk. *annanna*) placeholder self-introductory formula (see Mayer 1976: 51) and an *attalû*-formula (see Mayer 1976: 100-102), that is, a formula relating to the evils of a lunar eclipse (see lines 17a-17d of the edition). BabaNA1 inserts the name of king Ashurbanipal’s brother, Shamash-shum-ukin, who ruled Babylon from 668 to 648 BCE, into the self-introductory formula and includes a lament concerning the evil announced by some broken part on the supplicant’s (*viz.* the king’s) chariot (see lines 17ˊa-17ˊf). HuzNA2 inserts into its self-introductory formula the name Aplutu, about whom we know nothing beyond the lines customized for him in this prayer, followed by a multi-pronged lament about the evils announced by a broken chariot part, the appearance of red ants, and the appearance of worrisome signs and portents in the supplicant’s house (see lines 17ˊA-17ˊH). These insertions in these three textual witnesses suggest Šamaš 1 was used in various kinds of *namburbi*-rituals to release the announced evil. A *namburbi*-ritual against the evil announced by a broken chariot is edited in Maul 1994: 387-399. The opening lines of the diagnostic section of this ritual (see Maul 1994: 189, lines 1-4) very much recall the situation described in the insertions in BabaNA1 and HuzNA2, though the latter lists other signs as well (see Maul 1994: 387; Frechette 2012: 187). Šamaš 1, however, is not prescribed in the *namburbi*’s ritual instructions; rather, Šamaš 5 is. See the introduction to that prayer below. (Contrary to Maul’s interpretation \[1998: 387\], which Frechette follows \[2012: 187, 193\], I do not think the lines written on the left edge of K.2296+ \[= Šamaš 5’s NinNA1\] belong to Šamaš 1. See my note on the edition of Šamaš 5, line 7, under NinNA1, obv. 9ˊa.) For a *namburbi*-ritual specifically against the appearance of ants, which are mentioned, among other signs, in the inserted lament in HuzNA2, see Maul 1994: 349-353. Yet once again the ritual instructions for this *namburbi* do not prescribe the recitation of Šamaš 1.The *šuʾila*-prayer’s link to *namburbi*-rituals is quite clear, however, in a *namburbi* against *uḫḫu*, “slime, phlegm” (see CAD U/W, 41 and Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 413) in KAR 72, obv. 1-25. (Ebeling 1954: 182-185 is still the most recent edition.) The ritual instructions indeed prescribe the recitation of Šamaš 1, citing its incipit in obv. 24. (Frechette 2012: 188 follows Ebeling \[1954: 183\] in taking UḪ-ḪU in obv. 2, as  a logographic spelling of Akk. *ašāšu*, “moth,” but this is not recognized in CAD A/2, 422\]. Maul 1994: 175,n. 162 is too uncertain about the word’s meaning to indicate the ritual’s precise purpose.)Another indicator of the prayer’s association with *namburbi*-rituals is the text’s inclusion on UrkHel1, which is the *pirsu maḫrû*, “first section,” in a series entitled *ana* ḪUL A₂-MEŠ GISKIM-MEŠ \[ḪUL-MEŠ *ša ina* E₂ NA GAL₂-MEŠ DU₈\] (*ana lumun idāti ittāti* \[*lemnēti ša ina bīt amēli ittanabšâ šupṭuri*\]), “to release the evil of \[unfavorable\] signs *and* omens \[which keep occurring in a man’s house” (rev. 30ˊ, restored according to Maul 1994: 203 with n.393; see also 498, and 499-500, lines 21-22). The full content of [UrkHel1](http://shuilas.org/P348623.html) runs as follows: ritual instructions to release an evil sign in a man’s house (obv. 1-5), ditto (obv. 6-7), ritual instructions against an evil sign drawing near to a man (obv. 8-10), ritual instructions that an evil sign not draw near to a man and his house (obv. 11-13), ditto (obv. 14-16), ritual instructions (obv. 17-18; there is a scribal annotation, AL.TIL, “finished,” inserted in a smaller script just below obv. 18), an Akkadian incantation-prayer to Shamash (obv. 19-27, rev. 1ˊ-8ˊ with broken rubric in rev. 9ˊ \[likely not a Kiʾutu-prayer\]), Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Šamaš 1 (rev. 10ˊ-25ˊ with *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 26ˊ), incipit to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Ea 1a (rev. 27ˊ), incipit to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Marduk 2 (rev. 28ˊ), incipit to incantation-prayer to River 1a (rev. 29ˊ), series information with one line of ritual instructions (rev. 30ˊ-31ˊ), and colophon (l.e. 1). It may be that the scribal annotation in obv. 18, AL.TIL, indicates that the ritual materials in obv. 1-18 came from a different source than the prayers that follow (see Simkó 2025: 151). Still, the placement of Šamaš 1 with the *namburbi*-material establishes an association with *namburbi*-rituals. (Frechette \[2012: 192-193\] sees the listing of the three *šuʾila*-prayers in UrkHel1 as supporting evidence for his idea that *šuʾila*-prayers were recited in *namburbi*-rituals more often than ritual instructions indicate.)As for *Bīt salāʾ mê*: Šamaš 1 is prescribed twice in an Assyrian version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet, once in the night cycle (see Ambos 2013: 162 \[B₂ 49\], see also 163, 174, 175, with discussion on pp. 61-62; Frechette 2012: 168, 169, 171, 271) and again as the first *šuʾila*-prayer in the dawn cycle (see Ambos 2013: 166 \[y + 8ˊ (= B₂ 3ˊˊ)\]). In other versions of the Ritual Tablet, the prayer is only prescribed in the morning (see Ambos 2013: 166 \[y + 8ˊ (= A₂ 6; C 6ˊˊb; E 2ˊb)\]; Frechette 2012: 168, 169, 271), followed by Ea 1a and Marduk 2 (note the same order in UrkHel1, rev. 27ˊ-28ˊ above; Frechette 2012: 171; Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 332). Interestingly, NinNA1 presents a series of *šuʾila*-prayers, including Anu 1, Nusku 3, Sîn 3, Gula 1a, Šamaš 1, and the catchline to Papsukkal 1, which follows the order of prescribed *šuʾila*-prayers in an Assyrian version of the night cycle (see Ambos 2013: 203 and 162, lines B₂ 44-B₂ 50), suggesting it is a tablet of *recitanda* for that series. Indeed, Ambos has labeled NinNA1 the ninth *pirsu* of the series (2013: 203), based on the fact that the catchline for Anu 1 appears on [K.2396+](http://shuilas.org/P397497.html), rev. 33 just before the colophon, which labels the tablet the eighth *pirsu* of *Bīt salāʾ mê*. The Assyrian night cycle may also be reflected in the tiny fragments comprising [NinNA6](http://shuilas.org/P401693.html), if *ludlul*, the only preserved word in the prayer that precedes Šamaš 1, belongs to Gula 1a. But with so little to go on, this remains very uncertain.[BabLB3](http://shuilas.org/P549618.html) likely provides *recitanda* for some other version of *Bīt salāʾ mê* that includes a recitation of Sîn 3 (obv. 1ˊ-23ˊ with *šuʾila*-rubric, obv. 24ˊ), followed immediately by Šamaš 1 (obv. 25ˊ-28ˊ), and then, after a break, Adad 1a (rev. 1ˊ-28ˊ), as I have argued in the Introduction to the *šuʾila*-prayer to Adad 1a (Šamaš 1’s BabLB3 = Adad 1a’s BabLB1). See [there](https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/Mag/2/1). [BabLB2](http://shuilas.org/P545379.html) likewise places Sîn 3 (obv. 1ˊ-19ˊ, rev. 1-6, with *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 7) immediately before Šamaš 1 (rev. 8-24), which may suggest it presents *recitanda* for the same version of the series.Finally, the content of [NinNA2](http://shuilas.org/P238568.html) may also suggest a (loose) connection to *Bīt salāʾ mê*. The fragmentary tablet includes the final lines of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Marduk 3 (obv. 1ˊ-5ˊ, with *šuʾila*-rubric in obv. 6ˊ), Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Šamaš 1 (o7ˊ-25ˊ, with *šuʾila*-rubric in obv. 26ˊ), and then the incantation-prayer to Šamaš 90 (obv. 27ˊ, rev. 1-6), with an incomplete rubric (rev. 7), which reads: ka-inim-ma gim^?^ a-⸢meš⸣ \[...\]. This is the only witness to Marduk 3. The text of this prayer is nearly identical to Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer to Ea 1a, and thus some have thought the divine name in the rubric is a mistake for Ea (see Mayer 1976: 395; Frechette 2012: 172; and Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 332). If so, then the tablet’s content shows the order Ea 1a, Šamaš 1, and then Šamaš 90. All three of these prayers are prescribed recitations in one version of the *Bīt salāʾ mê* Ritual Tablet (see Ambos 2013: 166 \[Šamaš 90 at x + 35ˊ (= D11ˊˊ), where the incantation is to be recited *kīma mê ana qāt Šamaš tattadnu*, “after you have given water for *washing* the hands of Shamash”; Šamaš 1 at y + 8ˊ (= A₂ 6; B₂ 3ˊˊ; C 6ˊˊb; E 2ˊb)\], 168 \[Ea 1a at y + 9ˊ (= A₂ 7; B₂ 4ˊˊ; C 7ˊˊa)\]). Although their order on NinNA2 is reversed in comparison to the Ritual Tablet’s order and some Sumerian incantations are also prescribed before Ea 1a, Frechette suggests the *recitanda* on NinNA2 may be connected to *Bīt salāʾ mê* or some similar ritual (2012: 172; similarly, Abusch and Schwemer 2016: 332).As for other ritual uses, our prayer is prescribed by incipit in a short medical prescription preserved only on [BAM 322](https://www.geschkult.fu-berlin.de/e/babmed/Corpora/BAM-4/BAM-4_-322/index.html). This tablet is a large compendium of medical material from the house of the exorcist in Neo-Assyrian Ashur (see rev. 40-43; Pedersén 1986: 64). The text itself provides rubrics that divides the tablet into two sections, according to the originals’ sources: obv. 1-28 from the palace of Hammurabi (obv. 29) and obv. 30-52, rev. 1-38 from the palace of Esarhaddon (rev. 39). The second part provides a series of nine short prescriptions to reconcile a person to various deities, to gain favor and success among people, to avoid illness, and to undo evil signs (see Steinert 2015: 128-129 for a brief discussion). Šamaš 1 is cited by incipit (rev. 12) as part of the fifth prescription (rev. 7-12) to help a patient gain a successful hearing with deities and social elites. After other prescribed ritual actions and ingestion of medicinals, the patient recites Šamaš 1 over a bath, salve, and fumigants (Akk. *ana narmakti napšalti qutāri*). Finally, Frechette speculates that the content of Šamaš 1 suggests it would be an appropriate recitation in a dream ritual; but, as he admits, there is currently no evidence for its use in such a ritual (Frechette 2012: 196).**Šamaš 2**The only textual witness for Šamaš 2, AššNA1, comes from the house of the exorcist in Neo-Assyrian Ashur (Pedersén 1986: 62). This exemplar of the prayer has been customized for Ashurbanipal, who lived from about 685 to 627 BCE and reigned as king from 668 BCE on (see lines 7a and 14a, as edited here). Šamaš 2 is the only text inscribed on this tablet. Although this witness clearly bears a *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 8, there are no ritual instructions provided with the prayer, even though half of the reverse is blank and could have easily accommodated such instructions. Thus, its precise ritual use or association with other ritual texts is unknown. Rather than a colophon proper, the tablet bears three repetitive lines in a small, shallow script, likely inscribed when the tablet was nearly dry. They read *ša ilu* (*u*) \[...\], “who the god (and) \[. . .\].” The purpose of these lines is unclear. It is worth noting that several scholars have pointed out the similarities between this *šuʾila*-prayer and a Kiʾutu-prayer used in *Bīt rimki* (Mayer 1976: 410; Seux 1976: 286,n.1; and see especially Baragli 2022: 404-405).**Šamaš 3**There are only two textual witnesses for Šamaš 3, both from Neo-Assyrian sites. The main witness is from Ashur (AššNA1). It only bears the text of Šamaš 3. After the *šuʾila*-rubric in rev. 14, the remainder of its reverse is blank. There are no ritual instructions. The other textual witness is from Nineveh (NinNA1); it is a corner fragment of a tablet, bearing eight partial lines on both its obverse and reverse. This textual material duplicates the ends of lines 25-41 (as edited here) but offers no substantive help for restoring the lines AššNA1 leaves wanting. Thus, lines 19-27 of the prayer are quite fragmentary. NinNA1 offers the tiniest of clues for the attachment of a *šuʾila*-rubric: It preserves only the final vertical wedge of what is taken to be ILA₂ before the deity’s name, ^d^UTU, in rev. 8. Given that this rubric, set off by rulings both before and after, occurs so close to the top edge of the fragment’s reverse, it is likely that either ritual instructions or another text followed Šamaš 3. But, at present, we can say nothing more due to our lack of evidence.**Šamaš 4**The only textual witness for Šamaš 4, AššNA1, comes from Neo-Assyrian Ashur. Not a single line of the fourteen lines bearing witness to Šamaš 4 on this fragment’s reverse is complete. And six of these fourteen lines produce nothing sensible at all (compare Ebeling 1953: 150, “Rest vorläufig unbrauchbar”). As best as can be determined, the lines contain hymnic material, though there is little to go on. Rev. 1 may refer to the lifting of hands. The prayer has no rubric attached to it, *šuʾila* or otherwise. The [obverse](http://shuilas.org/P369223.html) of this tablet contains text from Sipazianna 3(?) and Zappu 3. Both have a rubric attached to them. The rubric to the first prayer is very likely a *šuʾila*-rubric; it reads ka-inim-ma š\[u-il₂-la₂ ...\]). The defining element of the *šuʾila*-rubric is missing in the one attached to the second prayer, Zappu 3, though its restoration is likely. Given this very meager evidence, Šamaš 4 can only very tentatively be included in the corpus of Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayers. Aside from the textual association with the two prayers just mentioned, nothing more is known about Šamaš 4 or its ritual use.**Šamaš 5**There are four first-millennium textual witnesses available for the reconstruction of Šamaš 5. Two witnesses are from Neo-Assyrian Nineveh. NinNA1, comprising K.2296 + K.2776, preserves the *recitanda* known to be prescribed in a *namburbi*-ritual to counter the evil announced by the breaking of a part of the king’s chariot in the course of a campaign (for which, see Maul 1994: 387-399). This fragment has been associated with and/or believed to be indirectly joined to K.2495 (as asserted by Loretz and Mayer 1978: XIV and considered probable by Maul 1994: 388). If the indirect join is correct, about half of the original tablet, which would have contained the text of two *namburbi*-rituals, is now missing from its middle area. Thus, about twenty-five lines would be missing on both obverse and reverse — a rough estimate based on the curvature of the fragments. If not, as seems more likely (see below), then much more is missing from each fragment and they should be treated as separate textual witnesses. In any case, NinNA1, considered here to be only the obverse and reverse of K.2296 + K.2776, provides the main textual witness for Šamaš 5. NinNA2 is a tiny fragment, attesting only eight fragmentary lines of Šamaš 5. Although largely only duplicating text already known from NinNA1, the fragment does fill some gaps at the ends of lines 6, 7, and 10 of the prayer (as edited here). The other two witnesses are from Babylonia, one from perhaps Neo-Babylonian Babylon (BabNB1) and the other from Hellenistic Uruk (UrkHel1). Both witnesses duplicate (variously) parts of the *namburbi*-related textual materials attested on NinNA1 and K.2495, including parts of Šamaš 5. But neither tablet contributes significantly to the reconstruction of the prayer beyond what is permitted by NinNA1. Two of these four witnesses provide evidence of a *šuʾila*-rubric attached to Šamaš 5 (see NinNA1, rev. 4 and BabNB1, rev. 12ˊ). The other two witnesses break off before the end of the prayer.*Why K.2495 is likely not part of the same tablet as K.2296 + K.2776*: Baragli’s work on the Kiʾutu-prayer corpus has called the indirect joining of K.2296 + K.2776 with K.2495 into question. The matter turns on the identification of the Kiʾutu-prayer prescribed by incipit in the *namburbi*’s ritual instructions just before the prescription of Šamaš 5 and Nergal 4 (see Maul 1994: 391, lines 21, 22, 25) versus the actual text of the Kiʾutu-prayer that is later provided as *recitanda* on some textual witnesses related to this *namburbi*-ritual. First, all the manuscripts attesting the ritual instructions (see Maul’s edition \[1994: 391\], line 20, MSS A, obv. 21; B = K.2495, obv. 10; C = UrkHel1, obv. 15; and D = BabNB1, obv. 22ˊ) prescribe a Kiʾutu-prayer that has been reasonably identified with one used in the *Bīt rimki* ritual, Kiʾutu br 3 in Baragli’s taxonomy (2022: 427-477; see also Maul 1994: 391,n.19). She estimates that this prayer would have run to about seventy lines (2022: 278). The obverse of K.2495 (the upper part of a tablet) breaks off just as it is providing the *recitanda* of this Kiʾutu-prayer (see obv. 14-17). The obverse of K.2296 + K.2776 (the lower part of a tablet), however, abruptly begins with the final lines of a Kiʾutu-prayer that has been identified as Kiʾutu D in Baragli’s taxonomy (2022: 276-288), a prayer she reconstructs in fifty-nine lines total. Given these identifications, Baragli treats the two fragments as separate witnesses to the same chariot-related *namburbi*-ritual, which would have differed in terms of which Kiʾutu-prayer was prescribed by incipit in the ritual instructions (see Baragli 2022: 146-150). I think this is a reasonable conclusion and likely the best inference from the present evidence. It is theoretically possible, of course, that both prayers might have been written sequentially, the first as the prescribed recitation while the second might have been labeled an alternative tradition. But the cumulative length of both prayers (c. 130 lines; admittedly, an estimate) and the space between the two fragments (perhaps twenty-five lines on the obverse; also an estimate) argue against this. (Even if we posit that the copyist continued to inscribe the tablet in a small script and ignoring line breaks \[note that he used only nine lines on K.2296 + K.2776 to inscribe Šamaš 5’s twenty-three lines of text, as reconstructed here\], he still could note have squeezed both prayers into the space available in the estimated gap.) It is also possible that the identification of these prayers is incorrect and that some (mostly) unknown prayer, one that begins as does Kiʾutu br 3 and ends like Kiʾutu D, in fact bridged what really should be considered a gap between K.2495 and K.2296 + K.2776. But on present evidence, even with all the uncertainties and estimates, this seems unlikely.As already mentioned above, Šamaš 5 was a prescribed recitation in a *namburbi*-ritual to avert the evil announced by an equipment failure on a royal chariot (see Maul 1994: 387-399 for an edition). The ritual instructions as presented in lines 20-25 (see Maul 1994: 391, 397) call for a ritual assemblage (*riksu*) to be laid out before Shamash and then the recitation of two prayers, cited by incipit, to the same deity. The first prayer is a Kiʾutu (see line 21 in Maul’s edition, attested in his MSS A, B, C, and D), which, as mentioned above, is likely to be identified with Kiʾutu br 3, according to Baragli’s taxonomy (see 2022: 146-150 for discussion and 427-477 for her edition); the second is Šamaš 5 (line 22, attested in Maul’s MSS A, B, C, and D). The ritual instructions then call for a second ritual assemblage for Nergal and the gods of the steppe. After instructing the exorcist to raise his hands, the instructions prescribe the recitation of the Akkadian *šuʾila*-prayer Nergal 4 (line 25, attested in Maul’s MSS A, B, and C \[D is broken\]) by incipit. If the ritual instructions on the reverse of K.2495 (Maul’s MS B) and AO.6471 (Maul’s MS C = UrkHel1 here) belong to the same ritual (as Maul reasonably assumes; 1994: 398,n.41), then there are further instructions about offerings and a brief recitation, beginning with *mimma lemnu*, which concludes with the exorcist himself offering praise to the deity. (It is not clear if this final recitation and praise are directed at Nergal or Shamash.) Although NinNA1 attests no ritual instructions for the *namburbi*, it does preserve the prescribed *recitanda* in the same order as prescribed by the ritual instructions on other tablets (though, it varies, as described already above, in the Kiʾutu-prayer). BabNB1, which does attest some of the ritual instructions for this *namburbi*-ritual (in its obv. 9ˊ-23ˊ), also shows Šamaš 5 followed by Nergal 4 (cited by incipit as the tablet’s catchline, see rev. 13ˊ). (UrkHel1 begins to provide the text of Šamaš 5 in obv. 19-22, directly after the ritual instructions, before it breaks off. This witness preserves nothing of the text of the Kiʾutu-prayer or Nergal 4, though its ritual instructions prescribe both \[see its obv. 14-18\].) As Frechette has noted, adopting Maul’s terminology, Šamaš 5 seems to function as an intial offering in the *namburbi*-ritual, while Nergal 4 provided the litigation offering (2012: 186). (As argued in the introduction to Šamaš 1 above, that *šuʾila*-prayer was not used in this chariot-related *namburbi*-ritual.)**Šamaš 6**There are three textual witnesses to Šamaš 6, all of which are from Neo-Assyrian sites. Two are from Ashur (AššNA1 and AššNA2), and one from Nineveh (NinNA1). AššNA2 and NinNA1 are both rather fragmentary. AššNA1, a copy of the prayer that was personalized for one Upāqa-ana-ištarāti (see Baker 2011: 1389), is the main textual witness, preserving nearly the entire prayer and accompanying ritual. Šamaš 6 is the only text inscribed on all three witnesses. Only AššNA1 attests a *šuʾila*-rubric (see rev. 12-13), though it has been expanded to include a purpose clause: ka-inim-ma šu-il₂-la₂-kam₂ *ṣibit tulî ša munatti*, “It is the wording of a lifted-hand prayer related to the seizing of the chest during *munattu*.” AššNA1 (in rev. 14-22) and NinNA1 (in its quite fragmentary rev. 8ˊ-12ˊ) both attest ritual instructions, though they vary significantly enough to be treated separately in the present edition (compare lines 32-40 and the very incomplete lines 32ˊ-36ˊ).In terms of its ritual purpose, Šamaš 6 was formulated to dispel two oath-related evils that have announced themselves in a dream, *ṣibit māmīti*, “seizure of *māmīti*,” and *ṣibit tulî*, “seizure of the chest.” As I interpret the text elsewhere (see Lenzi, forthcoming), the supplicant’s legal opponent has inflicted these two evils on him unjustly via a dream in which the supplicant took an oath and subsequently broke it, thus incurring the evils that the ritual-prayer seeks to dispel via an appeal to Shamash. Thus, the supplicant is the victim of sorcery. The text as a whole is a *namburbi*-ritual with close affinities to anti-witchcraft rituals. And, in fact, the prayer’s incipit is listed in a Ninevite catalog of *namburbi*-rituals (see Maul 1994: 197 with n.346, 201). Some scholars contend that this ritual purpose gives reason to suspect the validity or correctness of the *šuʾila*-rubric attached to the prayer in AššNA1 (Ebeling 1954: 5; Ebeling 1955: 147,n.2; Mayer 1976: 411; and Abusch 2018: 82). But other examples of *šuʾila*-prayers in *namburbi*-rituals (see, e.g., the introductions to Šamaš 1 and 5 above) suggest this suspicion is misplaced (see Frechette 2012: 133, 139,n.58, 180-194, especially 189-190).

name: Marduk’s Address to the Demons
intro:
*Marduk’s Address to the Demons* is a text of some 260 lines, whose goal is to protect humans from the attack of demons. Two facts set *Marduk’s Address* apart from most incantations: on the one hand, its exceptional length; on the other, the fact that a large section is spoken by the god Marduk, in his role as the healing god Asalluḫi.  
The text falls into five sections. The first (ll. 1–9) is an incantation known from other compilations, such as the fumigation series *Qutāru*; the second (ll. 10–107) begins all its lines with the statement “I am Asalluḫi,” followed by an epithet describing Asalluḫi’s exorcistic prowess. The third section contains a small myth (ll. 108–115) in which Asalluḫi speaks with his vizier Nabû, and enlists the intervention of other divinities to expel the demons. The next section (ll. 116–99′) is a long litany describing the habitual actions of demons who attack a sick person, or else of ghosts who were denied entry into the Netherworld. The final segment of the text (ll. 100′–128′) is the properly exorcistic segment, which  summons Asalluḫi to extirpate the threatening demons and confine them to the Netherworld.  
The text is known in very many “library” manuscripts, from Assyria and Babylonia. It was also one of the most popular texts in northern Babylonian schools: no fewer than 15 school tablets with excerpts from it are known. The popularity of *Marduk’s Address* is also shown by the multiplicity of commentaries it received, both in Assyria and Babylonia. Some editions of the exorcistic compendium *Udugḫul* incorporated *Marduk’s Address* as the eleventh tablet of the series.  
*Marduk’s Address* was first recognized as an independent composition by G. Meier, and its first modern edition was presented by Lambert in 1956. Lambert continued to work on the text over the ensuing decades with the view of publishing a new edition, which appeared posthumously in Geller’s edition of *Udugḫul*. The eBL edition includes multiple new fragments, most importantly the only known manuscript from Nippur.

name: Great Prayer to Šamaš
intro:
The *Great Prayer to Šamaš* is a 200-line hymnic composition dedicated to the Sun God, which belongs to the group of the so-called ‘Great Hymns’. Like other ‘Great Hymns’, the *Great Prayer to Šamaš* uses a high-register literary style, numerous rhetorical devices, and topics borrowed from wisdom literature. Perhaps the most noticeable element within the text is the wisdom section (*ca*. ll. 83–127), in which several examples of honest and dishonest behavior are listed: in his capacity as divine judge, Šamaš punishes unethical conduct and rewards good deeds.  
The most common rhetorical device used in the hymn is parallelism: parallel structures can be found within the same verse (e.g. 39), as well as over two (e.g. 180–181) or more verses (e.g. 112–115, 171–173). Most manuscripts divide the text into poetic couplets by means of horizontal rulings. These rulings, however, do not always match the content of the lines, and often represent a merely mechanical division of the text.  
There are thirty-five manuscripts of the Hymn, nineteen of which are school tablets. The majority come from Babylonia, but eleven fragments (representing possibly four different manuscripts) come from the Nineveh libraries and four from Sippar. All manuscripts date from the first millennium BCE, though internal evidence points to the Old Babylonian period as a possible date of composition: judging from style, language, and content, the *Šamaš Hymn* appears to have been reworked and expanded over time. The hymn’s popularity, as evidenced by the large number of copies, long transmission, and numerous school manuscripts, indicates that it was a literary “classic,” like the *Prayer to Marduk 1* ([III.1](/corpus/L/3/1)) and *Ludlul* ([II.2](/corpus/L/2/2)).
