name: Great Prayer to Nabû
intro:
The *Great Prayer to Nabû* belongs to the small group of the ‘Great Hymns’, Akkadian literary hymns and prayers characterized by their unusual length (200 lines or more), use of a special poetic idiom (so-called “hymno-epic dialect”), and themes that resemble wisdom literature. The *Nabû Prayer* with its 236-lines, sophisticated language with hymno-epic forms and hapax legomena, and  poetic imagery, exemplifies well these features.  
The text opens with a hymnic introduction in which the god is invoked and praised; the first portion of the text is then followed by a long lamentation in which the supplicant describes his pitiful condition and asks Nabû to put an end to his suffering. Afterwards, a short wisdom passage (ll. 173-185) develops the thought that initial suffering is necessary for future happiness. The closing section includes further praises to Nabû and a final salutation to the god.  
The text survives in one fragmentary two-column tablet (NinNA1, the main witness) and in two small fragments that do not join directly, but might belong to the same manuscript (NinNA2a and NinNA2b). All sources come from the Nineveh libraries. In both manuscripts, the text falls into couplets marked by horizontal rulings; in addition, NinNA1 exhibits a metrical caesura in the first column, represented either by a *spatium* between the hemistichs or by a vertical line drawn in the middle of verses. Despite the elaborate language and the stylistic affectations that might suggest a late date for the composition, it is possible that this text, like the *Prayer to Marduk 1* ([§III.1](/corpus/L/3/1)) and possibly the *Great Prayer to Šamaš* ([§III.4](/corpus/L/3/4)), was originally composed at an earlier date and then progressively reworked.  
In his edition (1971), von Soden included two additional fragments of NinNA1 (NinNA2a and [K.11373](/fragmentarium/K.11373)); the latter is part of a divination text. The present edition includes the previously unknown fragment NinNA2b and a join to NinNA1 ([K.18434](/fragmentarium/K.18434)), which, having been discovered later, was not included in any edition.

name: Hymn to the Queen of Nippur
intro:
The *Hymn to the Queen of Nippur* is a hymn praising Ištar in her various aspects and functions, with special emphasis on her Nippur hypostasis Šarrat-Nippuri “Queen of Nippur”. The text consists of at least 250 verses, around one-third of which containing two hemistichs with two metrical feet each; but verses with three feet also appear. Due to the existing gaps, the structure of the text cannot be reconstructed yet. Since the contents of the known sections are very miscellaneous, it has been suggested that the hymn is a conflation of several originally independent compositions.  
Although the text was probably composed in Nippur, no copy of it from that city has been discovered yet. Most manuscripts of the composition come from Ashurbanipal’s libraries; however, some of the most important tablets are written in Babylonian script (NinNB1 from Nineveh and SipNB1 from Sippar). The known manuscripts show a modest degree of variation, especially between the Nineveh and the Sippar versions. The text may be mentioned in the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([§0 a+5](/corpus/L/0/0/NA/-#a%2B5)), but no excerpt of the text on elementary school tablets has yet been found.  
The Sippar manuscript was first published by Scheil in 1895, and one of the Nineveh manuscripts was added by Langdon (1923). The first modern comprehensive edition is Lambert’s (1982); the eBL edition incorporates several newly identified fragments.

name: Bullussa-rabi’s Hymn to Gula
intro:
*Bullussa-rabi’s Hymn to Gula* is a hymn to several gods and goddesses, which in the text are identified either with the healing goddess Gula or with her consort. The composition can thus be considered an expression of Mesopotamian religious syncretism.  
The text consists of 200 verses, divided in most manuscripts into 20 sections by means of rulings. 19 of them enumerate epithets and deeds of a goddess (who praises herself in the first person) or of her consort: in both cases, the deity praised is identified in the last line of the section. In the 20ᵗʰ section the author pleads with the goddess for his health.  
The hymn was probably composed in the Middle Babylonian period, but all preserved manuscripts date to the first millennium BCE: in addition to an almost completely preserved but poorly written manuscript from Babylonia (BabaLB1), several manuscripts from Nineveh, Babylon and Sippar are known. They show a modest degree of variation: thus some manuscripts read “Ninazu” instead of “Ninurta” in l. 53, and “Ninkarrak” instead of “Gula” in 197. A fragment from Huzirina ([SU-1952.138](/fragmentarium/SU-1952.138)) contains some common phraseology, and may belong to a related composition.  
The *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* (§[0](/corpus/L/0/0/NA/-#d%2B6)) attributes the *Hymn* to a certain Bullussa-rabi, an exorcist and scholar of Babylon. The name “Bullussa-rabi” is otherwise born only by women in the Middle Babylonian period, which may suggest that the author of the text (in the *Hymn* a male) may originally have been a woman. Two lines of the text (100 and 123) are quoted in commentaries from Borsippa and Babylon, and an excerpt of the text on a school tablet from Sippar indicates that the *Hymn* was occasionally used in elementary education.  
The first edition of the *Hymn*, based on a large tablet that preserves the whole text (BabaLB1), as well as on several smaller fragments, was published in 1967; several more manuscripts were added in 2019.

name: A Syncretistic Hymn to Ištar
intro:
The *Syncretistic Hymn to Ištar* is a hymn addressed to a series of goddesses, most of them local hypostases of the goddess Ištar. The text ostensibly subsumes these goddesses under Ištar, which reflects syncretistic tendencies that were perhaps current in the early first millennium BCE. The hymn consists of 36 long lines, most of which enumerate the deeds or epithets of a goddess and end by providing her name. The end of the text contains a rubric describing its contents as “(…) names of goddesses”.  
The composition is known from an almost completely preserved 4ᵗʰ c. BCE manuscript from Borsippa, to which a Neo-Assyrian fragment from Nineveh has recently been added. The only difference between the Borsippa and the Nineveh manuscripts so far is the omission of l. 14 in the latter. The text is not mentioned in catalogues nor was it copied in the framework of scribal education, but some of its lines have parallels in other texts, such as the *Exaltation of Ištar* (l. 22) and the *Syncretistic Hymn to Gula* (ll. 30–31).  
The Borsippa manuscript, re-assembled from four pieces, was published by W.G. Lambert in 2003; his translation has been slightly adapted for the eBL edition.

name: Hymn to Ištar (“Ištar 2”)
intro:
The *Great Hymn of Ištar* is a long Akkadian literary composition dedicated to the goddess Ištar, originally 247 lines long. Like other ‘Great Hymns’, the text displays several ‘hymno-epic’ forms and a highly literary vocabulary.  
It is possible to reconstruct the general structure and content of the text, despite its fragmentary state of preservation. The first part of the hymn seems to contain an invocation and praise of the goddess Ištar. After the hymnic introduction, the lion’s share of the text is a long lament in which the penitent expresses his suffering, confesses his words and deeds, and asks for mercy. The text alternates first and third person, using motifs and phrases typical of Akkadian prayers.  
The *Hymn* survives in two manuscripts, from Nineveh and Babylon. In neither of these tablets is the text divided into couplets, in contrast to other manuscripts of the ‘Great Hymns’. Instead, the Nineveh manuscript has a horizontal line every ten lines, which is probably a librarian’s mark.  
Although it survives in only two manuscripts, the *Hymn* was probably a well-known text. Its incipit is cited in the Babylonian *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* [§0](/corpus/L/0/0/Neo-Babylonian/-), which attributes the text to a scholar called Aba-ninnu-dari. It is possible that the *Hymn*, like other ‘Great Hymns’, was composed in the second millennium, but nothing can be said with certainty.

name: Hymn to Ninurta as Savior
intro:
The *Hymn to Ninurta as a Savior* is a hymnic prayer that exalts Ninurta’s capacity of helping those in dire straits. Although the poetic structure of the text is not rigid, the hymn includes several stanzas consisting of the description of an individual in need, an epithet of Ninurta, and a description of how the god saved the individual in question. The underlying message of the text is that the wellbeing of humans depends on the god’s mercy, albeit humans in their hybris may not always be aware of it. The hymn ends with a plea to Ninurta to spare his city Nippur and the supplicant.  
With the focus of the composition on the god Ninurta and the explicit mention of his city Nippur, it is probable that the text originates in the scholarly environment of this city, at some point prior to the 8ᵗʰ or 7ᵗʰ century BCE, the date of the earliest known manuscript (Sultantepe). All other manuscripts stem from Babylon and Sippar; the palaeography of some of them suggests that they date to the last centuries of cuneiform culture. Some of the manuscripts are barrel-shaped school copies, a format reminiscent of royal inscriptions that is used for very few compositions, most of them concerned with the god Nabû. All barrel-shaped manuscripts have a paratextual note in the shape of a frame that identifies the text as a “royal inscription (of Nabû)”.  
The text circulated widely among the Babylonian literate elite, as witnessed by the quotation of one line in a copy of a letter relating to king Ashurbanipal’s tablet collecting ([BM.28825](/fragmentarium/BM.28825#o%2014)). Furthermore, the hymn is listed in the Babylonian version of the *Catalogue of Texts and Authors* ([§0](/corpus/L/0/0/)) together with a hymn to the goddess Gula ([*STT* 128+](/fragmentarium/SU-1951.207) and dupls.) and one to Nabû ([*STT* 71](/fragmentarium/SU-1951.42) and dupls.)

name: Saĝba
intro:
*Saĝba* (Sumerian: “curse”) is a bilingual Sumerian-Akkadian incantation series comprising two tablets that employ curse formulas to protect against demons. The ancient title of the series was perhaps zì-sur-ra-meš (Sumerian zì-sur-ra, “flour paste”), referring to a ritual substance used to draw magical protective lines. In the text, demons are threatened with destruction if they violate boundaries drawn with this substance, creating an effective magical ban.  
The series consists of two tablets with distinct functions. Tablet I belongs to the “prophylactic type” of Sumerian incantations, protecting the patient’s house from demonic attack through extensive curse formulas (lines 23–120) that threaten demons with annihilation for any transgression. Tablet II serves a different purpose: it protects the exorcist himself during ritual performance, employing elements of incantations of the “legitimation type.” Both tablets begin with identical opening words (saĝ-ba saĝ-ba), though this repetition represents an abbreviated citation form rather than the series title itself.  
The textual witnesses date primarily to the first millennium BCE. The Nineveh manuscripts belong to the 7th century BCE; slightly older are the texts from Sultantepe and Assur. Babylonian exemplars are Neo- or Late Babylonian, including texts from Uruk. Despite the late manuscript tradition, the literary origins likely lie in the Old Babylonian period, as is generally assumed for first-millennium bilingual incantations. The text was popular in scribal education, and many school tablets with excerpts from it are known. 
*Saĝba* incantations appear in ritual contexts at the conclusion of major therapeutic ceremonies. The [*Muššuʾu* ritual tablet]( /library/K.3996) prescribes reciting saĝ-ba saĝ-ba while drawing flour-paste lines around the patient’s bed. Similarly, the [*Maqlû* Ritual Tablet](/corpus/Mag/1/1) and *Lamaštu* III employ the incantation at the end of ritual sections, followed by *tummu bītu* and [ab-ta nam-mu-un-da-ku₄-ku₄-dè]( /library/K.156#r%20iii%20166). An [Assur incantation catalogue]( /library/VAT.13723#r%20iii%2032) lists both tablets’ opening lines with the series designation *zì-sur-ra-meš*.  
Thompson first published manuscripts of the text in CT 17 (1903). A complete edition of Tablet I was published by Römer (1989); the first comprehensive edition of the series was Schramm’s (2001). The present edition relies heavily on that by Schramm, who was kind enough to share the original files of his edition and consent to their publication here. In addition, it incorporates many new manuscripts identified mostly in the course of the eBL project.

name: Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk (*Eriš šummi*)
intro:
*Eriš šummi* is a Babylonian hymn in which the major gods of the Mesopotamian pantheon are explained as just bynames of Marduk. The first section of the text, a hymnic prologue, celebrates Marduk as the sage of the gods (ll. 1–17); the second identifies several major gods of the Mesopotamian pantheon with Marduk (ll. 18–60); and the final segment (61–86) praises Marduk as king of the universe under some of his traditional names, such as Lugal-dimmer-ankia, Asalluḫi, Šazu, and Enbilulu. All manuscripts contain a bilingual line after this last section (l. 87 f.), which exhorts the audience to extol Marduk.  
The hymn, written in elevated prose, is clearly derivative of other traditional texts, in particular *Enūma eliš* ([L I.2](/corpus/L/1/2)), a text of which it can be considered a pastiche. While it is presently not possible to date the composition of *Eriš šummi*, it seems clear that it must post-date *Enūma eliš* (12ᵗʰ century BCE?) and, of course, pre-date its earliest known manuscript, AššNA1 (8ᵗʰ century BCE?).  
The equation of major gods with Marduk, the most arresting aspect of *Eriš šummi*, appears prima facie to be a manifesto of monotheism. Careful study, however, reveals that the hymn represents no dramatic departure from the spirit of texts such as *Enūma eliš*, in that it develops ideas that can be found in traditional Babylonian texts.  
The incipit of *Eriš šummi* is cited, along with other hymns to Marduk, in an inventory tablet that in all likelihood stems from Nineveh ([SEM.1092](/fragmentarium/SEM.1092)). The tablet refers perhaps to the Nineveh manuscript of the text known to us, [BM.141781](/fragmentarium/BM.141781). The text was formerly known from the fragment from Aššur. The first complete edition of the text was published in 2022.

name: Syncretistic Hymn to Gula
intro:
This composition is a hymn (or perhaps a prayer) to the healing goddess Gula in which, in praise of her preeminence and her universal powers, the goddess is identified with other goddesses and associated with cities and temples across Southern Babylonia and portrayed as the goddess of each. Like Bullussa-rabi’s Hymn to Gula ([III.7](/corpus/L/3/7)), the composition is thus an expression of Mesopotamian religious syncretism. Over 200 lines long (although the text is still incomplete), it was evidently a major Babylonian hymn, taking its place alongside Bullussa-rabi’s hymn and other so-called “Great Hymns”.  
The hymn is characterised by lengthy passages (18-40, A+75- B+19) in which names of deities, cities and towns, temples and shrines sacred to them are explained and explored by techniques of Babylonian scholarship found in the exposition of Marduk’s names (*Enūma eliš* VI, VII) and elsewhere. The variety and sophistication of the interpretive techniques mark the composition as a work of exceptional scholarship.   
The hymn was probably composed in the Middle Babylonian period. Its manuscripts, dating from the first millennium BCE, are known from Kuyunjik and Aššur in Assyria, and Sippar and Babylon in Babylonia. Copied for the great libraries of Assyria and as a school text in Babylonia, the work was evidently important in scribal circles. A Late Babylonian manuscript indicates the enduring popularity of this composition.  
First editions of different parts of the composition were published in 1900, 1918 and 1953. Part of the work has sometimes been understood as a hymn to Ištar since then. The first modern edition of the hymn, with additional manuscripts and now evidently in praise of the healing goddess, was published in 2021.

name: Macranthropic Hymn to Ninurta
intro:
This hymn to Ninurta is of the finest piece of Mesopotamian religious literature. It presents Ninurta  as a ‘macranthrope’, a being who embodies the entire universe and incorporates various deities into his body. While earlier scholars criticized the hymn for its “crude anthropomorphism,” and have dismissed it as “very explicit and distasteful,” , recent studies have highlighted its creative imagery.  
The text begins with an introductory praise of Ninurta (ll. 1–8), followed by a detailed enumeration of Ninurta’s body parts from head to toe, each associated with a deity or divine pair (ll. 9–31). It then describes his attire (l. 32). After a brief hymnic intermission (ll. 33–34), the text elaborates on Ninurta’s formidable weaponry (ll. 35–62), illustrating its devastating power. It concludes with a succinct depiction of Ninurta’s steed (ll. 63–67) and an almost lost rubric (l. 68). The list of body parts, clothing and weaponry fits well with Ninurta’s iconography, and it seems possible that it is an inventory of the components of a cult image of the god.   
The composition likely originated in Nippur and in the late second millennium BCE. Its creative language suggests it might be the work of the Rīmūt-Gula, who, among others, penned the *Hymn to Ninurta as Savior* ([L III.10](/corpus/L/3/10)). Manuscripts of the text have been found in Assur, Nineveh, Huzirina, and Sippar. In the Sippar Library, it was stored in the same niche as the *Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk* (*Eriš šummi*) ([L III.11](/corpus/L/3/11)).    
The hymn was first published, using the Assur manuscript alone, in 1918. The most important manuscript of the text, from the Sippar Library, was published in 2023. This edition incorporates two manuscripts, from Nineveh and Sultantepe, which were not utilized in that study.
